### Attitude control system

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Attitude control system")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Shuttle_front_RCS.jpg/250px-Shuttle_front_RCS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shuttle_front_RCS.jpg)

_Discovery_'s forward reaction control thrusters

The [Reaction Control System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaction_Control_System "Reaction Control System") (RCS) was composed of 44 small [liquid-fueled rocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid-fuel_rocket "Liquid-fuel rocket") thrusters and their very sophisticated [fly-by-wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly-by-wire "Fly-by-wire")[flight control system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_control_system "Flight control system"), which utilized computationally intensive digital [Kalman filtering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalman_filter "Kalman filter"). This control system carried out the usual [attitude control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_attitude "Aircraft attitude") along the pitch, roll, and yaw axes during all of the flight phases of launching, [orbiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit "Orbit"), and re-entry. This system also executed any needed orbital maneuvers, including all changes in the orbit's altitude, [orbital plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_plane_(astronomy) "Orbital plane (astronomy)"), and [eccentricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_eccentricity "Orbital eccentricity"). These were all operations that required more thrust and [impulse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse_(physics) "Impulse (physics)") than mere attitude control.

The forward rockets of the Reaction Control System, located near the nose of the Space Shuttle orbiter, included 14 primary and two [vernier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernier_thruster "Vernier thruster") RCS rockets. The aft RCS engines were located in the two [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") (OMS) pods at the rear of the orbiter, and these included 12 primary (PRCS) and two vernier (VRCS) engines in each pod. The PRCS system provided the pointing control of the Orbiter, and the VRCS was used for fine maneuvering during the rendezvous, docking, and undocking maneuvers with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), or formerly with the Russian [Mir space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_space_station "Mir space station"). The RCS also controlled the attitude of the orbiter during most of its re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere – until the air became dense enough that the rudder, elevons and body flap became effective.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-8)

The orbiter's OMS and RCS fuel is [monomethyl hydrazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomethylhydrazine "Monomethylhydrazine") (CH 3 NHNH 2), and the oxidizer is [dinitrogen tetroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinitrogen_tetroxide "Dinitrogen tetroxide") (N 2 O 4). This particular propellant combination is extremely reactive and spontaneously ignites on contact (hypergolic) with each other. This chemical reaction (4CH 3 NHNH 2 + 5N 2 O 4 → 9N 2 + 4CO 2 + 12H 2 O) occurs within the engine's combustion chamber. The reaction products are then expanded and accelerated in the engine bell to provide thrust. Due to their hypergolic characteristics these two chemicals are easily started and restarted without an ignition source, which makes them ideal for spacecraft maneuvering systems.

During the early design process of the orbiter, the forward RCS thrusters were to be hidden underneath retractable doors, which would open once the orbiter reached space. These were omitted in favor of flush-mounted thrusters for fear that the RCS doors would remain stuck open and endanger the crew and orbiter during re-entry.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-9)

### Pressurized cabin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pressurized cabin")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/STSCPanel.jpg/250px-STSCPanel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STSCPanel.jpg)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/S123_Linnehan_through_the_window.jpg/250px-S123_Linnehan_through_the_window.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S123_Linnehan_through_the_window.jpg)

A window on _Endeavour_'s aft flight deck

The orbiter's flight deck or cockpit originally had 2,214 controls and displays, about three times as many as the [Apollo command module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_command_module "Apollo command module").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-stevens19810406-2) The crew cabin consisted of the flight deck, the mid-deck, and the utility area. The uppermost of these was the flight deck, in which sat the Space Shuttle's commander and pilot in permanently fixed seats with up to two mission specialists seated behind them in stowable seats.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-10) The mission specialist in seat four (located behind and between commander and pilot) served as the flight engineer during ascent and landing, tracking information from CAPCOM and calling out milestones.

The mid-deck, which was below the flight deck, was normally equipped with up to three additional stowable seats, depending on the crew requirements of the mission.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-orbiter-11) One mission carried four seats ([STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A")) and NASA drew up plans that were never used to carry up to seven seats in the case of an emergency rescue ([STS-400](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-400 "STS-400")).

The galley, toilet, sleep locations, storage lockers, and the side hatch for entering and exiting the orbiter were also located on the mid-deck, as well as the [airlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airlock "Airlock"). The airlock had an additional hatch into the payload bay. This airlock allowed two or three astronauts, wearing their [Extravehicular Mobility Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_Mobility_Unit "Extravehicular Mobility Unit") (EMU) space suits, to depressurize before a [walk in space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") ([EVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity")), and also to repressurize and re-enter the orbiter at the conclusion of the EVA.

The utility area was located under the floor of the mid-deck and contained air and water tanks in addition to the [carbon dioxide scrubbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide_scrubber "Carbon dioxide scrubber") system.

### Propulsion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Propulsion")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/020408_STS110_Atlantis_launch.jpg/250px-020408_STS110_Atlantis_launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:020408_STS110_Atlantis_launch.jpg)

_Atlantis'_ s main engines during launch

Three [Space Shuttle Main Engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Main_Engine "Space Shuttle Main Engine") (SSMEs) were mounted on the orbiter's aft fuselage in the pattern of an [equilateral triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equilateral_triangle "Equilateral triangle"). These three liquid-fueled engines [could be swiveled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_vectoring "Thrust vectoring") 10.5 degrees vertically and 8.5 degrees horizontally during the rocket-powered ascent of the orbiter in order to change the direction of their thrust. Hence, they steered the entire Space Shuttle, as well as providing rocket thrust towards orbit. The aft fuselage also housed three [auxiliary power units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit") (APU). The APUs chemically converted [hydrazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrazine "Hydrazine") fuel from a [liquid state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_state "Liquid state") to a [gas state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_state "Gas state"), powering a [hydraulic pump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydraulic_pump "Hydraulic pump") which supplied pressure for all of the hydraulic system, including the hydraulic sub-system that pointed the three main liquid-fueled rocket engines, under computerized flight control. The hydraulic pressure generated was also used to control all of the orbiter's [flight control surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_control_surfaces "Flight control surfaces") (the elevons, rudder, speed brake, etc.), to deploy the landing gear of the orbiter, and to retract the umbilical hose connection doors located near the rear landing gear, which supplied the orbiter's SSMEs with liquid hydrogen and oxygen from the external tank.

Two [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") (OMS) thrusters were mounted in two separate removable pods on the orbiter's aft fuselage, located between the SSMEs and the vertical stabilizer. The OMS engines provided significant thrust for course [orbital maneuvers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_maneuver "Orbital maneuver"), including insertion, circularization, transfer, rendezvous, deorbit, [abort to orbit, and to abort once around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_abort_modes "Space Shuttle abort modes").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-12) At lift-off, two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_boosters "Solid rocket boosters") (SRBs) were used to take the vehicle to an altitude of roughly 140,000 feet.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-Kulkarni2005-13)

### Electrical power

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Electrical power")]

Electric power for the orbiter's [subsystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsystem "Subsystem") was provided by a set of three hydrogen-oxygen [fuel cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_cell "Fuel cell") which produced 28 volt [DC power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_power "DC power") and was also converted into 115 volt 400 Hz AC [three-phase electric power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-phase_electric_power "Three-phase electric power") (for systems that used [AC power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_power "AC power")).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-Electrical_Power_System-14) These provided power to the entire Shuttle stack (including the SRBs and ET) from T-minus 3m30s up through the end of the mission. The hydrogen and oxygen for the fuel cells was kept in pairs of [cryogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenic "Cryogenic") storage tanks in the mid-fuselage underneath the payload bay liner, and a variable number of such tank sets could be installed (up to five pairs) depending on the requirements of the mission. The three fuel cells were capable of generating 21 kilowatts of power continuously (or a 15-minute peak of 36 kilowatts) with the orbiter consuming an average of about 14 kilowatts of that power (leaving 7 kilowatts for the payload).

Additionally, the fuel cells provided [potable water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potable_water "Potable water") for the crew during the mission.

### Computer systems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Computer systems")]

The orbiter's computer system consisted of five identical [IBM AP-101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_AP-101 "IBM AP-101")[avionics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avionics "Avionics") computers, which redundantly controlled the vehicle's on-board systems. The specialized [HAL/S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HAL/S "HAL/S") programming language was used for orbiter systems.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-nasagpc-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-nyt20030207-16)

### Thermal protection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Thermal protection")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/STS-114_Discovery_thermal_protection_system_%28S114-E-6412%29.jpg/250px-STS-114_Discovery_thermal_protection_system_%28S114-E-6412%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-114_Discovery_thermal_protection_system_(S114-E-6412).jpg)

_Discovery_'s ventral thermal protection system

The orbiters were protected by [Thermal Protection System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") (TPS) materials (developed by [Rockwell Space Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_International "Rockwell International")) inside and out, from the orbiter's outer surface to the payload bay.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-NASA_Tech_Briefs-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-Oakes_2003-18) The TPS protected it from the cold soak of −121°C (−186°F) in space to the 1,649°C (3,000°F) heat of re-entry. The tile materials comprising much of the orbiter's outermost layer were mostly air held within near-pure [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica "Silica") fibers, which made the tiles efficient at [refractory insulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_entry#Refractory_insulation "Atmospheric entry") that absorbed and redirected heat back out into the air. The tiles were coated in [silicon borides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_boride "Silicon boride") and [borosilicate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate_glass "Borosilicate glass"), with blacker tiles covering the lower surface, and whiter tiles covering the tail, parts of the upper wing and crew cabin surfaces, and the outsides of the payload bay doors. The nose cap, nose landing gear doors, and leading edges were made of [reinforced carbon–carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_carbon%E2%80%93carbon "Reinforced carbon–carbon"), which is [rayon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayon "Rayon") impregnated with [graphite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite "Graphite")-filled resins and coated in [silicon carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_carbide "Silicon carbide").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-Lyle_Fasanella_2009_pp._702%E2%80%93708-19) The upper, white materials that were not in tiles were mostly made of either [Nomex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomex "Nomex") felt coated in [silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon "Silicon")-rich [elastomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elastomer "Elastomer") or [beta cloth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_cloth "Beta cloth"), woven silica fibers covered in [Teflon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teflon "Teflon"). This was especially true in the interior of the payload bay.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-Finckenor_Dooling_1999-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-nasareport-22)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-Oakes_2003-18)

### Structure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Structure")]

The orbiter's structure was made primarily from [aluminum alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminum_alloy "Aluminum alloy"), although the engine thrust structure was made from [titanium alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium_alloy "Titanium alloy"). The later orbiters (_Discovery_, _Atlantis_ and _Endeavour_) substituted [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") for aluminum in some structural elements in order to reduce weight. The windows were made of [aluminum silicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminum_silicate "Aluminum silicate") glass and [fused silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fused_silica "Fused silica") glass, and comprised an internal pressure pane, a 1.3-inch-thick (33 mm) optical pane, and an external thermal pane.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-23) The windows were tinted with the same ink used to make [American banknotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Note "Federal Reserve Note").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-24)

### Landing gear

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Landing gear")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis_landing_at_KSC_following_STS-122_%28crop%29.jpg/250px-Space_Shuttle_Atlantis_landing_at_KSC_following_STS-122_%28crop%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Space_Shuttle_Atlantis_landing_at_KSC_following_STS-122_(crop).jpg)

_Atlantis_'s landing gear are deployed following STS-122.

The Space Shuttle orbiter had tricycle [landing gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_gear "Landing gear") which emerged downwards through doors in the heat shield. As a weight-saving measure, the gear could not be retracted once deployed. Since any premature extension of the landing gear would very likely have been catastrophic (as it opened through the heat shield layers), the landing gear could only be lowered by manual controls, and not by any automatic system.

Similarly, since the Shuttle landed at high speed and could not abort its landing attempt, the gear had to deploy reliably on the first try every time. The gear were unlocked and deployed by triple redundant hydraulics, with the gear doors actuated by mechanical linkages to the gear strut. If all three hydraulic systems failed to release the landing gear uplocks within one second of the release command, pyrotechnic charges automatically cut the lock hooks and a set of springs deployed the gear.

During landing, the Shuttle nose wheel could be steered with the [rudder pedals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder_pedal "Rudder pedal") in the cockpit. During the construction of [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")[_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour"), an improved nose wheel steering system was developed which allowed easier and more effective nose wheel steering. After _Endeavour_'s roll-out, the system was installed on the other shuttles during their overhauls in the early 1990s.

### Lack of navigational lights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Lack of navigational lights")]

The Space Shuttle orbiter did not carry [anti-collision lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strobe_light "Strobe light"), [navigational lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_light "Navigation light"), or [landing lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_landing_lights "Aircraft landing lights"), because the orbiter always landed in areas that had been specially cleared by both the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") (FAA) and the [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force"). The orbiter always landed at either [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") or at the Kennedy Space Center [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility"), Florida, except [STS-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-3 "STS-3") at the [White Sands Space Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Sands_Space_Harbor "White Sands Space Harbor") in New Mexico. Similar special clearances (no-fly zones) were also in effect at potential emergency landing sites, such as in [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") and in [West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa") during all launches.

When an orbiter landing was carried out at night, the runway was always strongly illuminated with light from [floodlights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-intensity_discharge_lamp "High-intensity discharge lamp") and [spotlights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Searchlight "Searchlight") on the ground, making landing lights on the orbiter unnecessary and also an unneeded spaceflight weight load. A total of 26 landings took place at night, the first being [STS-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-8 "STS-8") in September 1983.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-25)

### Markings and insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Markings and insignia")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/World%27s_First_Five_Spaceplanes.PNG/250px-World%27s_First_Five_Spaceplanes.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World's_First_Five_Spaceplanes.PNG)

The [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") orbiter ranks second among the world's first [spaceplanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane"), preceded only by the [North American X-15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_X-15 "North American X-15") and followed by the [Buran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buran_(spacecraft) "Buran (spacecraft)"), [SpaceShipOne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceShipOne "SpaceShipOne"), and the [Boeing X-37](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_X-37 "Boeing X-37").

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Enterprise_free_flight.jpg/250px-Enterprise_free_flight.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Enterprise_free_flight.jpg)

_Enterprise_ displaying the orbiter markings.

The [typeface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typeface "Typeface") used on the Space Shuttle orbiter was [Helvetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvetica "Helvetica").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-26)

The prototype orbiter _Enterprise_ originally had a [flag of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_the_United_States "Flag of the United States") on the upper surface of the left wing and the letters "USA" in black on the right wing. The name "Enterprise" in black was painted on the payload bay doors just above the forwardmost hinge and behind the crew module; on the aft end of the payload bay doors was the [NASA "worm" logotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_insignia "NASA insignia") in gray. Underneath the rear of the payload bay doors on the side of the fuselage just above the wing was the text "United States" in black with a flag of the United States ahead of it.

The first operational orbiter, _Columbia_, originally had the same markings as _Enterprise_, although the letters "USA" on the right wing were slightly larger and spaced farther apart. _Columbia_ also had black tiles which _Enterprise_ lacked on its forward RCS module, around the cockpit windows, and on its vertical stabilizer. _Columbia_ also had distinctive black [chines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chine_(aeronautics) "Chine (aeronautics)") on the forward part of its upper wing surfaces, which none of the other orbiters had.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/NASA_Worm_logo_%28gray%29.svg/250px-NASA_Worm_logo_%28gray%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NASA_Worm_logo_(gray).svg)

Gray NASA "worm" logotype used on the orbiters from 1982 to 1998.

_Challenger_ established a modified marking scheme for the shuttle fleet that would be matched by _Discovery_, _Atlantis_ and _Endeavour_. The letters "USA" in black above an American flag were displayed on the left wing, with the NASA "worm" logotype in gray centered above the name of the orbiter in black on the right wing. Also, the name of the orbiter was inscribed not on the payload bay doors, but on the forward fuselage just below and behind the cockpit windows. This would make the name visible when the orbiter was photographed in orbit with the doors open. _Challenger_ also had black tiles on the tip of its vertical stabilizer much like _Columbia_, which the other orbiters lacked.

In 1983, _Enterprise_ had its wing markings changed to match _Challenger_, and the NASA "worm" logotype on the aft end of the payload bay doors was changed from gray to black. Some black markings were added to the nose, cockpit windows and vertical tail to more closely resemble the flight vehicles, but the name "Enterprise" remained on the payload bay doors as there was never any need to open them. _Columbia_ had its name moved to the forward fuselage to match the other flight vehicles after [STS-61-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-C "STS-61-C"), during the 1986–1988 hiatus when the shuttle fleet was grounded following the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), but retained its original wing markings until its last overhaul (after [STS-93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-93 "STS-93")), and its unique black chines for the remainder of its operational life.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/NASA_logo_%282023_colors%29.svg/250px-NASA_logo_%282023_colors%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NASA_logo_(2023_colors).svg)

NASA "meatball" insignia used on the operational Space Shuttle orbiters after 1998.

Beginning in [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") (1998), the flight vehicles' markings were modified to incorporate the NASA ["meatball" insignia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_insignia "NASA insignia"). The "worm" logotype, which the agency had phased out, was removed from the payload bay doors and the "meatball" insignia was added aft of the "United States" text on the lower aft fuselage. The "meatball" insignia was also displayed on the left wing, with the American flag above the orbiter's name, left-justified rather than centered, on the right wing. The three surviving flight vehicles, _Discovery_, _Atlantis_ and _Endeavour_, still bear these markings as museum displays. _Enterprise_ became the property of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution") in 1985 and was no longer under NASA's control when these changes were made, hence the prototype orbiter still has its 1983 markings and still has its name on the payload bay doors.

### Retirement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Retirement")]

With the end of the Shuttle program, plans were made to place the three remaining Space Shuttle orbiters on permanent display. NASA Administrator [Charles F. Bolden Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bolden "Charles Bolden") announced the disposition location of the orbiters on April 12, 2011, the 50th anniversary of the [first human space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 "Vostok 1") and the 30th anniversary of the [first flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1") of _Columbia_.

_Discovery_ went to the Smithsonian's [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. ## Shuttle Orbiter Specifications (OV-105)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_orbiter&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Shuttle Orbiter Specifications (OV-105)")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/STS_orbiter_4-view_diagram_%28EG-0076-07%29.png/250px-STS_orbiter_4-view_diagram_%28EG-0076-07%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS_orbiter_4-view_diagram_(EG-0076-07).png)

_Data from_[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-esa.shuttle-36)

**General characteristics**

*   **Crew:** 2 (commander and pilot)
*   **Capacity:** 6 passengers (up to three mission and up to three payload specialists) _or_ 25,060 kg (55,250 lb)
*   **Length:** 122 ft 2.0 in (37.237 m)
*   **Wingspan:** 78 ft 1 in (23.79 m)
*   **Height:** 58 ft 7 in (17.86 m)
*   **Wing area:** 2,690 sq ft (249.9 m 2) [[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-TM-X-3492-37)
*   **Empty weight:** 171,961 lb (78,000 kg)
*   **Max takeoff weight:** 242,508 lb (110,000 kg)
*   **Payload to [LEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit")**: 24,310 kg (53,590 lb)

*   **Cargo bay dimensions**: 60×15 ft (18.3×4.6 m)
*   **Powerplant:** 3 × [Rocketdyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocketdyne "Rocketdyne") Block 2-A [RS-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RS-25 "RS-25")[liquid-fuelled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid-propellant_rocket "Liquid-propellant rocket")[rocket engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_engine "Rocket engine"), 418,000 lbf (1,860 kN) thrust each
*   **Powerplant:** 2 × [Aerojet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerojet "Aerojet")[AJ10-190](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AJ10 "AJ10")[liquid-fuelled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid-propellant_rocket "Liquid-propellant rocket")[rocket engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_engine "Rocket engine"), 6,000 lbf (26.7 kN) thrust each

**Performance**

*   **Maximum speed:** 17,320 mph (27,870 km/h, 15,050 kn)
*   **Range:** 120–600 mi (190–960 km, 100–520 nmi)
*   **Service ceiling:** 607,000–2,110,000 ft (185,000–643,000 m)
*   **Maximum glide ratio:** Variable with speed, 1:1 at [hypersonic speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_speed "Hypersonic speed") - 2:1 at [supersonic speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersonic_speed "Supersonic speed") - 4.5:1 at [subsonic speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsonic_speed "Subsonic speed")[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-SSTC-38)

The cargo bay is 60 ft (18 m) by 15 ft (4.6 m),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-SP-2010-3409-39) and could transport 24,400 kg (53,800 lb) to 204 km (127 mi), or 12,500 kg (27,600 lb) to the ISS at 407 km (253 mi).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-astrx.shuttle-40) The most massive payload launched by the Space Shuttle was the [Chandra X-ray Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-ray_Observatory "Chandra X-ray Observatory") in 1999 at 50,162 lb (22,753 kg), including its [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS) and support equipment.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-chandra-quick-facts-41) The Shuttle was capable of returning approximately 16,000 kg (35,000 lb) of cargo to Earth.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-SP-2006-557-42)

The orbiter's maximum [glide ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glide_ratio "Glide ratio") / [lift-to-drag ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lift-to-drag_ratio "Lift-to-drag ratio") varied considerably with speed, ranging from 1:1 at [hypersonic speeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_speed "Hypersonic speed"), 2:1 at [supersonic speeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersonic_speed "Supersonic speed"), and reaching 4.5:1 at subsonic speeds during approach and landing.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-SSTC-38)

## Fleet

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Shuttle_profiles.jpg/960px-Shuttle_profiles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shuttle_profiles.jpg)

Shuttle launch profiles. From left to right: _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_, _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_, _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_, _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_, and _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_.

Individual Space Shuttle orbiters were named in honor of historic sailing ships of the navies of the world (though the test orbiter _Enterprise_, originally to be named "_Constitution_", was ultimately instead given the name of [the _Star Trek_ starship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Enterprise_(NCC-1701) "USS Enterprise (NCC-1701)"), itself named after [a series of US Navy ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ships_of_the_United_States_Navy_named_Enterprise "List of ships of the United States Navy named Enterprise")), and they were also numbered using the NASA [Orbiter Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation") designation system. Three of the names had also been given to Apollo spacecraft between 1969 and 1972: [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11") Command Module _Columbia_, [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15") Command Module _Endeavour_, and [Apollo 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_17 "Apollo 17") Lunar Module _Challenger_.

While all of the orbiters were externally practically identical, they had minor differences in their interiors. New equipment for the orbiters was installed in the same order that they underwent maintenance work, and the newer orbiters were constructed by Rockwell International, under NASA supervision, with some more advanced, lighter-in-weight structural elements. Thus, the newer orbiters (_Discovery_, _Atlantis_ and _Endeavour_) had slightly more cargo capacity than _Columbia_ or _Challenger_.

The Space Shuttle orbiters were assembled at Rockwell's assembly facility in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-Assembly-4) at the federally owned [Plant 42](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_42 "Plant 42") complex.

Each [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") designation was composed of a [prefix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_spacecraft_prefixes "List of spacecraft prefixes") and suffix separated by a dash. The prefix for operational shuttles is OV, for **Orbiter Vehicle**. The suffix is composed of two parts: the series and the vehicle number; "0" was used for non-flight ready orbiters, and "1" was used for flight-ready orbiters. The vehicle number is sequentially assigned within the series, beginning with 1. Therefore, there can never be an OV-100 as it would read "Orbiter Vehicle Series 1 Vehicle 0". Many proposals to build a second generation of orbiters, externally compatible with the current system but internally new, refer to them as "OV-200" or "OV-2xx" in order to differentiate them from the "first generation", the OV-100s. This terminology is informal, and it is unlikely that any Shuttle-derived vehicle built will be given such designation. _Challenger_ was originally intended to be used as a Structural Test Article (STA), rather than a flight-capable orbiter; as such, the numbering was changed when it was rebuilt. _Enterprise_, on the other hand, was intended to be rebuilt into a flight-capable orbiter; it was found to be cheaper to rebuild STA-099 than OV-101, so it remained unflown. The designations were not altered, despite these changes in plans. An "OV-106" designation was given to the set of structural components manufactured to replace those used in the construction of _Endeavour_; however, the contract for these was canceled shortly afterwards, and they were never completed.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-43) The "096" and "097" designators were given to structural test articles that were canceled, but while they exist in some NASA records, the NASA History Office has no official record of STA-096 and STA-097.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter#cite_note-44)

On February 1, 2003, _Columbia_[disintegrated during re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") on its 28th spaceflight.

*   _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_ was first launched on April 4, 1983. On January 28, 1986, it [disintegrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") 73 seconds after launch on its 10th mission.

*   _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ was first launched on August 30, 1984. It flew 39 missions, and was NASA's "Return to Flight" vehicle, following the accidental destructions of _Challenger_ and _Columbia_. _Discovery_ completed its last mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), in March 2011. It is currently on display at the [Smithsonian's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")[National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center, near [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport").

*   _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ was first launched on October 3, 1985. It flew 33 spaceflights including the final Space Shuttle mission, [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), in July 2011.

*   _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ was first launched on May 7, 1992. It flew 25 spaceflights, the final being [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134"), launched May 16, 2011.

**STS-41-D** (formerly STS-14) was the 12th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the maiden flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. It was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on August 30, 1984, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on September 5, 1984. Three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") were deployed into orbit during the six-day mission, and a number of scientific experiments were conducted, including a prototype [extendable solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_system_of_the_International_Space_Station "Electrical system of the International Space Station") that would eventually form the basis of the main solar arrays on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS).

The mission was delayed by more than two months from its original planned launch date, having experienced the Space Shuttle program's first launch abort at T−4 seconds on June 26, 1984.

## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission background")]

The launch was originally planned for June 25, 1984, but because of a variety of technical problems, including rollback to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) to replace a faulty [Space Shuttle Main Engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Main_Engine "Space Shuttle Main Engine") (SSME), the launch was delayed by over two months. The June 26, 1984, launch attempt marked the first time since [Gemini 6A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_6A "Gemini 6A") that a crewed spacecraft had experienced a shutdown of its engines just prior to launch.

### June 1984 launch attempt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: June 1984 launch attempt")]

During the June 26, 1984, launch attempt, there was a launch abort at T−4 seconds, followed by a pad fire about ten minutes later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-STS-41-4) Because the center engine had not started when the abort was triggered, confusion ensued as the [flight controllers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller "Flight controller") were unable to verify its state:

> Commentary: "We have a cut off".  
>  "NTD [_NASA Test Director_] we have a RSLS [_Redundant Set Launch Sequencer_] abort".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We have an abort by the onboard computers of the orbiter Discovery".  
>  "Break break, break break, GLS [_Ground Launch Sequencer_] shows engine one not shut down".  
>  "OK, PLT [_pilot_]?"  
>  "CSME [_Space Shuttle Main Engines_] verify engine one".  
>  "You want me to shut down engine one?"  
>  "We do not show engine start on one".  
>  "OTC [_Orbiter test conductor_] I can verify shutdown on verify on engine one, we haven't start prepped engine one".  
>  "All engines shut down I can verify that".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We can now verify all three engines have been shut down".  
>  "We have red lights on engines two and three in the cockpit, not on one".  
>  "All right, CSME verify engine one safe for APU [_[auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary\_power\_unit "Auxiliary power unit")_] shutdown".  
>  "If I can verify that?"  
>  "OTC GPC [_General Purpose Computer_] go for APU shutdown".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-5)

Mission Specialist Steve Hawley was reported as saying following the abort: "Gee, I thought we'd be a lot higher at MECO (Main Engine Cut-Off)!".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6) About ten minutes later, the following was heard on live TV coverage:

> "We have indication two of our fire detectors on the zero level; no response. They're side by side right next to the engine area. The engineer requested that we turn on the heat shield fire water which is what could be seen spraying up in the vicinity of the engine bells of _Discovery_'s three main engines".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-7)

While evacuating the shuttle 20 minutes later, the crew was doused with water from the pad deluge system, which was activated due to a hydrogen fire on the launch pad caused by the free hydrogen (fuel) that had collected around the engine nozzles following the shutdown and engine anomaly.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-8) Because the fire was invisible to humans, had the astronauts used the normal emergency escape procedure across the service arm to the slidewire escape baskets, they would have run into the fire.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050317-9)

Changes to procedures resulting from the abort included more practicing of "safing" the orbiter following aborts at various points, the use of the fire suppression system in all pad aborts, and the testing of the slidewire escape system with a real person ([Charles F. Bolden Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bolden "Charles Bolden")). It emerged that launch controllers were reluctant to order the crew to evacuate during the STS-41-D abort, as the slidewire had not been ridden by a human.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)

Examination of telemetry data indicated that the engine malfunction had been caused by a stuck valve that prevented proper flow of LOX into the combustion chamber.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

STS-41-D launched at 08:41:50 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on August 30, 1984, after a six-minute, fifty-second delay when a private aircraft flew into the restricted airspace near the launch pad. It was the fourth launch attempt for _Discovery_. Because of the two-month delay, the [STS-41-F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") mission was canceled (STS-41-E had already been canceled), and its primary payloads were included on the STS-41-D flight. The combined cargo weighed over 18,681 kg (41,185 lb), a record for a Space Shuttle payload up to that time.

The six-person flight crew consisted of [Henry W. Hartsfield Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_W._Hartsfield_Jr. "Henry W. Hartsfield Jr."), commander, making his second shuttle mission; pilot [Michael L. Coats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Coats "Michael Coats"); three mission specialists – [Judith A. Resnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Resnik "Judith Resnik"), [Richard M. Mullane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mullane "Mike Mullane") and [Steven A. Hawley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hawley "Steven Hawley"); and a payload specialist, [Charles D. Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_D._Walker "Charles D. Walker"), an employee of [McDonnell Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas "McDonnell Douglas"). Walker was the first commercially sponsored payload specialist to fly aboard the Space Shuttle. Resnik became the second American woman to fly any NASA space mission, after [Sally K. Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Ride "Sally Ride").

Primary cargo of _Discovery_ consisted of three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"): SBS-4 for [Satellite Business Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_Business_Systems "Satellite Business Systems"), [Telstar 302](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telstar_302 "Telstar 302") for [Telesat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telesat "Telesat") of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-2, or [Leasat-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom"), a [Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft_Company "Hughes Aircraft Company")-built satellite leased to the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy"); all three were Hughes-built satellites. Leasat-2 was the first large communications satellite designed specifically to be deployed from the Space Shuttle. All three satellites were deployed successfully and became operational.

Another payload was the OAST-1 [solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_module "Photovoltaic module"), a device 4 m (13 ft) wide and 31 m (102 ft) high, which folded into a package 18 cm (7.1 in) deep. The array carried a number of different types of experimental [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cell "Solar cell") and was extended to its full height several times during the mission. At the time, it was the largest structure ever extended from a crewed spacecraft, and it demonstrated the feasibility of large lightweight solar arrays for use on future orbital installations, such as the International Space Station (ISS).

The McDonnell Douglas-sponsored Continuous Flow Electrophoresis System (CFES) experiment, using living cells, was more elaborate than the one flown on previous missions, and payload specialist Walker operated it for more than 100 hours during the flight. A student experiment to study [crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") growth in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") was also carried out. The highlights of the mission were filmed using an [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX")[motion picture camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie_camera "Movie camera"), and later appeared in the 1985 documentary film _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_. On September 3, 1984, concern arose over the formation of ice on the waste dump nozzle of the shuttle. The cause was an obstruction in the shuttle's external wastewater dumping system that caused a 61 cm (24 in) "[pee-sicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine "Urine")" to form during the mission; Hartsfield removed it with the Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) the following day.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050414-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-11)

The mission lasted 6 days, 0 hour, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds, with landing taking place on Runway 17 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 06:37:54 a.m. PDT on September 5, 1984. During STS-41-D, _Discovery_ traveled a total of 4,010,000 km (2,490,000 mi) and made 97 orbits. The orbiter was transported back to KSC on September 10, 1984. Ominously, STS-41-D was the first Shuttle mission in which blow-by damage to the SRB O-rings was discovered, with a small amount of soot found beyond the primary O-ring. Following the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), [Morton Thiokol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiokol "Thiokol") engineer Brian Russell called this finding the first "big red flag" on SRB Joint and O-ring safety.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-12)

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The 12 stars within the blue field indicate the flight's original numerical designation as STS-12 in the Space Transportation System's mission sequence. A representation of _Discovery's_ namesake is manifested in a sailing ship, which is linked to the Shuttle (with the OAST solar array in the payload bay) via a red, white, and blue path, signifying its maiden voyage.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-chronology-16)

**STS-41-D** (formerly STS-14) was the 12th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the maiden flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. It was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on August 30, 1984, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on September 5, 1984. Three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") were deployed into orbit during the six-day mission, and a number of scientific experiments were conducted, including a prototype [extendable solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_system_of_the_International_Space_Station "Electrical system of the International Space Station") that would eventually form the basis of the main solar arrays on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS).

The mission was delayed by more than two months from its original planned launch date, having experienced the Space Shuttle program's first launch abort at T−4 seconds on June 26, 1984.

## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission background")]

The launch was originally planned for June 25, 1984, but because of a variety of technical problems, including rollback to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) to replace a faulty [Space Shuttle Main Engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Main_Engine "Space Shuttle Main Engine") (SSME), the launch was delayed by over two months. The June 26, 1984, launch attempt marked the first time since [Gemini 6A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_6A "Gemini 6A") that a crewed spacecraft had experienced a shutdown of its engines just prior to launch.

### June 1984 launch attempt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: June 1984 launch attempt")]

During the June 26, 1984, launch attempt, there was a launch abort at T−4 seconds, followed by a pad fire about ten minutes later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-STS-41-4) Because the center engine had not started when the abort was triggered, confusion ensued as the [flight controllers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller "Flight controller") were unable to verify its state:

> Commentary: "We have a cut off".  
>  "NTD [_NASA Test Director_] we have a RSLS [_Redundant Set Launch Sequencer_] abort".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We have an abort by the onboard computers of the orbiter Discovery".  
>  "Break break, break break, GLS [_Ground Launch Sequencer_] shows engine one not shut down".  
>  "OK, PLT [_pilot_]?"  
>  "CSME [_Space Shuttle Main Engines_] verify engine one".  
>  "You want me to shut down engine one?"  
>  "We do not show engine start on one".  
>  "OTC [_Orbiter test conductor_] I can verify shutdown on verify on engine one, we haven't start prepped engine one".  
>  "All engines shut down I can verify that".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We can now verify all three engines have been shut down".  
>  "We have red lights on engines two and three in the cockpit, not on one".  
>  "All right, CSME verify engine one safe for APU [_[auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary\_power\_unit "Auxiliary power unit")_] shutdown".  
>  "If I can verify that?"  
>  "OTC GPC [_General Purpose Computer_] go for APU shutdown".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-5)

Mission Specialist Steve Hawley was reported as saying following the abort: "Gee, I thought we'd be a lot higher at MECO (Main Engine Cut-Off)!".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6) About ten minutes later, the following was heard on live TV coverage:

> "We have indication two of our fire detectors on the zero level; no response. They're side by side right next to the engine area. The engineer requested that we turn on the heat shield fire water which is what could be seen spraying up in the vicinity of the engine bells of _Discovery_'s three main engines".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-7)

While evacuating the shuttle 20 minutes later, the crew was doused with water from the pad deluge system, which was activated due to a hydrogen fire on the launch pad caused by the free hydrogen (fuel) that had collected around the engine nozzles following the shutdown and engine anomaly.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-8) Because the fire was invisible to humans, had the astronauts used the normal emergency escape procedure across the service arm to the slidewire escape baskets, they would have run into the fire.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050317-9)

Changes to procedures resulting from the abort included more practicing of "safing" the orbiter following aborts at various points, the use of the fire suppression system in all pad aborts, and the testing of the slidewire escape system with a real person ([Charles F. Bolden Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bolden "Charles Bolden")). It emerged that launch controllers were reluctant to order the crew to evacuate during the STS-41-D abort, as the slidewire had not been ridden by a human.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)

Examination of telemetry data indicated that the engine malfunction had been caused by a stuck valve that prevented proper flow of LOX into the combustion chamber.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

STS-41-D launched at 08:41:50 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on August 30, 1984, after a six-minute, fifty-second delay when a private aircraft flew into the restricted airspace near the launch pad. It was the fourth launch attempt for _Discovery_. Because of the two-month delay, the [STS-41-F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") mission was canceled (STS-41-E had already been canceled), and its primary payloads were included on the STS-41-D flight. The combined cargo weighed over 18,681 kg (41,185 lb), a record for a Space Shuttle payload up to that time.

The six-person flight crew consisted of [Henry W. Hartsfield Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_W._Hartsfield_Jr. "Henry W. Hartsfield Jr."), commander, making his second shuttle mission; pilot [Michael L. Coats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Coats "Michael Coats"); three mission specialists – [Judith A. Resnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Resnik "Judith Resnik"), [Richard M. Mullane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mullane "Mike Mullane") and [Steven A. Hawley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hawley "Steven Hawley"); and a payload specialist, [Charles D. Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_D._Walker "Charles D. Walker"), an employee of [McDonnell Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas "McDonnell Douglas"). Walker was the first commercially sponsored payload specialist to fly aboard the Space Shuttle. Resnik became the second American woman to fly any NASA space mission, after [Sally K. Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Ride "Sally Ride").

Primary cargo of _Discovery_ consisted of three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"): SBS-4 for [Satellite Business Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_Business_Systems "Satellite Business Systems"), [Telstar 302](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telstar_302 "Telstar 302") for [Telesat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telesat "Telesat") of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-2, or [Leasat-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom"), a [Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft_Company "Hughes Aircraft Company")-built satellite leased to the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy"); all three were Hughes-built satellites. Leasat-2 was the first large communications satellite designed specifically to be deployed from the Space Shuttle. All three satellites were deployed successfully and became operational.

Another payload was the OAST-1 [solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_module "Photovoltaic module"), a device 4 m (13 ft) wide and 31 m (102 ft) high, which folded into a package 18 cm (7.1 in) deep. The array carried a number of different types of experimental [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cell "Solar cell") and was extended to its full height several times during the mission. At the time, it was the largest structure ever extended from a crewed spacecraft, and it demonstrated the feasibility of large lightweight solar arrays for use on future orbital installations, such as the International Space Station (ISS).

The McDonnell Douglas-sponsored Continuous Flow Electrophoresis System (CFES) experiment, using living cells, was more elaborate than the one flown on previous missions, and payload specialist Walker operated it for more than 100 hours during the flight. A student experiment to study [crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") growth in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") was also carried out. The highlights of the mission were filmed using an [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX")[motion picture camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie_camera "Movie camera"), and later appeared in the 1985 documentary film _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_. On September 3, 1984, concern arose over the formation of ice on the waste dump nozzle of the shuttle. The cause was an obstruction in the shuttle's external wastewater dumping system that caused a 61 cm (24 in) "[pee-sicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine "Urine")" to form during the mission; Hartsfield removed it with the Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) the following day.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050414-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-11)

The mission lasted 6 days, 0 hour, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds, with landing taking place on Runway 17 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 06:37:54 a.m. PDT on September 5, 1984. During STS-41-D, _Discovery_ traveled a total of 4,010,000 km (2,490,000 mi) and made 97 orbits. The orbiter was transported back to KSC on September 10, 1984. Ominously, STS-41-D was the first Shuttle mission in which blow-by damage to the SRB O-rings was discovered, with a small amount of soot found beyond the primary O-ring. Following the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), [Morton Thiokol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiokol "Thiokol") engineer Brian Russell called this finding the first "big red flag" on SRB Joint and O-ring safety.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-12)

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The 12 stars within the blue field indicate the flight's original numerical designation as STS-12 in the Space Transportation System's mission sequence. A representation of _Discovery's_ namesake is manifested in a sailing ship, which is linked to the Shuttle (with the OAST solar array in the payload bay) via a red, white, and blue path, signifying its maiden voyage.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-chronology-16)

This is a list of persons who served aboard **Space Shuttles**, arranged in chronological order by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions.

Abbreviations:

*   **PC** = Payload Commander
*   **MSE** = [USAF Manned Spaceflight Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Spaceflight_Engineer_Program "Manned Spaceflight Engineer Program")
*   **Mir** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") Space Station
*   **ISS** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

Names of astronauts returning from the Mir or ISS on the Space Shuttle are shown in _italics_. They did not have specific crew roles, but are listed in the Payload Specialist columns for reasons of space.

Only two flights have carried more than seven crew members for either launch or landing. [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A") in 1985 is the only flight to have both launched and landed with a crew of eight, and [STS-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-71 "STS-71") in 1995 is the only other flight to have landed with a crew of eight.

This is a list of persons who served aboard **Space Shuttles**, arranged in chronological order by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions.

Abbreviations:

*   **PC** = Payload Commander
*   **MSE** = [USAF Manned Spaceflight Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Spaceflight_Engineer_Program "Manned Spaceflight Engineer Program")
*   **Mir** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") Space Station
*   **ISS** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

Names of astronauts returning from the Mir or ISS on the Space Shuttle are shown in _italics_. They did not have specific crew roles, but are listed in the Payload Specialist columns for reasons of space.

Only two flights have carried more than seven crew members for either launch or landing. [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A") in 1985 is the only flight to have both launched and landed with a crew of eight, and [STS-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-71 "STS-71") in 1995 is the only other flight to have landed with a crew of eight.

This is a list of persons who served aboard **Space Shuttles**, arranged in chronological order by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions.

Abbreviations:

*   **PC** = Payload Commander
*   **MSE** = [USAF Manned Spaceflight Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Spaceflight_Engineer_Program "Manned Spaceflight Engineer Program")
*   **Mir** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") Space Station
*   **ISS** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

Names of astronauts returning from the Mir or ISS on the Space Shuttle are shown in _italics_. They did not have specific crew roles, but are listed in the Payload Specialist columns for reasons of space.

Only two flights have carried more than seven crew members for either launch or landing. [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A") in 1985 is the only flight to have both launched and landed with a crew of eight, and [STS-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-71 "STS-71") in 1995 is the only other flight to have landed with a crew of eight.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching.jpg/330px-Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching.jpg)

Launch of Space Shuttle _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ on 12 April 1981 at Pad 39A for mission [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")

The [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") was a partially reusable [low Earth orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit")[spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft") system operated by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration). Its official program name was [Space Transportation System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System "Space Transportation System") (STS), taken from a 1969 plan for a system of reusable spacecraft of which it was the only item funded for development.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-taskGroup-1) Operational missions launched numerous [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite"), conducted science experiments in orbit, and participated in construction and servicing of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS). The first of four orbital test flights occurred in 1981, leading to operational flights beginning in 1982.

From 1981 to 2011 a total of 135 missions were flown, all launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). During that time period the fleet logged 1,322 days, 19 hours, 21 minutes and 23 seconds of flight time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-ShuttleByNumbers-2) The longest orbital flight of the Shuttle was [STS-80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-80 "STS-80") at 17 days 15 hours, while the shortest flight was [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") at one minute 13 seconds when the Space Shuttle _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_ broke apart during launch. The cold morning shrank an [O-ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-ring "O-ring") on the right [solid rocket booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster") causing the external fuel tank to explode. The shuttles docked with [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") space station _[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")_ nine times and visited the ISS thirty-seven times. The highest altitude ([apogee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apsis "Apsis")) achieved by the shuttle was 386 mi (621 km) when deploying the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-forbes-3) The program flew a total of 355 people representing 16 countries, and with 852 total shuttle fliers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-nasafacts-4) The Kennedy Space Center served as the landing site for 78 missions, while 54 missions landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") and one mission landed at [White Sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Sands,_New_Mexico "White Sands, New Mexico"), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-launch-5)

The first orbiter built, _[Enterprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise")_, was used for [atmospheric flight tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") (ALT) but future plans to upgrade it to orbital capability were ultimately canceled. Four fully operational orbiters were initially built: _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_, _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_, _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_, and _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ were destroyed in mission accidents in 1986 and 2003 respectively, killing a total of fourteen astronauts. A fifth operational orbiter, _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_, was built in 1991 to replace _Challenger_. The Space Shuttle was retired from service upon the conclusion of [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135") by _Atlantis_ on 21 July 2011.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6)

## Flight numbering

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Shuttle_profiles.jpg/330px-Shuttle_profiles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shuttle_profiles.jpg)

Profiles of all five orbiters at launch.

The U.S. Space Shuttle program was officially referred to as the Space Transportation System (STS). Specific shuttle missions were therefore designated with the prefix "STS".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-ShuttleByNumbers-2) Initially, the launches were given sequential numbers indicating order of launch, such as [STS-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-7 "STS-7"). Subsequent to the [Apollo 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13 "Apollo 13") mishap, due to [Administrator of NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA "Administrator of NASA")[James M. Beggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_M._Beggs "James M. Beggs")'s [triskaidekaphobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triskaidekaphobia "Triskaidekaphobia") and consequent unwillingness to number [a forthcoming flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-C "STS-41-C") as STS-13,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-crippenoh-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-hartoh-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-weitzoh-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-vanhoftenoh-10) beginning in 1984, each mission was assigned a code, such as [STS-41-B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-B "STS-41-B"), with the first digit (or pair of digits for years 1990 and beyond) indicating the federal [fiscal year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") offset into the program (so 41-B was scheduled for FY 1984, 51-A through 51-L originally for FY 1985, and the third flight in FY 1985 would have been named 51-C), the second digit indicating the launch site (1 was [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") and 2 was [Space Launch Complex 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Space_Launch_Complex_6 "Vandenberg Space Launch Complex 6") at [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Space_Force_Base "Vandenberg Space Force Base"), although Vandenberg was never used), and the letter indicating scheduling sequence.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-spacefacts-11) These codes were assigned when the launches were initially scheduled and were not changed as missions were delayed or rescheduled.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6) The codes were adopted from STS-41-B through STS-51-L (although the highest code used was actually [STS-61-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-C "STS-61-C")), and the sequential numbers were used internally at NASA on all processing paperwork.

After the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), NASA returned to using a sequential numbering system, with the number counting from the beginning of the STS program. Unlike the initial system, however, the numbers were assigned based on the initial mission schedule, and did not always reflect actual launch order. This numbering scheme started at 26, with the first flight as STS-26R—the R suffix stood for "reflight" to disambiguate from prior missions. The suffix was used for two years through STS-33R, then the R was dropped.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6) As a result of the changes in systems, flights under different numbering systems could have the same number with one having a letter appended, e.g. flight [STS-51](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51 "STS-51") (a mission carried out by _Discovery_ in 1993) was many years after [STS-51-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A "STS-51-A") (_Discovery's_ second flight in 1984).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6) It wasn't until [STS-127](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-127 "STS-127") in 2009 where the flight numbering system returned to a standard and consistent order.
