NASA flights of the partially reusable spacecraft

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching.jpg/330px-Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching.jpg)

Launch of Space Shuttle _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ on 12 April 1981 at Pad 39A for mission [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")

The [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") was a partially reusable [low Earth orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit")[spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft") system operated by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration). Its official program name was [Space Transportation System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System "Space Transportation System") (STS), taken from a 1969 plan for a system of reusable spacecraft of which it was the only item funded for development.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-taskGroup-1) Operational missions launched numerous [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite"), conducted science experiments in orbit, and participated in construction and servicing of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS). The first of four orbital test flights occurred in 1981, leading to operational flights beginning in 1982.

From 1981 to 2011 a total of 135 missions were flown, all launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). During that time period the fleet logged 1,322 days, 19 hours, 21 minutes and 23 seconds of flight time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-ShuttleByNumbers-2) The longest orbital flight of the Shuttle was [STS-80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-80 "STS-80") at 17 days 15 hours, while the shortest flight was [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") at one minute 13 seconds when the Space Shuttle _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_ broke apart during launch. The cold morning shrank an [O-ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-ring "O-ring") on the right [solid rocket booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster") causing the external fuel tank to explode. The shuttles docked with [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") space station _[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")_ nine times and visited the ISS thirty-seven times. The highest altitude ([apogee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apsis "Apsis")) achieved by the shuttle was 386 mi (621 km) when deploying the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-forbes-3) The program flew a total of 355 people representing 16 countries, and with 852 total shuttle fliers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-nasafacts-4) The Kennedy Space Center served as the landing site for 78 missions, while 54 missions landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") and one mission landed at [White Sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Sands,_New_Mexico "White Sands, New Mexico"), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-launch-5)

The first orbiter built, _[Enterprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise")_, was used for [atmospheric flight tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") (ALT) but future plans to upgrade it to orbital capability were ultimately canceled. Four fully operational orbiters were initially built: _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_, _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_, _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_, and _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ were destroyed in mission accidents in 1986 and 2003 respectively, killing a total of fourteen astronauts. A fifth operational orbiter, _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_, was built in 1991 to replace _Challenger_. The Space Shuttle was retired from service upon the conclusion of [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135") by _Atlantis_ on 21 July 2011.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6)

## Flight numbering

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Shuttle_profiles.jpg/330px-Shuttle_profiles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shuttle_profiles.jpg)

Profiles of all five orbiters at launch.

The U.S. Space Shuttle program was officially referred to as the Space Transportation System (STS). Specific shuttle missions were therefore designated with the prefix "STS".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-intro-ShuttleByNumbers-2) Initially, the launches were given sequential numbers indicating order of launch, such as [STS-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-7 "STS-7"). Subsequent to the [Apollo 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13 "Apollo 13") mishap, due to [Administrator of NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA "Administrator of NASA")[James M. Beggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_M._Beggs "James M. Beggs")'s [triskaidekaphobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triskaidekaphobia "Triskaidekaphobia") and consequent unwillingness to number [a forthcoming flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-C "STS-41-C") as STS-13,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-crippenoh-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-hartoh-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-weitzoh-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-vanhoftenoh-10) beginning in 1984, each mission was assigned a code, such as [STS-41-B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-B "STS-41-B"), with the first digit (or pair of digits for years 1990 and beyond) indicating the federal [fiscal year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") offset into the program (so 41-B was scheduled for FY 1984, 51-A through 51-L originally for FY 1985, and the third flight in FY 1985 would have been named 51-C), the second digit indicating the launch site (1 was [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") and 2 was [Space Launch Complex 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Space_Launch_Complex_6 "Vandenberg Space Launch Complex 6") at [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Space_Force_Base "Vandenberg Space Force Base"), although Vandenberg was never used), and the letter indicating scheduling sequence.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-numbering-spacefacts-11) These codes were assigned when the launches were initially scheduled and were not changed as missions were delayed or rescheduled.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6) The codes were adopted from STS-41-B through STS-51-L (although the highest code used was actually [STS-61-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-C "STS-61-C")), and the sequential numbers were used internally at NASA on all processing paperwork.

After the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), NASA returned to using a sequential numbering system, with the number counting from the beginning of the STS program. Unlike the initial system, however, the numbers were assigned based on the initial mission schedule, and did not always reflect actual launch order. This numbering scheme started at 26, with the first flight as STS-26R—the R suffix stood for "reflight" to disambiguate from prior missions. The suffix was used for two years through STS-33R, then the R was dropped.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6) As a result of the changes in systems, flights under different numbering systems could have the same number with one having a letter appended, e.g. flight [STS-51](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51 "STS-51") (a mission carried out by _Discovery_ in 1993) was many years after [STS-51-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A "STS-51-A") (_Discovery's_ second flight in 1984).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Space_Shuttle_missions&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkins524-6) It wasn't until [STS-127](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-127 "STS-127") in 2009 where the flight numbering system returned to a standard and consistent order.

**Space Shuttle _Discovery_** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-103**) is a retired American Space Shuttle orbiter. The [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") was one of the orbiters from [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ov103-2) Its first mission, STS-41-D, flew from August 30 to September 5, 1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times, aggregating more spaceflights than any other spacecraft as of December 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-Guinness_most_spaceflights-3) The Space Shuttle launch vehicle had three main components: the Space Shuttle orbiter, a single-use central fuel tank, and two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster"). Nearly 25,000 [heat-resistant tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") cover the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-4)

_Discovery_ became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded by _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ and _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-5) After the _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ accidents, _Discovery_ became the oldest surviving orbiter. It embarked on its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), on February 24, 2011, and touched down for the last time at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on March 9,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-6) having spent a cumulative total of nearly a full year in space. _Discovery_ performed both research and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) assembly missions, and also carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into orbit among other satellites.

_Discovery_ was the first operational shuttle to be retired, followed by _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ and then _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. The shuttle is now on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") of the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")[National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").

## History

The name _Discovery_ was chosen to carry on a tradition based on ships of exploration,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ov103-2) primarily [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1774) "HMS Discovery (1774)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-7) one of the ships commanded by Captain [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook") during his third and final major voyage from 1776 to 1779, and [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson")'s [_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(1602_ship) "Discovery (1602 ship)"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ov103-2) which was used in 1610–1611 to explore [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") and search for a [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage "Northwest Passage"). Other ships bearing the name have included [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1874) "HMS Discovery (1874)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-8) of the 1875–1876 [British Arctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Arctic_Expedition "British Arctic Expedition") to the North Pole, and [RRS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RRS_Discovery "RRS Discovery"), which carried the 1901–1904 [_Discovery_ Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Expedition "Discovery Expedition") to [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), led by [Captain Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Falcon_Scott "Robert Falcon Scott").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-pao-9)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") and conducted the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-103 "STS-103") Hubble service missions. It also launched the [_Ulysses_ probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_probe "Ulysses probe") and three [TDRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") satellites. Twice _Discovery_ was chosen as the "Return To Flight" Orbiter, first in 1988 after the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and then again for the twin "Return To Flight" missions in July 2005 and July 2006 after the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in 2003. [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") astronaut [John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"), who was 77 at the time, flew with _Discovery_ on [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") in 1998, making him the oldest person to go into space at that time in history.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)

Had plans to launch [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") payloads from [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") gone ahead, _Discovery_ would have become the dedicated [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") shuttle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-11) Its first West Coast mission, [STS-62-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A"), was scheduled for 1986, but [canceled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") in the aftermath of the _[Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger\_disaster "Challenger disaster")_.

On May 27, 1999, _Discovery_ was launched on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96"), the first shuttle mission to dock with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-12)

_Discovery_ was retired after completing its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") on March 9, 2011. The spacecraft is now on display in Virginia at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"), an annex of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-nasm-13)

During its construction, _Discovery_ was fitted with several black tiles near the middle starboard window where there should have been white tiles. It is unknown if this was the result of a harmless manufacturing mishap or done intentionally to give a distinctive look to the shuttle. This feature has been called 'teardrop' and allowed _Discovery_ to be told apart from the rest of the fleet without looking at its name, although often unnoticed by the uninitiated.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-14)

The spacecraft weighed roughly 6,870 lb (3,120 kg) less than _Columbia_ when it was brought into service due to optimalizations determined during the construction and testing of _Enterprise_, _Columbia_ and _Challenger_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)_Discovery_ weighs 6 pounds (2.7 kg) heavier than _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ and 363 pounds (165 kg) heavier than _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ after further weight-saving adjustments were made.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-FT_facts-15)

Part of the _Discovery_ weight optimizations included the greater use of quilted [AFRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Flexible_Insulation_Blankets/Advanced_Flexible_Reusable_Insulation_(FIB/AFRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") blankets rather than the white [LRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Low-temperature_reusable_surface_insulation_(LRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") tiles on the fuselage, and the use of [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") instead of aluminum for the payload bay doors and some of the wing spars and beams.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-16)

Upon its delivery to the Kennedy Space Center in 1983, _Discovery_ was modified alongside _Challenger_ to accommodate the liquid-fueled [Centaur-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centaur-G "Centaur-G") booster, which had been planned for use beginning in 1986 but was cancelled in the wake of the _Challenger_ disaster.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-17)

Beginning in late 1995, the orbiter underwent a nine-month Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). This included outfitting the vehicle with a fifth set of cryogenic tanks and an external airlock to support missions to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). As with all the orbiters, it could be attached to the top of specialized aircraft and did so in June 1996 when it returned to the Kennedy Space Center, and later in April 2012 when sent to the Udvar-Hazy Center, riding [piggy-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggy-back_(transportation) "Piggy-back (transportation)") on a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)

After [STS-105](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105 "STS-105"), _Discovery_ became the first of the orbiter fleet to undergo Orbiter Major Modification (OMM) period at the Kennedy Space Center. Work began in September 2002 to prepare the vehicle for Return to Flight. The work included scheduled upgrades and additional safety modifications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)

_Discovery_ was [decommissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_decommissioning "Ship decommissioning") on March 9, 2011.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-manifest-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-CSCS1-20) NASA offered _Discovery_ to the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") for public display and preservation, after a month-long [decontamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contamination_control "Contamination control") process,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-21) as part of the national collection.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-smithsonian-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-smithsonian-houston-chronical-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-24)_Discovery_ replaced [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), which was in the Smithsonian's display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until 2011.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-27)_Discovery_ was transported to [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") on April 17, 2012, and was transferred to the Udvar-Hazy Center on April 19 where a welcome ceremony was held. Afterwards, at around 5:30 pm, _Discovery_ was rolled to its "final wheels stop" in the Udvar-Hazy Center.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-29)

Texas senators [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") added a provision to the 2025 [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") to spend $85 million to relocate a space vehicle that has flown astronauts into space, presumably _Discovery_ because of the sponsors of the provision and previous legislation attempts, from the Udvar-Hazy Center to the [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston") Museum in Texas.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-31) While the Smithsonian estimated that the total cost of the transfer would be approximately $325 million, they also countered that ownership of the shuttle had been transferred to the museum and was no longer federal property, and that Congress did not have the ability to force a transfer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-33)

## Flights

By its last mission, _Discovery_ had flown 149 million mi (240 million km) in 39 missions, completed 5,830 orbits, and spent 365 days in orbit over 27 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-slt-34)_Discovery_ flew [more flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbiter#Flight_statistics "Space Shuttle Orbiter") than any other Orbiter Shuttle, including four in 1985 alone. _Discovery_ flew both "return to flight" missions after the _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster")_ and _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster")_ disasters: [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") in 1988, [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005, and [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") in 2006. _Discovery_ flew the ante-penultimate mission of the Space Shuttle program, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), having launched on February 24, 2011. _Endeavour_ flew [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") and _Atlantis_ performed [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), NASA's last Space Shuttle mission. On February 24, 2011, Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39-A to begin its final orbital flight.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ares6-35)

## Flow directors

The Flow Director was responsible for the overall preparation of the shuttle for launch and processing it after landing, and remained permanently assigned to head the spacecraft's ground crew while the astronaut flight crews changed for every mission. Each shuttle's Flow Director was supported by a Vehicle Manager for the same spacecraft. Space Shuttle _Discovery'_ s Flow Directors were:

*   Until 01/1991: John J. "Tip" Talone Jr. (afterwards Flow Director for _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   01/1991 – 09/1992: John C. "Chris" Fairey[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   09/1992 – 10/1996: [David A. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_A._King_(engineer) "David A. King (engineer)")[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-39)
*   10/1996 – 05/2000: W. Scott Cilento[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-40)
*   12/2000 – 03/2011: Stephanie S. Stilson[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-41)

**Space Shuttle _Discovery_** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-103**) is a retired American Space Shuttle orbiter. The [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") was one of the orbiters from [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ov103-2) Its first mission, STS-41-D, flew from August 30 to September 5, 1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times, aggregating more spaceflights than any other spacecraft as of December 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-Guinness_most_spaceflights-3) The Space Shuttle launch vehicle had three main components: the Space Shuttle orbiter, a single-use central fuel tank, and two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster"). Nearly 25,000 [heat-resistant tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") cover the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-4)

_Discovery_ became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded by _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ and _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-5) After the _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ accidents, _Discovery_ became the oldest surviving orbiter. It embarked on its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), on February 24, 2011, and touched down for the last time at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on March 9,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-6) having spent a cumulative total of nearly a full year in space. _Discovery_ performed both research and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) assembly missions, and also carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into orbit among other satellites.

_Discovery_ was the first operational shuttle to be retired, followed by _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ and then _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. The shuttle is now on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") of the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")[National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").

## History

The name _Discovery_ was chosen to carry on a tradition based on ships of exploration,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ov103-2) primarily [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1774) "HMS Discovery (1774)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-7) one of the ships commanded by Captain [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook") during his third and final major voyage from 1776 to 1779, and [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson")'s [_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(1602_ship) "Discovery (1602 ship)"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ov103-2) which was used in 1610–1611 to explore [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") and search for a [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage "Northwest Passage"). Other ships bearing the name have included [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1874) "HMS Discovery (1874)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-8) of the 1875–1876 [British Arctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Arctic_Expedition "British Arctic Expedition") to the North Pole, and [RRS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RRS_Discovery "RRS Discovery"), which carried the 1901–1904 [_Discovery_ Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Expedition "Discovery Expedition") to [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), led by [Captain Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Falcon_Scott "Robert Falcon Scott").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-pao-9)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") and conducted the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-103 "STS-103") Hubble service missions. It also launched the [_Ulysses_ probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_probe "Ulysses probe") and three [TDRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") satellites. Twice _Discovery_ was chosen as the "Return To Flight" Orbiter, first in 1988 after the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and then again for the twin "Return To Flight" missions in July 2005 and July 2006 after the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in 2003. [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") astronaut [John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"), who was 77 at the time, flew with _Discovery_ on [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") in 1998, making him the oldest person to go into space at that time in history.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)

Had plans to launch [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") payloads from [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") gone ahead, _Discovery_ would have become the dedicated [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") shuttle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-11) Its first West Coast mission, [STS-62-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A"), was scheduled for 1986, but [canceled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") in the aftermath of the _[Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger\_disaster "Challenger disaster")_.

On May 27, 1999, _Discovery_ was launched on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96"), the first shuttle mission to dock with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-12)

_Discovery_ was retired after completing its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") on March 9, 2011. The spacecraft is now on display in Virginia at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"), an annex of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-nasm-13)

During its construction, _Discovery_ was fitted with several black tiles near the middle starboard window where there should have been white tiles. It is unknown if this was the result of a harmless manufacturing mishap or done intentionally to give a distinctive look to the shuttle. This feature has been called 'teardrop' and allowed _Discovery_ to be told apart from the rest of the fleet without looking at its name, although often unnoticed by the uninitiated.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-14)

The spacecraft weighed roughly 6,870 lb (3,120 kg) less than _Columbia_ when it was brought into service due to optimalizations determined during the construction and testing of _Enterprise_, _Columbia_ and _Challenger_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)_Discovery_ weighs 6 pounds (2.7 kg) heavier than _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ and 363 pounds (165 kg) heavier than _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ after further weight-saving adjustments were made.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-FT_facts-15)

Part of the _Discovery_ weight optimizations included the greater use of quilted [AFRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Flexible_Insulation_Blankets/Advanced_Flexible_Reusable_Insulation_(FIB/AFRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") blankets rather than the white [LRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Low-temperature_reusable_surface_insulation_(LRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") tiles on the fuselage, and the use of [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") instead of aluminum for the payload bay doors and some of the wing spars and beams.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-16)

Upon its delivery to the Kennedy Space Center in 1983, _Discovery_ was modified alongside _Challenger_ to accommodate the liquid-fueled [Centaur-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centaur-G "Centaur-G") booster, which had been planned for use beginning in 1986 but was cancelled in the wake of the _Challenger_ disaster.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-17)

Beginning in late 1995, the orbiter underwent a nine-month Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). This included outfitting the vehicle with a fifth set of cryogenic tanks and an external airlock to support missions to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). As with all the orbiters, it could be attached to the top of specialized aircraft and did so in June 1996 when it returned to the Kennedy Space Center, and later in April 2012 when sent to the Udvar-Hazy Center, riding [piggy-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggy-back_(transportation) "Piggy-back (transportation)") on a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)

After [STS-105](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105 "STS-105"), _Discovery_ became the first of the orbiter fleet to undergo Orbiter Major Modification (OMM) period at the Kennedy Space Center. Work began in September 2002 to prepare the vehicle for Return to Flight. The work included scheduled upgrades and additional safety modifications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-over-10)

[SCA N905NA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") carrying _Discovery_ on the last flyover of the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall") at around 10:15 am EDT, during its 11:05 am landing at [Dulles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") airport on April 17, 2012[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-18)

_Discovery_ was [decommissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_decommissioning "Ship decommissioning") on March 9, 2011.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-manifest-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-CSCS1-20) NASA offered _Discovery_ to the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") for public display and preservation, after a month-long [decontamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contamination_control "Contamination control") process,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-21) as part of the national collection.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-smithsonian-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-smithsonian-houston-chronical-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-24)_Discovery_ replaced [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), which was in the Smithsonian's display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until 2011.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-27)_Discovery_ was transported to [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") on April 17, 2012, and was transferred to the Udvar-Hazy Center on April 19 where a welcome ceremony was held. Afterwards, at around 5:30 pm, _Discovery_ was rolled to its "final wheels stop" in the Udvar-Hazy Center.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-29)

Texas senators [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") added a provision to the 2025 [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") to spend $85 million to relocate a space vehicle that has flown astronauts into space, presumably _Discovery_ because of the sponsors of the provision and previous legislation attempts, from the Udvar-Hazy Center to the [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston") Museum in Texas.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-31) While the Smithsonian estimated that the total cost of the transfer would be approximately $325 million, they also countered that ownership of the shuttle had been transferred to the museum and was no longer federal property, and that Congress did not have the ability to force a transfer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-33)

## Flights

By its last mission, _Discovery_ had flown 149 million mi (240 million km) in 39 missions, completed 5,830 orbits, and spent 365 days in orbit over 27 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-slt-34)_Discovery_ flew [more flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbiter#Flight_statistics "Space Shuttle Orbiter") than any other Orbiter Shuttle, including four in 1985 alone. _Discovery_ flew both "return to flight" missions after the _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster")_ and _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster")_ disasters: [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") in 1988, [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005, and [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") in 2006. _Discovery_ flew the ante-penultimate mission of the Space Shuttle program, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), having launched on February 24, 2011. _Endeavour_ flew [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") and _Atlantis_ performed [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), NASA's last Space Shuttle mission. On February 24, 2011, Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39-A to begin its final orbital flight.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-ares6-35)

## Flow directors

The Flow Director was responsible for the overall preparation of the shuttle for launch and processing it after landing, and remained permanently assigned to head the spacecraft's ground crew while the astronaut flight crews changed for every mission. Each shuttle's Flow Director was supported by a Vehicle Manager for the same spacecraft. Space Shuttle _Discovery'_ s Flow Directors were:

*   Until 01/1991: John J. "Tip" Talone Jr. (afterwards Flow Director for _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   01/1991 – 09/1992: John C. "Chris" Fairey[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   09/1992 – 10/1996: [David A. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_A._King_(engineer) "David A. King (engineer)")[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-39)
*   10/1996 – 05/2000: W. Scott Cilento[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-40)
*   12/2000 – 03/2011: Stephanie S. Stilson[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&printable=yes&pagefrom=przewid?#cite_note-41)

**STS-51-A** (formerly STS-19) was the 14th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the second flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. The mission launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on November 8, 1984, and landed just under eight days later on November 16, 1984.

STS-51-A marked the first time a shuttle deployed two [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"), and retrieved from orbit two other communications satellites. The Canadian [Anik D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anik_(satellite) "Anik (satellite)") and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-1 satellites were both successfully deployed by the crew of _Discovery_. [Palapa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palapa "Palapa") B2 and [Westar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westar "Westar") 6, meanwhile, had been deployed during the [STS-41-B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-B "STS-41-B") mission earlier in the year, but had been placed into improper orbits due to the malfunctioning of their [kick motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apogee_kick_motor "Apogee kick motor"); they were both safely recovered and returned to [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") during STS-51-A.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-A&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

| Attempt | Planned | Result | Turnaround | Reason | Decision point | Weather go (%) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 7 Nov 1984, 8:23:00 am | Scrubbed | — | Weather | 7 Nov 1984, 7:51 am​(T−00:20:00 hold) |  | High windshear in the KSC area.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A#cite_note-3) |
| 2 | 8 Nov 1984, 7:15:00 am | Success | 0 days 22 hours 52 minutes |  |  |  |  |

STS-51-A was launched from [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida")'s Kennedy Space Center (KSC) at 7:15:00 a.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"), on November 8, 1984, less than a month after the [STS-41-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-G "STS-41-G") flight. A launch attempt the day before was scrubbed at T-minus 20 minutes due to high [shear winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_gradient "Wind gradient") in the [upper atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_atmosphere "Upper atmosphere").

The five-person flight crew consisted of Frederick H. Hauck, commander, on his second flight; pilot David M. Walker; and three mission specialists – Anna Lee Fisher, Dale A. Gardner and Joseph P. Allen. Both Gardner and Allen were making their second shuttle flights. STS-51-A marked the first flight of the Space Shuttle commanded by an astronaut from the 1978 class rather than the [Apollo era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program "Apollo program").

The two communications satellites successfully deployed were [Anik D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anik_(satellite) "Anik (satellite)") (on the second day of the mission) and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-1, also known as [Leasat 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") (on the third day); both were Hughes-built satellites. The orbiter then began a series of maneuvers to meet up with the first of the two satellites to be recovered, Palapa B2. The orbits of both satellites had been lowered by ground commands from about 970 km (600 mi) to 340 km (210 mi) to facilitate recovery operations. On day five of the mission, _Discovery_ rendezvoused with Palapa. Mission specialists Allen and Gardner performed an EVA, capturing the satellite with a device known as a "Stinger", or Apogee Capture Device (ACD),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A#cite_note-4) which was inserted into the satellite's [apogee motor nozzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apogee_kick_motor "Apogee kick motor") by Allen. The satellite's rotation was slowed to 1 [RPM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_per_minute "Revolutions per minute"), and Gardner, operating from a position on the end of the Remote Manipulator System (RMS) ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")), attempted unsuccessfully to grapple the satellite. Allen was able to manually maneuver the satellite into its cradle with Gardner's help, further aided by the Canadarm, which was operated by Fisher. The successful, improvised rescue effort took two hours.

The recovery of Westar 6 was not as difficult, and took place a day later. This time, Gardner, using the same muscle-power technique Allen had used for Palapa B2's rescue, easily captured the satellite. With Allen's help, he placed it in a cradle in the cargo bay. Following Westar 6's recovery, Gardner humorously held up a "For Sale" sign, as if trying to find someone to sell the malfunctioning satellites to, as a means to indicate the successful recovery and provide some comical relief for the troubled owners. The Westar satellite was, ironically enough, indeed later sold to Hong Kong–based [AsiaSat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AsiaSat "AsiaSat").

The STS-51-A mission also carried the Diffused Mixing of Organic Solutions (DMOS) experiment. It was the first of a series of comprehensive organic and [polymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymer "Polymer") science experiments sponsored by [3M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M "3M"). This mid-deck experiment was successful, and the proprietary results of the chemical mixes were turned over to 3M. One other experiment, a [radiation monitoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation_monitoring "Radiation monitoring") experiment, was also performed.

The satellite recoveries on STS-51-A were the last [untethered spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") until 1994, and marked the last use of the [Manned Maneuvering Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Maneuvering_Unit "Manned Maneuvering Unit") (MMU). In 1994, the [Simplified Aid For EVA Rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Aid_For_EVA_Rescue "Simplified Aid For EVA Rescue") (SAFER) was tested on [STS-64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-64 "STS-64"). On all subsequent spacewalks conducted by both NASA and the [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")/[Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") space agencies, the astronauts were tethered to the craft by some means.

The second mission of _Discovery_ ended at 6:59:56 a.m. EST on November 16, 1984, with a successful landing on Runway 15 at KSC. Footage of the landing was used in opening scene of the 1985 [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") movie _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_. The flight completed 127 orbits, and lasted 7 days, 23 hours, 44 minutes, and 56 seconds. It was the third shuttle landing at KSC, and the fifth and last shuttle mission of 1984.

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-A&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

STS-51-A Mission insignia depicts the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ en route to Earth orbit for NASA's STS-51-A mission and is reminiscent of a soaring eagle, shown in the insignia. The red and white trailing stripes, the blue background, and the presence of the Eagle, generate memories of America's 208 year-old history and traditions. The two satellites orbiting the Earth backgrounded amidst a celestial scene are a universal representation of the versatility of the Space Shuttle. The two satellites it is meant to retrieve are also included as a more specific reference to the mission's main objective and a highlight of what part of the Shuttle's versatile mission capabilities she would be covering this time. White lettering against the blue border lists the surnames of the five-member crew. The six stars represent the five astronauts aboard plus the daughter of Fisher, the first mother in space.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-A&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A#cite_note-chronology-5)

**STS-51-A** (formerly STS-19) was the 14th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the second flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. The mission launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on November 8, 1984, and landed just under eight days later on November 16, 1984.

STS-51-A marked the first time a shuttle deployed two [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"), and retrieved from orbit two other communications satellites. The Canadian [Anik D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anik_(satellite) "Anik (satellite)") and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-1 satellites were both successfully deployed by the crew of _Discovery_. [Palapa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palapa "Palapa") B2 and [Westar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westar "Westar") 6, meanwhile, had been deployed during the [STS-41-B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-B "STS-41-B") mission earlier in the year, but had been placed into improper orbits due to the malfunctioning of their [kick motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apogee_kick_motor "Apogee kick motor"); they were both safely recovered and returned to [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") during STS-51-A.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-A&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

| Attempt | Planned | Result | Turnaround | Reason | Decision point | Weather go (%) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 7 Nov 1984, 8:23:00 am | Scrubbed | — | Weather | 7 Nov 1984, 7:51 am​(T−00:20:00 hold) |  | High windshear in the KSC area.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A#cite_note-3) |
| 2 | 8 Nov 1984, 7:15:00 am | Success | 0 days 22 hours 52 minutes |  |  |  |  |

STS-51-A was launched from [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida")'s Kennedy Space Center (KSC) at 7:15:00 a.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"), on November 8, 1984, less than a month after the [STS-41-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-G "STS-41-G") flight. A launch attempt the day before was scrubbed at T-minus 20 minutes due to high [shear winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_gradient "Wind gradient") in the [upper atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_atmosphere "Upper atmosphere").

The five-person flight crew consisted of Frederick H. Hauck, commander, on his second flight; pilot David M. Walker; and three mission specialists – Anna Lee Fisher, Dale A. Gardner and Joseph P. Allen. Both Gardner and Allen were making their second shuttle flights. STS-51-A marked the first flight of the Space Shuttle commanded by an astronaut from the 1978 class rather than the [Apollo era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program "Apollo program").

The two communications satellites successfully deployed were [Anik D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anik_(satellite) "Anik (satellite)") (on the second day of the mission) and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-1, also known as [Leasat 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") (on the third day); both were Hughes-built satellites. The orbiter then began a series of maneuvers to meet up with the first of the two satellites to be recovered, Palapa B2. The orbits of both satellites had been lowered by ground commands from about 970 km (600 mi) to 340 km (210 mi) to facilitate recovery operations. On day five of the mission, _Discovery_ rendezvoused with Palapa. Mission specialists Allen and Gardner performed an EVA, capturing the satellite with a device known as a "Stinger", or Apogee Capture Device (ACD),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A#cite_note-4) which was inserted into the satellite's [apogee motor nozzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apogee_kick_motor "Apogee kick motor") by Allen. The satellite's rotation was slowed to 1 [RPM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_per_minute "Revolutions per minute"), and Gardner, operating from a position on the end of the Remote Manipulator System (RMS) ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")), attempted unsuccessfully to grapple the satellite. Allen was able to manually maneuver the satellite into its cradle with Gardner's help, further aided by the Canadarm, which was operated by Fisher. The successful, improvised rescue effort took two hours.

The recovery of Westar 6 was not as difficult, and took place a day later. This time, Gardner, using the same muscle-power technique Allen had used for Palapa B2's rescue, easily captured the satellite. With Allen's help, he placed it in a cradle in the cargo bay. Following Westar 6's recovery, Gardner humorously held up a "For Sale" sign, as if trying to find someone to sell the malfunctioning satellites to, as a means to indicate the successful recovery and provide some comical relief for the troubled owners. The Westar satellite was, ironically enough, indeed later sold to Hong Kong–based [AsiaSat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AsiaSat "AsiaSat").

The STS-51-A mission also carried the Diffused Mixing of Organic Solutions (DMOS) experiment. It was the first of a series of comprehensive organic and [polymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymer "Polymer") science experiments sponsored by [3M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M "3M"). This mid-deck experiment was successful, and the proprietary results of the chemical mixes were turned over to 3M. One other experiment, a [radiation monitoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation_monitoring "Radiation monitoring") experiment, was also performed.

The satellite recoveries on STS-51-A were the last [untethered spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") until 1994, and marked the last use of the [Manned Maneuvering Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Maneuvering_Unit "Manned Maneuvering Unit") (MMU). In 1994, the [Simplified Aid For EVA Rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Aid_For_EVA_Rescue "Simplified Aid For EVA Rescue") (SAFER) was tested on [STS-64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-64 "STS-64"). On all subsequent spacewalks conducted by both NASA and the [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")/[Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") space agencies, the astronauts were tethered to the craft by some means.

The second mission of _Discovery_ ended at 6:59:56 a.m. EST on November 16, 1984, with a successful landing on Runway 15 at KSC. Footage of the landing was used in opening scene of the 1985 [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") movie _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_. The flight completed 127 orbits, and lasted 7 days, 23 hours, 44 minutes, and 56 seconds. It was the third shuttle landing at KSC, and the fifth and last shuttle mission of 1984.

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-A&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

STS-51-A Mission insignia depicts the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ en route to Earth orbit for NASA's STS-51-A mission and is reminiscent of a soaring eagle, shown in the insignia. The red and white trailing stripes, the blue background, and the presence of the Eagle, generate memories of America's 208 year-old history and traditions. The two satellites orbiting the Earth backgrounded amidst a celestial scene are a universal representation of the versatility of the Space Shuttle. The two satellites it is meant to retrieve are also included as a more specific reference to the mission's main objective and a highlight of what part of the Shuttle's versatile mission capabilities she would be covering this time. White lettering against the blue border lists the surnames of the five-member crew. The six stars represent the five astronauts aboard plus the daughter of Fisher, the first mother in space.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-A&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-A#cite_note-chronology-5)

**Space Shuttle _Discovery_** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-103**) is a retired American Space Shuttle orbiter. The [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") was one of the orbiters from [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ov103-2) Its first mission, STS-41-D, flew from August 30 to September 5, 1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times, aggregating more spaceflights than any other spacecraft as of December 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-Guinness_most_spaceflights-3) The Space Shuttle launch vehicle had three main components: the Space Shuttle orbiter, a single-use central fuel tank, and two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster"). Nearly 25,000 [heat-resistant tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") cover the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-4)

_Discovery_ became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded by _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ and _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-5) After the _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ accidents, _Discovery_ became the oldest surviving orbiter. It embarked on its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), on February 24, 2011, and touched down for the last time at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on March 9,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-6) having spent a cumulative total of nearly a full year in space. _Discovery_ performed both research and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) assembly missions, and also carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into orbit among other satellites.

_Discovery_ was the first operational shuttle to be retired, followed by _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ and then _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. The shuttle is now on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") of the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")[National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The name _Discovery_ was chosen to carry on a tradition based on ships of exploration,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ov103-2) primarily [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1774) "HMS Discovery (1774)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-7) one of the ships commanded by Captain [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook") during his third and final major voyage from 1776 to 1779, and [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson")'s [_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(1602_ship) "Discovery (1602 ship)"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ov103-2) which was used in 1610–1611 to explore [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") and search for a [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage "Northwest Passage"). Other ships bearing the name have included [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1874) "HMS Discovery (1874)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-8) of the 1875–1876 [British Arctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Arctic_Expedition "British Arctic Expedition") to the North Pole, and [RRS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RRS_Discovery "RRS Discovery"), which carried the 1901–1904 [_Discovery_ Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Expedition "Discovery Expedition") to [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), led by [Captain Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Falcon_Scott "Robert Falcon Scott").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-pao-9)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") and conducted the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-103 "STS-103") Hubble service missions. It also launched the [_Ulysses_ probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_probe "Ulysses probe") and three [TDRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") satellites. Twice _Discovery_ was chosen as the "Return To Flight" Orbiter, first in 1988 after the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and then again for the twin "Return To Flight" missions in July 2005 and July 2006 after the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in 2003. [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") astronaut [John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"), who was 77 at the time, flew with _Discovery_ on [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") in 1998, making him the oldest person to go into space at that time in history.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)

Had plans to launch [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") payloads from [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") gone ahead, _Discovery_ would have become the dedicated [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") shuttle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-11) Its first West Coast mission, [STS-62-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A"), was scheduled for 1986, but [canceled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") in the aftermath of the _[Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger\_disaster "Challenger disaster")_.

On May 27, 1999, _Discovery_ was launched on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96"), the first shuttle mission to dock with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-12)

_Discovery_ was retired after completing its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") on March 9, 2011. The spacecraft is now on display in Virginia at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"), an annex of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-nasm-13)
