During its construction, _Discovery_ was fitted with several black tiles near the middle starboard window where there should have been white tiles. It is unknown if this was the result of a harmless manufacturing mishap or done intentionally to give a distinctive look to the shuttle. This feature has been called 'teardrop' and allowed _Discovery_ to be told apart from the rest of the fleet without looking at its name, although often unnoticed by the uninitiated.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-14)

The spacecraft weighed roughly 6,870 lb (3,120 kg) less than _Columbia_ when it was brought into service due to optimalizations determined during the construction and testing of _Enterprise_, _Columbia_ and _Challenger_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)_Discovery_ weighs 6 pounds (2.7 kg) heavier than _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ and 363 pounds (165 kg) heavier than _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ after further weight-saving adjustments were made.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-FT_facts-15)

Part of the _Discovery_ weight optimizations included the greater use of quilted [AFRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Flexible_Insulation_Blankets/Advanced_Flexible_Reusable_Insulation_(FIB/AFRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") blankets rather than the white [LRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Low-temperature_reusable_surface_insulation_(LRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") tiles on the fuselage, and the use of [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") instead of aluminum for the payload bay doors and some of the wing spars and beams.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-16)

Upon its delivery to the Kennedy Space Center in 1983, _Discovery_ was modified alongside _Challenger_ to accommodate the liquid-fueled [Centaur-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centaur-G "Centaur-G") booster, which had been planned for use beginning in 1986 but was cancelled in the wake of the _Challenger_ disaster.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-17)

Beginning in late 1995, the orbiter underwent a nine-month Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). This included outfitting the vehicle with a fifth set of cryogenic tanks and an external airlock to support missions to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). As with all the orbiters, it could be attached to the top of specialized aircraft and did so in June 1996 when it returned to the Kennedy Space Center, and later in April 2012 when sent to the Udvar-Hazy Center, riding [piggy-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggy-back_(transportation) "Piggy-back (transportation)") on a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)

After [STS-105](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105 "STS-105"), _Discovery_ became the first of the orbiter fleet to undergo Orbiter Major Modification (OMM) period at the Kennedy Space Center. Work began in September 2002 to prepare the vehicle for Return to Flight. The work included scheduled upgrades and additional safety modifications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)

Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until 2011.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-27)_Discovery_ was transported to [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") on April 17, 2012, and was transferred to the Udvar-Hazy Center on April 19 where a welcome ceremony was held. Afterwards, at around 5:30 pm, _Discovery_ was rolled to its "final wheels stop" in the Udvar-Hazy Center.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-29)

Texas senators [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") added a provision to the 2025 [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") to spend $85 million to relocate a space vehicle that has flown astronauts into space, presumably _Discovery_ because of the sponsors of the provision and previous legislation attempts, from the Udvar-Hazy Center to the [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston") Museum in Texas.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-31) While the Smithsonian estimated that the total cost of the transfer would be approximately $325 million, they also countered that ownership of the shuttle had been transferred to the museum and was no longer federal property, and that Congress did not have the ability to force a transfer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-33)

## Flights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Flights")]

By its last mission, _Discovery_ had flown 149 million mi (240 million km) in 39 missions, completed 5,830 orbits, and spent 365 days in orbit over 27 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-slt-34)_Discovery_ flew [more flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbiter#Flight_statistics "Space Shuttle Orbiter") than any other Orbiter Shuttle, including four in 1985 alone. _Discovery_ flew both "return to flight" missions after the _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster")_ and _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster")_ disasters: [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") in 1988, [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005, and [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") in 2006. _Discovery_ flew the ante-penultimate mission of the Space Shuttle program, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), having launched on February 24, 2011. _Endeavour_ flew [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") and _Atlantis_ performed [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), NASA's last Space Shuttle mission. On February 24, 2011, Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39-A to begin its final orbital flight.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ares6-35)

## Flow directors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Flow directors")]

The Flow Director was responsible for the overall preparation of the shuttle for launch and processing it after landing, and remained permanently assigned to head the spacecraft's ground crew while the astronaut flight crews changed for every mission. Each shuttle's Flow Director was supported by a Vehicle Manager for the same spacecraft. Space Shuttle _Discovery'_ s Flow Directors were:

*   Until 01/1991: John J. "Tip" Talone Jr. (afterwards Flow Director for _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   01/1991 – 09/1992: John C. "Chris" Fairey[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   09/1992 – 10/1996: [David A. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_A._King_(engineer) "David A. King (engineer)")[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-39)
*   10/1996 – 05/2000: W. Scott Cilento[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-40)
*   12/2000 – 03/2011: Stephanie S. Stilson[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-41)

**Space Shuttle _Discovery_** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-103**) is a retired American Space Shuttle orbiter. The [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") was one of the orbiters from [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ov103-2) Its first mission, STS-41-D, flew from August 30 to September 5, 1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times, aggregating more spaceflights than any other spacecraft as of December 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-Guinness_most_spaceflights-3) The Space Shuttle launch vehicle had three main components: the Space Shuttle orbiter, a single-use central fuel tank, and two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster"). Nearly 25,000 [heat-resistant tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") cover the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-4)

_Discovery_ became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded by _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ and _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-5) After the _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ accidents, _Discovery_ became the oldest surviving orbiter. It embarked on its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), on February 24, 2011, and touched down for the last time at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on March 9,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-6) having spent a cumulative total of nearly a full year in space. _Discovery_ performed both research and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) assembly missions, and also carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into orbit among other satellites.

_Discovery_ was the first operational shuttle to be retired, followed by _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ and then _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. The shuttle is now on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") of the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")[National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The name _Discovery_ was chosen to carry on a tradition based on ships of exploration,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ov103-2) primarily [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1774) "HMS Discovery (1774)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-7) one of the ships commanded by Captain [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook") during his third and final major voyage from 1776 to 1779, and [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson")'s [_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(1602_ship) "Discovery (1602 ship)"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ov103-2) which was used in 1610–1611 to explore [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") and search for a [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage "Northwest Passage"). Other ships bearing the name have included [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1874) "HMS Discovery (1874)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-8) of the 1875–1876 [British Arctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Arctic_Expedition "British Arctic Expedition") to the North Pole, and [RRS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RRS_Discovery "RRS Discovery"), which carried the 1901–1904 [_Discovery_ Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Expedition "Discovery Expedition") to [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), led by [Captain Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Falcon_Scott "Robert Falcon Scott").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-pao-9)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") and conducted the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-103 "STS-103") Hubble service missions. It also launched the [_Ulysses_ probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_probe "Ulysses probe") and three [TDRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") satellites. Twice _Discovery_ was chosen as the "Return To Flight" Orbiter, first in 1988 after the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and then again for the twin "Return To Flight" missions in July 2005 and July 2006 after the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in 2003. [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") astronaut [John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"), who was 77 at the time, flew with _Discovery_ on [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") in 1998, making him the oldest person to go into space at that time in history.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)

Had plans to launch [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") payloads from [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") gone ahead, _Discovery_ would have become the dedicated [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") shuttle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-11) Its first West Coast mission, [STS-62-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A"), was scheduled for 1986, but [canceled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") in the aftermath of the _[Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger\_disaster "Challenger disaster")_.

On May 27, 1999, _Discovery_ was launched on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96"), the first shuttle mission to dock with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-12)

_Discovery_ was retired after completing its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") on March 9, 2011. The spacecraft is now on display in Virginia at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"), an annex of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-nasm-13)

During its construction, _Discovery_ was fitted with several black tiles near the middle starboard window where there should have been white tiles. It is unknown if this was the result of a harmless manufacturing mishap or done intentionally to give a distinctive look to the shuttle. This feature has been called 'teardrop' and allowed _Discovery_ to be told apart from the rest of the fleet without looking at its name, although often unnoticed by the uninitiated.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-14)

The spacecraft weighed roughly 6,870 lb (3,120 kg) less than _Columbia_ when it was brought into service due to optimalizations determined during the construction and testing of _Enterprise_, _Columbia_ and _Challenger_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)_Discovery_ weighs 6 pounds (2.7 kg) heavier than _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ and 363 pounds (165 kg) heavier than _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ after further weight-saving adjustments were made.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-FT_facts-15)

Part of the _Discovery_ weight optimizations included the greater use of quilted [AFRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Flexible_Insulation_Blankets/Advanced_Flexible_Reusable_Insulation_(FIB/AFRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") blankets rather than the white [LRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Low-temperature_reusable_surface_insulation_(LRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") tiles on the fuselage, and the use of [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") instead of aluminum for the payload bay doors and some of the wing spars and beams.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-16)

Upon its delivery to the Kennedy Space Center in 1983, _Discovery_ was modified alongside _Challenger_ to accommodate the liquid-fueled [Centaur-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centaur-G "Centaur-G") booster, which had been planned for use beginning in 1986 but was cancelled in the wake of the _Challenger_ disaster.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-17)

Beginning in late 1995, the orbiter underwent a nine-month Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). This included outfitting the vehicle with a fifth set of cryogenic tanks and an external airlock to support missions to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). As with all the orbiters, it could be attached to the top of specialized aircraft and did so in June 1996 when it returned to the Kennedy Space Center, and later in April 2012 when sent to the Udvar-Hazy Center, riding [piggy-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggy-back_(transportation) "Piggy-back (transportation)") on a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)

After [STS-105](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105 "STS-105"), _Discovery_ became the first of the orbiter fleet to undergo Orbiter Major Modification (OMM) period at the Kennedy Space Center. Work began in September 2002 to prepare the vehicle for Return to Flight. The work included scheduled upgrades and additional safety modifications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-over-10)

_Discovery_ was [decommissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_decommissioning "Ship decommissioning") on March 9, 2011.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-manifest-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-CSCS1-20) NASA offered _Discovery_ to the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") for public display and preservation, after a month-long [decontamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contamination_control "Contamination control") process,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-21) as part of the national collection.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-smithsonian-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-smithsonian-houston-chronical-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-24)_Discovery_ replaced [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), which was in the Smithsonian's display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until 2011.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-27)_Discovery_ was transported to [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") on April 17, 2012, and was transferred to the Udvar-Hazy Center on April 19 where a welcome ceremony was held. Afterwards, at around 5:30 pm, _Discovery_ was rolled to its "final wheels stop" in the Udvar-Hazy Center.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-29)

Texas senators [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") added a provision to the 2025 [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") to spend $85 million to relocate a space vehicle that has flown astronauts into space, presumably _Discovery_ because of the sponsors of the provision and previous legislation attempts, from the Udvar-Hazy Center to the [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston") Museum in Texas.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-31) While the Smithsonian estimated that the total cost of the transfer would be approximately $325 million, they also countered that ownership of the shuttle had been transferred to the museum and was no longer federal property, and that Congress did not have the ability to force a transfer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-33)

## Flights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Flights")]

By its last mission, _Discovery_ had flown 149 million mi (240 million km) in 39 missions, completed 5,830 orbits, and spent 365 days in orbit over 27 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-slt-34)_Discovery_ flew [more flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbiter#Flight_statistics "Space Shuttle Orbiter") than any other Orbiter Shuttle, including four in 1985 alone. _Discovery_ flew both "return to flight" missions after the _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster")_ and _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster")_ disasters: [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") in 1988, [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005, and [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") in 2006. _Discovery_ flew the ante-penultimate mission of the Space Shuttle program, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), having launched on February 24, 2011. _Endeavour_ flew [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") and _Atlantis_ performed [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), NASA's last Space Shuttle mission. On February 24, 2011, Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39-A to begin its final orbital flight.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-ares6-35)

## Flow directors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Flow directors")]

The Flow Director was responsible for the overall preparation of the shuttle for launch and processing it after landing, and remained permanently assigned to head the spacecraft's ground crew while the astronaut flight crews changed for every mission. Each shuttle's Flow Director was supported by a Vehicle Manager for the same spacecraft. Space Shuttle _Discovery'_ s Flow Directors were:

*   Until 01/1991: John J. "Tip" Talone Jr. (afterwards Flow Director for _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   01/1991 – 09/1992: John C. "Chris" Fairey[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   09/1992 – 10/1996: [David A. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_A._King_(engineer) "David A. King (engineer)")[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-39)
*   10/1996 – 05/2000: W. Scott Cilento[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-40)
*   12/2000 – 03/2011: Stephanie S. Stilson[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(space_shuttle)#cite_note-41)

**STS-51-C** (formerly STS-10) was the 15th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the third flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. It launched on January 24, 1985, and made the fourth shuttle landing at the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") on January 27, 1985. STS-51-C was the first shuttle mission dedicated to the [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD), and consequently many details remain classified. NASA reported that a satellite ([USA-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites")) was deployed during the mission using an [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") booster and met mission objectives. At just over three days, the mission was shorter in duration than most civilian missions and was the shortest of _Discovery_'s career.

STS-51-C launched from Kennedy Space Center (KSC) on January 24, 1985, at 19:50:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time"), and was the first of nine shuttle missions in 1985. It was originally scheduled for January 23, 1985, but was delayed because of freezing weather. [_Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger") had been scheduled for this flight, but _Discovery_ was substituted when problems were encountered with _Challenger's_[thermal protection tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system"). STS-51-C marked the 100th [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_human_spaceflights "List of human spaceflights") to achieve orbit.

The mission's length of three days was shorter than the week or longer of most civilian shuttle flights. It was the first dedicated to the [U.S. Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-blakeslee-5) and most information about it remains classified. For the first time, NASA did not provide pre-launch commentary to the public until nine minutes before liftoff.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-Uri-3) The [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") only stated that the shuttle successfully launched its payload with an [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS) on the mission's seventh orbit. It is believed that the payload was a [Magnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_(satellite) "Magnum (satellite)")[SIGINT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signals_intelligence "Signals intelligence") satellite into [geosynchronous orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-6) Other DoD flights [STS-33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-33 "STS-33") and [STS-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-38 "STS-38") could have carried similar payloads. Payton stated in 2009 that STS-51-C's payload is "still up there, and still operating".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-cassutt200908-7) Payton was a USAF [Manned Spaceflight Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Spaceflight_Engineer "Manned Spaceflight Engineer") (MSE); the USAF declined a NASA offer to fly another MSE on the mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-cassutt1989-8)

Also, according to _Aviation Week_, the shuttle initially entered a 204×519 km (127×322 mi) orbit, at an [inclination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_inclination "Orbital inclination") of 28.45° to the [equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator "Equator"). It then executed three [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") (OMS) burns, the last being executed on the fourth orbit. The first burn was conducted to circularize the shuttle's orbit at 519 km (322 mi).

The mission lasted 3 days, 1 hour, 33 minutes, and 23 seconds. _Discovery_ touched down on [SLF Runway 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at KSC on January 27, 1985, at 21:23:23 UTC. IMAX footage of the STS-51-C launch was used in the 1985 movie _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_.

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-C&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The crew insignia for STS Flight 51-C includes the names of its five crewmembers. The STS 51-C mission marked the third trip of the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ into space, which is referenced by the three colored trailing strips behind the orbiter in the United States red, white and blue. It was the first Space Shuttle mission totally dedicated to the U.S. Department of Defense, hence the DoD central eagle on the mission patch. The five stars on the upper part of the golden band of the DoD insignia represent the five astronauts. As this mission was classified, the patch includes no further detail as to the mission's payload or nature. For similar reasons, the name of the used orbiter was omitted from the patch.

## Connection to the _Challenger_ disaster

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-C&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Connection to the Challenger disaster")]

Almost exactly a year after STS-51-C, [Space Shuttle _Challenger_ was destroyed with all hands on board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") during the [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") mission including [Ellison Onizuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellison_Onizuka "Ellison Onizuka"), a crew member on both flights. As part of the investigation into the disaster, it was reported to the [Rogers Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers_Commission_Report "Rogers Commission Report") that during the launch of STS-51-C, the worst [Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster") (SRB) blow-by effects of any mission prior to STS-51-L occurred, indicating conclusively that the [Viton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FKM "FKM")[O-rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-ring "O-ring") were not sufficiently sealing the hot gases inside the [combustion chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combustion_chamber "Combustion chamber") of the SRBs while firing. After they were recovered post-flight, the O-rings in both the right and left SRBs showed some degree of charring, but analysis of the center field joint of the right SRB showed an unprecedented penetration of the primary O-ring and heavy charring on the secondary O-ring.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-Rogers_vol6-9)

This information is significant to the established consensus that low air temperature was a major factor in _Challenger_'s destruction because the temperature at STS-51-C's launch was also, up to its time, the coldest recorded during a shuttle launch, at only 12°C (54°F).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-Rogers_vol6-9)

**STS-51-C** (formerly STS-10) was the 15th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the third flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. It launched on January 24, 1985, and made the fourth shuttle landing at the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") on January 27, 1985. STS-51-C was the first shuttle mission dedicated to the [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD), and consequently many details remain classified. NASA reported that a satellite ([USA-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites")) was deployed during the mission using an [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") booster and met mission objectives. At just over three days, the mission was shorter in duration than most civilian missions and was the shortest of _Discovery_'s career.

Launch of STS-51-C as seen from an IMAX camera attached to the Fixed Service Structure

STS-51-C launched from Kennedy Space Center (KSC) on January 24, 1985, at 19:50:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time"), and was the first of nine shuttle missions in 1985. It was originally scheduled for January 23, 1985, but was delayed because of freezing weather. [_Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger") had been scheduled for this flight, but _Discovery_ was substituted when problems were encountered with _Challenger's_[thermal protection tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system"). STS-51-C marked the 100th [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_human_spaceflights "List of human spaceflights") to achieve orbit.

The mission's length of three days was shorter than the week or longer of most civilian shuttle flights. It was the first dedicated to the [U.S. Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-blakeslee-5) and most information about it remains classified. For the first time, NASA did not provide pre-launch commentary to the public until nine minutes before liftoff.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-Uri-3) The [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") only stated that the shuttle successfully launched its payload with an [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS) on the mission's seventh orbit. It is believed that the payload was a [Magnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_(satellite) "Magnum (satellite)")[SIGINT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signals_intelligence "Signals intelligence") satellite into [geosynchronous orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-6) Other DoD flights [STS-33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-33 "STS-33") and [STS-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-38 "STS-38") could have carried similar payloads. Payton stated in 2009 that STS-51-C's payload is "still up there, and still operating".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-cassutt200908-7) Payton was a USAF [Manned Spaceflight Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Spaceflight_Engineer "Manned Spaceflight Engineer") (MSE); the USAF declined a NASA offer to fly another MSE on the mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-cassutt1989-8)

Also, according to _Aviation Week_, the shuttle initially entered a 204×519 km (127×322 mi) orbit, at an [inclination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_inclination "Orbital inclination") of 28.45° to the [equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator "Equator"). It then executed three [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") (OMS) burns, the last being executed on the fourth orbit. The first burn was conducted to circularize the shuttle's orbit at 519 km (322 mi).

The mission lasted 3 days, 1 hour, 33 minutes, and 23 seconds. _Discovery_ touched down on [SLF Runway 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at KSC on January 27, 1985, at 21:23:23 UTC. IMAX footage of the STS-51-C launch was used in the 1985 movie _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_.

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-C&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The crew insignia for STS Flight 51-C includes the names of its five crewmembers. The STS 51-C mission marked the third trip of the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ into space, which is referenced by the three colored trailing strips behind the orbiter in the United States red, white and blue. It was the first Space Shuttle mission totally dedicated to the U.S. Department of Defense, hence the DoD central eagle on the mission patch. The five stars on the upper part of the golden band of the DoD insignia represent the five astronauts. As this mission was classified, the patch includes no further detail as to the mission's payload or nature. For similar reasons, the name of the used orbiter was omitted from the patch.

## Connection to the _Challenger_ disaster

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-C&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Connection to the Challenger disaster")]

Almost exactly a year after STS-51-C, [Space Shuttle _Challenger_ was destroyed with all hands on board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") during the [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") mission including [Ellison Onizuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellison_Onizuka "Ellison Onizuka"), a crew member on both flights. As part of the investigation into the disaster, it was reported to the [Rogers Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers_Commission_Report "Rogers Commission Report") that during the launch of STS-51-C, the worst [Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster") (SRB) blow-by effects of any mission prior to STS-51-L occurred, indicating conclusively that the [Viton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FKM "FKM")[O-rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-ring "O-ring") were not sufficiently sealing the hot gases inside the [combustion chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combustion_chamber "Combustion chamber") of the SRBs while firing. After they were recovered post-flight, the O-rings in both the right and left SRBs showed some degree of charring, but analysis of the center field joint of the right SRB showed an unprecedented penetration of the primary O-ring and heavy charring on the secondary O-ring.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-Rogers_vol6-9)

This information is significant to the established consensus that low air temperature was a major factor in _Challenger_'s destruction because the temperature at STS-51-C's launch was also, up to its time, the coldest recorded during a shuttle launch, at only 12°C (54°F).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C#cite_note-Rogers_vol6-9)

**STS-51-D** was the 16th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the fourth flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-press_kit-2) The launch of STS-51-D from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on April 12, 1985, was delayed by 55 minutes, after a boat strayed into the restricted [Solid Rocket Booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_Rocket_Booster "Solid Rocket Booster") (SRB) recovery zone. STS-51-D was the third shuttle mission to be extended.

On April 19, 1985, after a week-long flight, _Discovery_ conducted the fifth shuttle landing at KSC. The shuttle suffered extensive brake damage and a ruptured tire during landing. This forced shuttle landings to be done at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") for the next five years until the development and implementation of nose wheel steering made landings at KSC more feasible.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-D&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

During STS-51-D, the shuttle crew deployed two [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"): Telesat-I ([Anik C1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anik_(satellite) "Anik (satellite)")) and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-3 (also known as [Leasat-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom")); both were Hughes-built satellites. Telesat-I was attached to a [Payload Assist Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Assist_Module "Payload Assist Module") (PAM-D) motor and successfully deployed. [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-3, however, failed to initiate antenna deployment and spin-up, or ignite its [perigee kick motor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apogee_kick_motor "Apogee kick motor") upon deployment. The mission was consequently extended by two days to ensure that the satellite's spacecraft sequencer start lever was in its proper position. Griggs and Hoffman performed an unscheduled [Extravehicular Activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") (EVA) to attach homemade "Flyswatter" devices to the shuttle's Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")). Seddon then engaged the satellite's start lever using the RMS, but again the post-deployment sequence did not begin.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-walker20050414-4) The satellite was subsequently retrieved, repaired and successfully redeployed during the [STS-51-I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I "STS-51-I") mission later that year.

_Discovery_'s other mission payloads included the Continuous Flow Electrophoresis System III (CFES-III), which was flying for the sixth time; two Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) experiments; the American Flight Echo-cardiograph (AFE); two [Getaway specials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getaway_special "Getaway special") (GASs); a set of Phase Partitioning Experiments (PPE); an astronomical photography verification test; various medical experiments; and "Toys in Space", an informal study of the behavior of simple toys in a [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") environment, with the results being made available to school students upon the shuttle's return.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-5)

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 33 of the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at Kennedy Space Center at 13:54:28 UTC (8:54:28 am EST local time at the landing site). As the orbiter approached the runway, it was buffeted by a 10-mile-per-hour (16 km/h; 8.7 kn)[crosswind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosswind "Crosswind") from the right, which pushed the orbiter 19 feet (5.8 m) left of the runway's [center line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway#Markings "Runway") as the rear landing gear touched down. As the orbiter rolled out, the crosswind continued to push it towards the left, causing it to drift 65 feet (20 m) from the center line of the 300-foot-wide (91 m) runway. At this point, Commander Bobko began to counteract the drift by applying more pressure to the right-wheel brakes, a technique called [differential steering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_steering "Differential steering"), which brought the orbiter back to the center of the runway. However, he had to apply twice as much force to the right brakes and about 134 feet (41 m) before stopping the brakes on the right-side inboard tire locked up and 5 feet (1.5 m) before stopping the brakes on the right-side outboard tire locked up and the inboard tire blew. The incident prompted NASA to add nose wheel steering to the orbiters, which was complete by late 1985.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-6) Until that work was completed, NASA would land the orbiters at the Edwards Air Force Base which offered the option of landing on a long and wide dry lake bed from more directions. Nose wheel steering was also implemented shortly before the Challenger disaster, which would ground the shuttle program for a time. Ultimately, it would be five years until a mission would again land at the SLF, when [STS-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-38 "STS-38") had to divert there due to bad weather at Edwards.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-D&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-chronology-7)

**STS-51-D** was the 16th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the fourth flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-press_kit-2) The launch of STS-51-D from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on April 12, 1985, was delayed by 55 minutes, after a boat strayed into the restricted [Solid Rocket Booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_Rocket_Booster "Solid Rocket Booster") (SRB) recovery zone. STS-51-D was the third shuttle mission to be extended.

On April 19, 1985, after a week-long flight, _Discovery_ conducted the fifth shuttle landing at KSC. The shuttle suffered extensive brake damage and a ruptured tire during landing. This forced shuttle landings to be done at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") for the next five years until the development and implementation of nose wheel steering made landings at KSC more feasible.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-D&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

During STS-51-D, the shuttle crew deployed two [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"): Telesat-I ([Anik C1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anik_(satellite) "Anik (satellite)")) and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-3 (also known as [Leasat-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom")); both were Hughes-built satellites. Telesat-I was attached to a [Payload Assist Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Assist_Module "Payload Assist Module") (PAM-D) motor and successfully deployed. [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-3, however, failed to initiate antenna deployment and spin-up, or ignite its [perigee kick motor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apogee_kick_motor "Apogee kick motor") upon deployment. The mission was consequently extended by two days to ensure that the satellite's spacecraft sequencer start lever was in its proper position. Griggs and Hoffman performed an unscheduled [Extravehicular Activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") (EVA) to attach homemade "Flyswatter" devices to the shuttle's Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")). Seddon then engaged the satellite's start lever using the RMS, but again the post-deployment sequence did not begin.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-walker20050414-4) The satellite was subsequently retrieved, repaired and successfully redeployed during the [STS-51-I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I "STS-51-I") mission later that year.

_Discovery_'s other mission payloads included the Continuous Flow Electrophoresis System III (CFES-III), which was flying for the sixth time; two Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) experiments; the American Flight Echo-cardiograph (AFE); two [Getaway specials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getaway_special "Getaway special") (GASs); a set of Phase Partitioning Experiments (PPE); an astronomical photography verification test; various medical experiments; and "Toys in Space", an informal study of the behavior of simple toys in a [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") environment, with the results being made available to school students upon the shuttle's return.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-5)

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 33 of the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at Kennedy Space Center at 13:54:28 UTC (8:54:28 am EST local time at the landing site). As the orbiter approached the runway, it was buffeted by a 10-mile-per-hour (16 km/h; 8.7 kn)[crosswind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosswind "Crosswind") from the right, which pushed the orbiter 19 feet (5.8 m) left of the runway's [center line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway#Markings "Runway") as the rear landing gear touched down. As the orbiter rolled out, the crosswind continued to push it towards the left, causing it to drift 65 feet (20 m) from the center line of the 300-foot-wide (91 m) runway. At this point, Commander Bobko began to counteract the drift by applying more pressure to the right-wheel brakes, a technique called [differential steering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_steering "Differential steering"), which brought the orbiter back to the center of the runway. However, he had to apply twice as much force to the right brakes and about 134 feet (41 m) before stopping the brakes on the right-side inboard tire locked up and 5 feet (1.5 m) before stopping the brakes on the right-side outboard tire locked up and the inboard tire blew. The incident prompted NASA to add nose wheel steering to the orbiters, which was complete by late 1985.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-6) Until that work was completed, NASA would land the orbiters at the Edwards Air Force Base which offered the option of landing on a long and wide dry lake bed from more directions. Nose wheel steering was also implemented shortly before the Challenger disaster, which would ground the shuttle program for a time. Ultimately, it would be five years until a mission would again land at the SLF, when [STS-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-38 "STS-38") had to divert there due to bad weather at Edwards.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-D&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-D#cite_note-chronology-7)

**STS-51-G** was the 18th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the fifth flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. The seven-day mission launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on June 17, 1985, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on June 24, 1985. [Sultan bin Salman Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_bin_Salman_Al_Saud "Sultan bin Salman Al Saud") from [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") was on board as a [payload specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_specialist "Payload specialist"); Al Saud became the first [Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab "Arab"), the first [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim"), and the first member of a [royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_family "Royal family") to fly into space.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G#cite_note-ARAMCO-2) It was also the first Space Shuttle mission which flew without at least one astronaut from the pre-Shuttle era among its crew.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-G&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

_Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A"), [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC), at 7:33 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on June 17, 1985. The mission's crew members included [Daniel C. Brandenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Brandenstein "Daniel Brandenstein"), commander; [John O. Creighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Oliver_Creighton "John Oliver Creighton"), pilot; [Shannon W. Lucid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Lucid "Shannon Lucid"), [Steven R. Nagel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_R._Nagel "Steven R. Nagel"), and [John M. Fabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Fabian "John M. Fabian"), mission specialists; and [Patrick Baudry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Baudry "Patrick Baudry"), from [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), and Prince Sultan [Sultan bin Salman Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_bin_Salman_Al_Saud "Sultan bin Salman Al Saud"), from [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), both payload specialists.

STS-51-G carried three [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") as its primary cargo. These were [Arabsat-1B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabsat-1B "Arabsat-1B") ([Arab Satellite Communications Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Satellite_Communications_Organization "Arab Satellite Communications Organization")); [Morelos-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morelos_Satellite_System "Morelos Satellite System") ([Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")); and [Telstar-303](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telstar_303 "Telstar 303") ([AT&T Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT&T_Corporation "AT&T Corporation")). All three successfully utilized [Payload Assist Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Assist_Module "Payload Assist Module") (PAM-D) booster stages to achieve [geostationary transfer orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geostationary_transfer_orbit "Geostationary transfer orbit") (GTO) after being deployed from _Discovery_.

Also carried was the SPARTAN-1 (Shuttle Pointed Autonomous Research Tool for AstroNomy) a deployable/retrievable carrier module, designed to be deployed from the orbiter and fly free in space before being retrieved. SPARTAN-1 included 140 kg (310 lb) of astronomy experiments. It was deployed and operated successfully, independent of the orbiter, before being retrieved. _Discovery_ furthermore carried an experimental materials-processing furnace, two French biomedical experiments (French Echocardiograph Experiment (FEE) and French Postural Experiment (FPE)),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G#cite_note-SF51G-3) and six [Getaway Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getaway_Special "Getaway Special") (GAS) experiments, which were all successfully performed, although the GO34 Getaway Special shut down prematurely. This mission was also the first flight test of the OEX advanced autopilot which gave the orbiter capabilities above and beyond those of the baseline system.

The mission's final payload element was a High Precision Tracking Experiment (HPTE) for the [Strategic Defense Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Defense_Initiative "Strategic Defense Initiative") (SDI) (nicknamed "Star Wars"); the HPTE failed to deploy properly during its first try on the mission's 37th orbit, because the orbiter was not at the correct attitude. It was successfully deployed on orbit 64.

_Discovery_ landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 9:11:52 a.m. EDT on June 24, 1985, after a mission duration of 7 days, 1 hour, 38 minutes, and 52 seconds.

## Mission Insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-G&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission Insignia")]

The STS-51-G insignia illustrates the advances in aviation technology in the United States within a relatively short span of the twentieth century with _Discovery_ flying over the _[Wright Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright\_Flyer "Wright Flyer")_. A gold-and-orange-flame eagle forms the base of the insigna. The surnames of the crewmembers for the _Discovery_'s mission appear near the center edge of the circular design, with the French and Saudi crewmembers added below, with a respective flag icon along their name. Although Baudry was the first French citizen to fly with a Space Shuttle mission into space, he was only the second Frenchman to go to space, following [Jean-Loup Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean-Loup Chrétien")'s earlier missions with [Soyuz capsule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)"), [Soyuz T-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6 "Soyuz T-6").

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-G&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G#cite_note-chronology-4)

**STS-51-G** was the 18th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the fifth flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. The seven-day mission launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on June 17, 1985, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on June 24, 1985. [Sultan bin Salman Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_bin_Salman_Al_Saud "Sultan bin Salman Al Saud") from [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") was on board as a [payload specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_specialist "Payload specialist"); Al Saud became the first [Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab "Arab"), the first [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim"), and the first member of a [royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_family "Royal family") to fly into space.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G#cite_note-ARAMCO-2) It was also the first Space Shuttle mission which flew without at least one astronaut from the pre-Shuttle era among its crew.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-G&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

_Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A"), [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC), at 7:33 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on June 17, 1985. The mission's crew members included [Daniel C. Brandenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Brandenstein "Daniel Brandenstein"), commander; [John O. Creighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Oliver_Creighton "John Oliver Creighton"), pilot; [Shannon W. Lucid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Lucid "Shannon Lucid"), [Steven R. Nagel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_R._Nagel "Steven R. Nagel"), and [John M. Fabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Fabian "John M. Fabian"), mission specialists; and [Patrick Baudry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Baudry "Patrick Baudry"), from [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), and Prince Sultan [Sultan bin Salman Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_bin_Salman_Al_Saud "Sultan bin Salman Al Saud"), from [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), both payload specialists.

STS-51-G carried three [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") as its primary cargo. These were [Arabsat-1B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabsat-1B "Arabsat-1B") ([Arab Satellite Communications Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Satellite_Communications_Organization "Arab Satellite Communications Organization")); [Morelos-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morelos_Satellite_System "Morelos Satellite System") ([Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")); and [Telstar-303](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telstar_303 "Telstar 303") ([AT&T Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT&T_Corporation "AT&T Corporation")). All three successfully utilized [Payload Assist Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Assist_Module "Payload Assist Module") (PAM-D) booster stages to achieve [geostationary transfer orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geostationary_transfer_orbit "Geostationary transfer orbit") (GTO) after being deployed from _Discovery_.

Also carried was the SPARTAN-1 (Shuttle Pointed Autonomous Research Tool for AstroNomy) a deployable/retrievable carrier module, designed to be deployed from the orbiter and fly free in space before being retrieved. SPARTAN-1 included 140 kg (310 lb) of astronomy experiments. It was deployed and operated successfully, independent of the orbiter, before being retrieved. _Discovery_ furthermore carried an experimental materials-processing furnace, two French biomedical experiments (French Echocardiograph Experiment (FEE) and French Postural Experiment (FPE)),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G#cite_note-SF51G-3) and six [Getaway Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getaway_Special "Getaway Special") (GAS) experiments, which were all successfully performed, although the GO34 Getaway Special shut down prematurely. This mission was also the first flight test of the OEX advanced autopilot which gave the orbiter capabilities above and beyond those of the baseline system.

The mission's final payload element was a High Precision Tracking Experiment (HPTE) for the [Strategic Defense Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Defense_Initiative "Strategic Defense Initiative") (SDI) (nicknamed "Star Wars"); the HPTE failed to deploy properly during its first try on the mission's 37th orbit, because the orbiter was not at the correct attitude. It was successfully deployed on orbit 64.

_Discovery_ landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 9:11:52 a.m. EDT on June 24, 1985, after a mission duration of 7 days, 1 hour, 38 minutes, and 52 seconds.

## Mission Insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-G&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission Insignia")]

The STS-51-G insignia illustrates the advances in aviation technology in the United States within a relatively short span of the twentieth century with _Discovery_ flying over the _[Wright Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright\_Flyer "Wright Flyer")_. A gold-and-orange-flame eagle forms the base of the insigna. The surnames of the crewmembers for the _Discovery_'s mission appear near the center edge of the circular design, with the French and Saudi crewmembers added below, with a respective flag icon along their name. Although Baudry was the first French citizen to fly with a Space Shuttle mission into space, he was only the second Frenchman to go to space, following [Jean-Loup Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean-Loup Chrétien")'s earlier missions with [Soyuz capsule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)"), [Soyuz T-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6 "Soyuz T-6").

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-G&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G#cite_note-chronology-4)

**STS-51-I** was the 20th mission of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") program and the sixth flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. During the mission, _Discovery_ deployed three [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") into orbit. The mission launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on August 27, 1985, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on September 3, 1985.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-I&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

_Discovery_ launched at 6:58 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on August 27, 1985. Two earlier launch attempts, one on August 24 and another on August 25, were scrubbed – the first because of poor weather,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I#cite_note-3) and the second because the backup orbiter computer failed and had to be replaced.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I#cite_note-4) The successful launch on August 27, 1985, took place just as an approaching [storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") front reached the launch pad area.

The five-man STS-51-I crew included Joe H. Engle, commander; Richard O. Covey, pilot; and James D. A. van Hoften, John M. Lounge, and William F. Fisher, mission specialists. Their primary mission was to deploy three [commercial communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") and retrieve and repair the [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-3 (Leasat-3) satellite, which had been deployed during the STS-51-D mission in April 1985, but had malfunctioned. In addition, a mid-deck materials processing experiment, the Physical Vapor Transport Organic Solid Experiment (PVTOS), was flown aboard _Discovery_.

The three communications satellites were [Aussat-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optus_(satellite) "Optus (satellite)"), a multi-purpose spacecraft owned by [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"); ASC-1, owned and operated by the [American Satellite Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Satellite_Corporation "American Satellite Corporation") (ASC); and Syncom IV-4 ([Leasat-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom")), leased to the [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD) by its builder, [Hughes Space and Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Space_and_Communications "Hughes Space and Communications"). Both Aussat-1 and ASC-1 were deployed on the day of the launch, August 27, 1985. Syncom IV-4 (Leasat-4) was deployed two days later. All three achieved their planned [geosynchronous orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit") and became operational.

On the fifth day of the mission, astronauts Fisher and van Hoften began repair efforts on the malfunctioning Syncom IV-3, following a successful rendezvous maneuver by _Discovery_. The effort was slowed by a problem with the Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) elbow joint. After a second EVA by Fisher and van Hoften, the satellite's control lever was repaired, permitting commands from the ground to activate the spacecraft's systems and eventually send it into its proper geosynchronous orbit. The two EVAs lasted a total of 11 hours and 46 minutes.

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 23 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 6:16 a.m. [PDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") on September 3, 1985. The flight lasted a total of 7 days, 2 hours, 18 minutes and 42 seconds, during which the shuttle completed 112 orbits of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-I&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The insignia depicts an American [bald eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bald_eagle "Bald eagle"), trailing red and white stripes, and pushing a boundary layer forward. The 19 stars, along with the eagle, are references to the 20th shuttle mission (with the eagle representing the orbiter and thus being the 20th "star"). Lining the patch are the surnames of the crew members.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-I&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I#cite_note-chronology-5)

**STS-51-I** was the 20th mission of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") program and the sixth flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. During the mission, _Discovery_ deployed three [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") into orbit. The mission launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on August 27, 1985, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on September 3, 1985.
