## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-I&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

_Discovery_ launched at 6:58 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on August 27, 1985. Two earlier launch attempts, one on August 24 and another on August 25, were scrubbed – the first because of poor weather,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I#cite_note-3) and the second because the backup orbiter computer failed and had to be replaced.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I#cite_note-4) The successful launch on August 27, 1985, took place just as an approaching [storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") front reached the launch pad area.

The five-man STS-51-I crew included Joe H. Engle, commander; Richard O. Covey, pilot; and James D. A. van Hoften, John M. Lounge, and William F. Fisher, mission specialists. Their primary mission was to deploy three [commercial communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") and retrieve and repair the [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-3 (Leasat-3) satellite, which had been deployed during the STS-51-D mission in April 1985, but had malfunctioned. In addition, a mid-deck materials processing experiment, the Physical Vapor Transport Organic Solid Experiment (PVTOS), was flown aboard _Discovery_.

The three communications satellites were [Aussat-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optus_(satellite) "Optus (satellite)"), a multi-purpose spacecraft owned by [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"); ASC-1, owned and operated by the [American Satellite Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Satellite_Corporation "American Satellite Corporation") (ASC); and Syncom IV-4 ([Leasat-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom")), leased to the [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD) by its builder, [Hughes Space and Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Space_and_Communications "Hughes Space and Communications"). Both Aussat-1 and ASC-1 were deployed on the day of the launch, August 27, 1985. Syncom IV-4 (Leasat-4) was deployed two days later. All three achieved their planned [geosynchronous orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit") and became operational.

On the fifth day of the mission, astronauts Fisher and van Hoften began repair efforts on the malfunctioning Syncom IV-3, following a successful rendezvous maneuver by _Discovery_. The effort was slowed by a problem with the Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) elbow joint. After a second EVA by Fisher and van Hoften, the satellite's control lever was repaired, permitting commands from the ground to activate the spacecraft's systems and eventually send it into its proper geosynchronous orbit. The two EVAs lasted a total of 11 hours and 46 minutes.

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 23 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 6:16 a.m. [PDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") on September 3, 1985. The flight lasted a total of 7 days, 2 hours, 18 minutes and 42 seconds, during which the shuttle completed 112 orbits of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-I&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The insignia depicts an American [bald eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bald_eagle "Bald eagle"), trailing red and white stripes, and pushing a boundary layer forward. The 19 stars, along with the eagle, are references to the 20th shuttle mission (with the eagle representing the orbiter and thus being the 20th "star"). Lining the patch are the surnames of the crew members.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-51-I&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-I#cite_note-chronology-5)

The **Space Shuttle program** was the fourth [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight "Human spaceflight") program carried out by the U.S. [National Aeronautics and Space Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Aeronautics_and_Space_Administration "National Aeronautics and Space Administration") (NASA), which accomplished routine transportation for Earth-to-orbit crew and cargo from 1981 to 2011. Its official program name was carried over from the 1969 plan for the [Space Transportation System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System "Space Transportation System") (STS) of reusable spacecraft. Only the shuttle and supporting rockets were funded for development; a proposed nuclear lunar shuttle in the plan was canceled in 1972.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-autogenerated1-3) It flew 135 missions and carried 355 astronauts from 16 countries, many on multiple trips.

The [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), composed of an orbiter launched with two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster") and a disposable [external fuel tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_fuel_tank "External fuel tank"), carried up to eight [astronauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") and up to 50,000 lb (23,000 kg) of [payload](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload "Payload") into [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit") (LEO). When its mission was complete, the orbiter would [reenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_reentry "Atmospheric reentry") the Earth's atmosphere and land like a [glider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glider_(aircraft) "Glider (aircraft)") at either the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") or [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base").

The Shuttle is the only winged crewed spacecraft to have achieved orbit and landing, and the first reusable crewed space vehicle that made multiple flights into orbit.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-4)Its missions involved carrying large payloads to various orbits including the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS), providing crew rotation for the space station, and performing service missions on the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope"). The orbiter also recovered [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite") and other payloads (e.g., from the ISS) from orbit and returned them to Earth, though its use in this capacity was rare. Each vehicle was designed with a projected lifespan of 100 launches, or 10 years' operational life. Original selling points on the shuttles were over 150 launches over a 15-year operational span with a 'launch per month' expected at the peak of the program, but extensive delays in the development of the International Space Station[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-iss-casis.org-5) never created such a peak demand for frequent flights.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Various shuttle concepts had been explored since the late 1960s. The program formally commenced in 1972, becoming the sole focus of NASA's [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight "Human spaceflight") operations after the [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program "Apollo program"), [Skylab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skylab "Skylab"), and [Apollo–Soyuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo%E2%80%93Soyuz "Apollo–Soyuz") programs in 1975. The Shuttle was originally conceived of and presented to the public in 1972 as a 'Space Truck' which would, among other things, be used to build a United States space station in [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit") during the 1980s and then be replaced by a new vehicle by the early 1990s. The stalled plans for a U.S. space station evolved into the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") and were formally initiated in 1983 by President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan"), but the ISS suffered from long delays, design changes and cost over-runs[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-iss-casis.org-5) and forced the service life of the Space Shuttle to be extended several times until 2011 when it was finally retired—serving twice as long as it was originally designed to do. In 2004, according to President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush")'s [Vision for Space Exploration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vision_for_Space_Exploration "Vision for Space Exploration"), use of the Space Shuttle was to be focused almost exclusively on completing assembly of the ISS, which was far behind schedule at that point.

The first experimental orbiter, [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), was a high-altitude glider, launched from the back of a specially modified Boeing 747, only for [initial atmospheric landing tests (ALT)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests"). _Enterprise'_ s first test flight was on February 18, 1977, only five years after the Shuttle program was formally initiated; leading to the launch of the first space-worthy shuttle _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ on April 12, 1981, on [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1"). The Space Shuttle program finished with its last mission, [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135") flown by [_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis"), in July 2011, retiring the final Shuttle in the fleet. The Space Shuttle program formally ended on August 31, 2011.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-6)

## Conception and development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Conception and development")]

This section is an excerpt from [Space Shuttle design process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_design_process "Space Shuttle design process").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_design_process&action=edit)]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Space_Shuttle_concepts.jpg/250px-Space_Shuttle_concepts.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Space_Shuttle_concepts.jpg)

Early U.S. space shuttle concepts

Before the [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11")[Moon landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crewed_Moon_landings "Crewed Moon landings") in [1969](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_in_spaceflight "1969 in spaceflight"), [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") began studies of [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") designs as early as October 1968. The early studies were denoted "Phase A", and in June 1970, "Phase B", which were more detailed and specific. The primary intended use of the Phase A Space Shuttle was supporting the future [space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station"), ferrying a minimum crew of four and about 20,000 pounds (9,100 kg) of cargo, and being able to be rapidly turned around for future flights, with larger payloads like space station modules being lifted by the [Saturn V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V "Saturn V").

Two designs emerged as front-runners. One was designed by engineers at the [Manned Spaceflight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_Space_Center "Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center"), and championed especially by [George Mueller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mueller_(NASA) "George Mueller (NASA)"). This was a two-stage system with delta-winged spacecraft, and generally complex. An attempt to re-simplify was made in the form of the [DC-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_DC-3 "North American DC-3"), designed by [Maxime Faget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Faget "Maxime Faget"), who had designed the Mercury capsule among other vehicles. Numerous offerings from a variety of commercial companies were also considered but generally fell by the wayside as each NASA lab pushed for its own version.

All of this was taking place in the midst of other NASA teams proposing a wide variety of post-Apollo missions, a number of which would cost as much as Apollo or more.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] As each of these projects fought for funding, the NASA budget was at the same time being severely constrained. Three were eventually presented to United States [Vice President Spiro Agnew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiro_T._Agnew "Spiro T. Agnew") in 1969. The shuttle project rose to the top, largely due to tireless campaigning by its supporters.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] By 1970 the shuttle had been selected as the one major project for the short-term post-Apollo time frame.

When funding for the program came into question, there were concerns that the project might be canceled. This became especially pressing as it became clear that the [Saturn V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V "Saturn V") would no longer be produced, which meant that the payload to orbit needed to be increased in both mass - all the way to 60,600 pounds (27,500 kg) - and size to supplement its heavy-lift capabilities, necessary for planned interplanetary probes and space station modules, which meant a bigger and costlier vehicle was needed during Phase B. Therefore, NASA tried to interest the [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") and a variety of other customers in using the shuttle for their missions as well. To lower the development costs of the proposed designs, boosters were added, a throw-away fuel tank was adopted, and many other changes were made that greatly lowered the reusability and greatly added to the vehicle and operational costs.

Shuttle approach and landing test crews, 1976

All Space Shuttle missions were launched from the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC) in Florida. Some civilian and military circumpolar Space Shuttle missions were planned for [Vandenberg AFB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base#Space_Shuttle "Vandenberg Air Force Base") in California. However, the use of Vandenberg AFB for Space Shuttle missions was canceled after the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986. The [weather criteria used for launch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_launch_commit_criteria "Space Shuttle launch commit criteria") included, but were not limited to: precipitation, temperatures, cloud cover, lightning forecast, wind, and humidity.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-weather_launch_criteria-7) The Shuttle was not launched under conditions where it could have been struck by [lightning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning "Lightning").

The first fully functional orbiter was _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ (designated OV-102), built in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). It was delivered to [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC) on March 25, 1979, and was first launched on April 12, 1981—the 20th anniversary of [Yuri Gagarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin "Yuri Gagarin")'s [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 "Vostok 1")—with a crew of two.

_[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_ (OV-099) was delivered to KSC in July 1982, _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ (OV-103) in November 1983, _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ (OV-104) in April 1985 and _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (OV-105) in May 1991. _Challenger_ was originally built and used as a Structural Test Article (STA-099), but was converted to a complete orbiter when this was found to be less expensive than converting _Enterprise_ from its Approach and Landing Test configuration into a spaceworthy vehicle.

On April 24, 1990, _Discovery_ carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into space during [STS-31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31 "STS-31").

In the course of 135 missions flown, two orbiters (_Columbia_ and _Challenger_) suffered catastrophic accidents, with the loss of all crew members, totaling 14 astronauts.

The accidents led to national level inquiries, detailed analysis of why the accidents occurred, and significant pauses where changes were made before the Shuttles returned to flight.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-space.com-8) After the _Challenger_ disaster in January 1986, there was a delay of 32 months before the next Shuttle launch.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-history.nasa.gov-9) A similar delay of 29 months occurred after the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in February 2003.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-space.com-8)

The longest Shuttle mission was [STS-80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-80 "STS-80") lasting 17 days, 15 hours. The final flight of the Space Shuttle program was [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135") on July 8, 2011.

Since the Shuttle's retirement in 2011, many of its original duties are performed by an assortment of government and private vessels. The European ATV [Automated Transfer Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_Transfer_Vehicle "Automated Transfer Vehicle") supplied the ISS between 2008 and 2015. Classified military missions are being flown by the US Air Force's uncrewed [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane"), the [X-37B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-37B "X-37B").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-10) By 2012, cargo to the International Space Station was already being delivered commercially under NASA's [Commercial Resupply Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Resupply_Services "Commercial Resupply Services") by SpaceX's partially reusable [Dragon spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon_spacecraft "Dragon spacecraft"), followed by Orbital Sciences' [Cygnus spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_spacecraft "Cygnus spacecraft") in late 2013. Crew service to the ISS is currently provided by the Russian [Soyuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)") and, since 2020, the [SpaceX Dragon 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Dragon_2 "SpaceX Dragon 2") crew capsule, launched on the company's reusable [Falcon 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9 "Falcon 9") rocket as part of NASA's [Commercial Crew Development program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Crew_Development "Commercial Crew Development").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-11)[Boeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Defense,_Space_&_Security "Boeing Defense, Space & Security")'s [Starliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Starliner "Boeing Starliner") capsule is scheduled to start ISS crew service from 2025. For missions beyond [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit"), NASA is building the [Space Launch System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Launch_System "Space Launch System") and the [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_spacecraft "Orion spacecraft"), part of the [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program").

## Budget

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Budget")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Atlantis_taking_off_on_STS-27.jpg/250px-Atlantis_taking_off_on_STS-27.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlantis_taking_off_on_STS-27.jpg)

Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ takes flight on the STS-27 mission on December 2, 1988. The Shuttle took about 8.5 minutes to accelerate to a speed of over 27,000 km/h (17000 mph) and achieve orbit.

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/950318_STS67_Endeavour_landing.jpg/250px-950318_STS67_Endeavour_landing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:950318_STS67_Endeavour_landing.jpg)

A drag chute is deployed by _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ as it completes a mission of almost 17 days in space on Runway 22 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in southern California. Landing occurred at 1:46 pm (EST), March 18, 1995.

Early during development of the Space Shuttle, NASA had estimated that the program would cost $7.45 billion ($43 billion in 2011 dollars, adjusting for inflation) in development/non-recurring costs, and $9.3M ($54M in 2011 dollars) per flight.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-14) Early estimates for the cost to deliver payload to low-Earth orbit were as low as $118 per pound ($260/kg) of payload ($635/lb or $1,400/kg in 2011 dollars), based on marginal or incremental launch costs, and assuming a 65,000 pound (30 000 kg) payload capacity and 50 launches per year.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-costbenefit-16) A more realistic projection of 12 flights per year for the 15-year service life combined with the initial development costs would have resulted in a total cost projection for the program of roughly $54 billion (in 2011 dollars).

The total cost of the actual 30-year service life of the Shuttle program through 2011, adjusted for inflation, was $196 billion.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_shuttle_program_costs-17) In 2010, the incremental cost per flight of the Space Shuttle was $409 million, or $14,186 per kilogram ($6,435 per pound) to [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit") (LEO). In contrast, the comparable [Proton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_(rocket) "Proton (rocket)") launch vehicle cost was $141 million, or $6,721 per kilogram ($3,049 per pound) to LEO and the [Soyuz 2.1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_2.1 "Soyuz 2.1") was $55 million, or $6,665 per kilogram ($3,023 per pound), despite these launch vehicles not being reusable.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Launch_Cost_Analy-18)

[NASA's budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Budget "NASA Budget") for 2005 allocated 30%, or $5 billion, to Space Shuttle operations;[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-nasa_2005_budget-19) this was decreased in 2006 to a request of $4.3 billion.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-nasa_2006_budget-20) Non-launch costs account for a significant part of the program budget: for example, during fiscal years 2004 to 2006, NASA spent around $13 billion on the Space Shuttle program,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-21) even though the fleet was grounded in the aftermath of the _Columbia_ disaster and there were a total of three launches during this period of time. In fiscal year 2009, NASA budget allocated $2.98 billion for 5 launches to the program, including $490 million for "program integration", $1.03 billion for "flight and ground operations", and $1.46 billion for "flight hardware" (which includes maintenance of orbiters, engines, and the external tank between flights.)

Per-launch costs can be measured by dividing the total cost over the life of the program (including buildings, facilities, training, salaries, etc.) by the number of launches. With 135 missions, and the total cost of US$192 billion (in 2010 dollars), this gives approximately $1.5 billion per launch over the life of the Shuttle program.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-pielke-22) A 2017 study found that carrying one kilogram of cargo to the ISS on the Shuttle cost $272,000 in 2017 dollars, twice the cost of Cygnus and three times that of Dragon.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-foust20171120-23)

NASA used a [management philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Management_philosophy "Management philosophy") known as success-oriented management during the Space Shuttle program which historian Alex Roland described in the aftermath of the _Columbia_ disaster as "hoping for the best".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-roland-24) Success-oriented management has since been studied by several analysts in the area.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-som1-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-som2-26)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-som3-27)

## Disasters

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Disasters")]

In the course of 135 missions flown, two orbiters were destroyed, with loss of crew totalling 14 astronauts:

*   _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_ – lost 73 seconds after liftoff, [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L"), January 28, 1986
*   _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ – lost approximately 16 minutes before its expected landing, [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), February 1, 2003

There was also one [abort-to-orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_abort_modes "Space Shuttle abort modes") and some fatal accidents on the ground during launch preparations.

### STS-51-L (_Challenger_, 1986)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: STS-51-L (Challenger, 1986)")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Challenger_explosion.jpg/250px-Challenger_explosion.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Challenger_explosion.jpg)

In 1986, _Challenger_ disintegrated one minute and 13 seconds after liftoff.

Close-up video footage of _Challenger_ during its final launch on January 28, 1986, clearly shows that the problems began due to an [O-ring failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") on the right solid rocket booster (SRB). The hot plume of gas leaking from the failed joint caused the collapse of the external tank, which then resulted in the orbiter's disintegration due to high aerodynamic stress. The accident resulted in the loss of all seven astronauts on board. _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (OV-105) was built to replace _Challenger_ (using structural spare parts originally intended for the other orbiters) and delivered in May 1991; it was first launched a year later.

After the loss of _Challenger_, NASA grounded the Space Shuttle program for over two years, making numerous safety changes recommended by the [Rogers Commission Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers_Commission_Report "Rogers Commission Report"), which included a redesign of the SRB joint that failed in the _Challenger_ accident. Other safety changes included a new escape system for use when the orbiter was in controlled flight, improved landing gear tires and brakes, and the reintroduction of pressure suits for Shuttle astronauts (these had been discontinued after [STS-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-4 "STS-4"); astronauts wore only coveralls and oxygen helmets from that point on until the _Challenger_ accident). The Shuttle program continued in September 1988 with the launch of _Discovery_ on [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26").

The accidents did not just affect the technical design of the orbiter, but also NASA.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-history.nasa.gov-9) Quoting some recommendations made by the post-_Challenger_ Rogers commission:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-history.nasa.gov-9)

> **Recommendation I** – The faulty Solid Rocket Motor joint and seal must be changed. This could be a new design eliminating the joint or a redesign of the current joint and seal. ... the Administrator of NASA should request the National Research Council to form an independent Solid Rocket Motor design oversight committee to implement the Commission's design recommendations and oversee the design effort.  
> **Recommendation II** – The Shuttle Program Structure should be reviewed. ... NASA should encourage the transition of qualified astronauts into agency management Positions.  
> **Recommendation III** – NASA and the primary shuttle contractors should review all Criticality 1, 1R, 2, and 2R items and hazard analyses.  
> **Recommendation IV** – NASA should establish an Office of Safety, Reliability and Quality Assurance to be headed by an Associate Administrator, reporting directly to the NASA Administrator.  
> **Recommendation VI** – NASA must take actions to improve landing safety. The tire, brake and nosewheel system must be improved.  
> **Recommendation VII** – Make all efforts to provide a crew escape system for use during controlled gliding flight.  
> **Recommendation VIII** – The nation's reliance on the shuttle as its principal space launch capability created a relentless pressure on NASA to increase the flight rate ... NASA must establish a flight rate that is consistent with its resources.

### STS-107 (_Columbia_, 2003)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: STS-107 (Columbia, 2003)")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Columbia disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/20/STS-107%2C_final_moments_in_cabin_%28Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster%29.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

Video of _Columbia_'s final moments, filmed by the crew.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Thermal_protection_system_inspections_from_ISS_-_Shuttle_nose.jpg/250px-Thermal_protection_system_inspections_from_ISS_-_Shuttle_nose.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thermal_protection_system_inspections_from_ISS_-_Shuttle_nose.jpg)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ as it approaches the International Space Station during [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") on July 28, 2005. This was the Shuttle's "return to flight" mission after the _Columbia_ disaster

The Shuttle program operated accident-free for seventeen years and 88 missions after the _Challenger_ disaster, until [_Columbia_ broke up on reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), killing all seven crew members, on February 1, 2003. The [ultimate cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_cause "Ultimate cause") of the accident was a piece of foam separating from the external tank moments after liftoff and striking the leading edge of the orbiter's left wing, puncturing one of the reinforced carbon-carbon (RCC) panels that covered the wing edge and protected it during reentry. As _Columbia_ reentered the atmosphere at the end of an otherwise normal mission, hot gas penetrated the wing and destroyed it from the inside out, causing the orbiter to lose control and disintegrate.

After the _Columbia_ disaster, the International Space Station operated on a skeleton crew of two for more than two years and was serviced primarily by Russian spacecraft. While the "Return to Flight" mission [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005 was successful, a similar piece of foam from a different portion of the tank was shed. Although the debris did not strike _Discovery_, the program was grounded once again for this reason.

The second "Return to Flight" mission, [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") launched on July 4, 2006, at 14:37 (EDT). Two previous launches were scrubbed because of lingering thunderstorms and high winds around the launch pad, and the launch took place despite objections from its chief engineer and safety head. A five-inch (13 cm) crack in the foam insulation of the external tank gave cause for concern; however, the Mission Management Team gave the go for launch.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-28) This mission increased the ISS crew to three. _Discovery_ touched down successfully on July 17, 2006, at 09:14 (EDT) on Runway 15 at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").

Following the success of [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121"), all subsequent missions were completed without major foam problems, and the construction of the ISS was completed (during the [STS-118](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-118 "STS-118") mission in August 2007, the orbiter was again struck by a foam fragment on liftoff, but this damage was minimal compared to the damage sustained by _Columbia_).

The _Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board, in its report, noted the reduced risk to the crew when a Shuttle flew to the International Space Station (ISS), as the station could be used as a safe haven for the crew awaiting rescue in the event that damage to the orbiter on ascent made it unsafe for reentry. The board recommended that for the remaining flights, the Shuttle always orbit with the station. Prior to STS-114, NASA Administrator Sean O'Keefe declared that all future flights of the Space Shuttle would go to the ISS, precluding the possibility of executing the final [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") servicing mission which had been scheduled before the _Columbia_ accident, despite the fact that millions of dollars' worth of upgrade equipment for Hubble were ready and waiting in NASA warehouses. Many dissenters, including astronauts [_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_], asked NASA management to reconsider allowing the mission, but initially the director stood firm. On October 31, 2006, [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") announced approval of the launch of _Atlantis_ for the fifth and final shuttle servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope, scheduled for August 28, 2008. However, SM4/[STS-125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-125 "STS-125") eventually launched in May 2009.

One impact of _Columbia_ was that future crewed launch vehicles, namely the [Ares I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares_I "Ares I"), had a special emphasis on crew safety compared to other considerations.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-29)

The Space Shuttle retirement was announced in January 2004.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-347 President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") announced his [Vision for Space Exploration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vision_for_Space_Exploration "Vision for Space Exploration"), which called for the retirement of the Space Shuttle once it completed construction of the ISS.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_vision-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_bush_speech-32) To ensure the ISS was properly assembled, the contributing partners determined the need for 16 remaining assembly missions in March 2006.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-349 One additional Hubble Space Telescope servicing mission was approved in October 2006.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-352 Originally, [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") was to be the final Space Shuttle mission. However, the _Columbia_ disaster resulted in additional orbiters being prepared for [launch on need](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-3xx "STS-3xx") in the event of a rescue mission. As _Atlantis_ was prepared for the final launch-on-need mission, the decision was made in September 2010 that it would fly as [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135") with a four-person crew that could remain at the ISS in the event of an emergency.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-355 STS-135 launched on July 8, 2011, and landed at the KSC on July 21, 2011, at 5:57 a.m.EDT (09:57 UTC).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-398 From then until the launch of [Crew Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Dragon_2#Crew_Dragon "SpaceX Dragon 2") Demo-2 on May 30, 2020, the US launched its astronauts aboard Russian Soyuz spacecraft.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_nytimes_crewdragon-33)

Following each orbiter's final flight, it was processed to make it safe for display. The OMS and RCS systems used presented the primary dangers due to their toxic [hypergolic propellant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergolic_propellant "Hypergolic propellant"), and most of their components were permanently removed to prevent any dangerous outgassing.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-443 _Atlantis_ is on display at the [Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Visitor_Complex "Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex") in Florida,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-456 _Discovery_ is on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") in Virginia,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-451 _Endeavour_ is on display at the [California Science Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Science_Center "California Science Center") in Los Angeles,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-457 and _Enterprise_ is displayed at the [_Intrepid_ Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrepid_Museum "Intrepid Museum") in New York.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-464 Components from the orbiters were transferred to the US Air Force, ISS program, and Russian and Canadian governments. The engines were removed to be used on the [Space Launch System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Launch_System "Space Launch System"), and spare RS-25 nozzles were attached for display purposes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III-445

For many [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program") missions, the Space Launch System's two solid rocket boosters' engines and casings and four main engines and the [Orion spacecraft's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(spacecraft) "Orion (spacecraft)") main engine will all be previously flown Space Shuttle main engines, solid rocket boosters, and [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") engines. They are refurbished legacy engines from the Space Shuttle program, some of which even date back to the early 1980s. For example, [Artemis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_I "Artemis I") had components that flew on 83 of the 135 Space Shuttle missions. From Artemis I to [Artemis IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_IV "Artemis IV") recycled Shuttle main engines will be used before manufacturing new engines. From Artemis I to [Artemis III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_III "Artemis III") recycled Shuttle solid rocket boosters' engines and steel casings are to be used before building new ones. From Artemis I to [Artemis VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_VI "Artemis VI") the Orion main engine will use six previously flown Space Shuttle OMS engines.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-34)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-36)

## Preservation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Preservation")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Space_Shuttle_Discovery_%40_Udvar_Hazy.png/250px-Space_Shuttle_Discovery_%40_Udvar_Hazy.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Space_Shuttle_Discovery_@_Udvar_Hazy.png)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ at the Udvar Hazy museum

Out of the five fully functional shuttle orbiters built, three remain. _Enterprise_, which was used for atmospheric test flights but not for orbital flight, had many parts taken out for use on the other orbiters. It was later visually restored and was on display at the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum")'s [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until April 19, 2012. _Enterprise_ was moved to New York City in April 2012 to be displayed at the [_Intrepid_ Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrepid_Museum "Intrepid Museum"), whose Space Shuttle Pavilion opened on July 19, 2012. _Discovery_ replaced _Enterprise_ at the National Air and Space Museum's Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center. _Atlantis_ formed part of the Space Shuttle Exhibit at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") visitor complex and has been on display there since June 29, 2013, following its refurbishment.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-37)

On October 14, 2012, _Endeavour_ completed an unprecedented 12 mi (19 km) drive on city streets from [Los Angeles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_International_Airport "Los Angeles International Airport") to the [California Science Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Science_Center "California Science Center"), where it was put on display later that year. The transport from the airport took two days and required major street closures, the removal of over 400 city trees, and extensive work to raise power lines, level the street, and temporarily remove street signs, lamp posts, and other obstacles. Hundreds of volunteers, and fire and police personnel, helped with the transport. Large crowds of spectators waited on the streets to see the shuttle as it passed through the city. _Endeavour_ was initially on display at the Science Center's temporary [Samuel Oschin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Oschin "Samuel Oschin") Pavilion (in a horizontal orientation) starting with its arrival in late 2012 until December 31, 2023, when it closed for the construction of its permanent home in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center (a planned addition to the California Science Center). Once moved, it will be displayed in launch configuration, along with genuine solid rocket boosters and the last flight-qualified external tank (ET-94).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-casc-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-39)As of April 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit), construction on the new facility has finished, though a reopening date has yet to be announced.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-40)

One area of Space Shuttle applications is an expanded crew.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-orbiter-41) Crews of up to eight have been flown in the Orbiter, but it could have held at least a crew of ten.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-orbiter-41) Various proposals for filling the payload bay with additional passengers were also made as early as 1979.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-reichert-42) One proposal by [Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_International "Rockwell International") provided seating for 74 passengers in the Orbiter payload bay, with support for three days in Earth orbit.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-reichert-42) With a smaller 64 seat orbiter, costs for the late 1980s would be around US$1.5 million per seat per launch.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-david-43) The Rockwell passenger module had two decks, four seats across on top and two on the bottom, including a 25-inch (63.5 cm) wide aisle and extra storage space.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-david-43)

Another design was Space Habitation Design Associates 1983 proposal for 72 passengers in the Space Shuttle Payload bay.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-david-43) Passengers were located in 6 sections, each with windows and its own loading ramp at launch, and with seats in different configurations for launch and landing.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-david-43) Another proposal was based on the Spacelab habitation modules, which provided 32 seats in the payload bay in addition to those in the cockpit area.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-david-43)

There were some efforts to analyze commercial operation of STS.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-44) Using the NASA figure for average cost to launch a Space Shuttle as of 2011 at about $450 million per mission,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-missionbudget-45) a cost per seat for a 74[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-rockwell74-46) seat module envisioned by Rockwell came to less than $6 million, not including the regular crew. Some passenger modules used hardware similar to existing equipment, such as the tunnel,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-rockwell74-46) which was also needed for [Spacehab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacehab "Spacehab") and Spacelab

## Successors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Successors")]

During the three decades of operation, various follow-on and replacements for the STS Space Shuttle were partially developed but not finished.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-ReferenceA-47)

Examples of possible future space vehicles to supplement or supplant STS:[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-ReferenceA-47)

*   Advanced Crewed Earth-to-Orbit Vehicle
*   [Shuttle II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_II "Shuttle II"), Johnson Space Center concept for a follow-on, with 2 boosters and 2 tanks mounted on its wings.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-48)
*   National Aero-Space Plane (NASP) 
    *   [Rockwell X-30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_X-30 "Rockwell X-30") (not funded)

*   [VentureStar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VentureStar "VentureStar"), SSTO spacelane concept using an aerospike engine. 
    *   [Lockheed Martin X-33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_X-33 "Lockheed Martin X-33") (cancelled 2001)

*   [Ares I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares_I "Ares I") (ended with Constellation cancellation)
*   [Orbital Space Plane Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Space_Plane_Program "Orbital Space Plane Program")

One effort in the direction of space transportation was the Reusable Launch Vehicle (RLV) program, initiated in 1994 by NASA.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-spinoff.nasa.gov-49) This led to work on the X-33 and X-34 vehicles.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-spinoff.nasa.gov-49) NASA spent about US$1 billion on developing the X-33 hoping for it be in operation by 2005.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-spinoff.nasa.gov-49) Another program around the turn of the millennium was the [Space Launch Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Launch_Initiative "Space Launch Initiative"), which was a next generation launch initiative.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-nasa.gov-50)

The Space Launch Initiative program was started in 2001, and in late 2002 it was evolved into two programs, the [Orbital Space Plane Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Space_Plane_Program "Orbital Space Plane Program") and the [Next Generation Launch Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Generation_Launch_Technology "Next Generation Launch Technology") program.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-nasa.gov-50) OSP was oriented towards provided access to the International Space Station.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-nasa.gov-50)

Other vehicles that would have taken over some of the Shuttles responsibilities were the [HL-20 Personnel Launch System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HL-20_Personnel_Launch_System "HL-20 Personnel Launch System") or the [NASA X-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_X-38 "NASA X-38") of the [Crew Return Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Return_Vehicle "Crew Return Vehicle") program, which were primarily for getting people down from ISS. The X-38 was cancelled in 2002,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-51) and the HL-20 was cancelled in 1993.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-52) Several other programs in this existed such as the Station Crew Return Alternative Module (SCRAM) and Assured Crew Return Vehicle (ACRV)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-53)

According to the 2004 Vision for Space Exploration, the next human NASA program was to be [Constellation program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation_program "Constellation program") with its [Ares I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares_I "Ares I") and [Ares V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares_V "Ares V") launch vehicles and the [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_spacecraft "Orion spacecraft"); however, the Constellation program was never fully funded, and in early 2010 the Obama administration asked Congress to instead endorse a plan with heavy reliance on the private sector for delivering cargo and crew to LEO.

The [Commercial Orbital Transportation Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Orbital_Transportation_Services "Commercial Orbital Transportation Services") (COTS) program began in 2006 with the purpose of creating commercially operated uncrewed cargo vehicles to service the ISS.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-54) The first of these vehicles, [SpaceX Dragon 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Dragon_1 "SpaceX Dragon 1"), became operational in 2012, and the second, [Orbital Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Sciences "Orbital Sciences")'s [Cygnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_(spacecraft) "Cygnus (spacecraft)") did so in 2014.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-55)

The [Commercial Crew Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Crew_Development "Commercial Crew Development") (CCDev) program was initiated in 2010 with the purpose of creating commercially operated crewed spacecraft capable of delivering at least four crew members to the ISS, staying docked for 180 days and then returning them back to Earth.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-56) These spacecraft, like [SpaceX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX "SpaceX")'s [Dragon 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon_2 "Dragon 2") and [Boeing CST-100 Starliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_CST-100_Starliner "Boeing CST-100 Starliner") were expected to become operational around 2020.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-57) On the [Crew Dragon Demo-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Dragon_Demo-2 "Crew Dragon Demo-2") mission, SpaceX's Dragon 2 sent astronauts to the ISS, restoring America's human launch capability. The [first operational SpaceX mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Crew-1 "SpaceX Crew-1") launched on November 15, 2020, at 7:27:17 p.m. ET, carrying four astronauts to the ISS.

Although the Constellation program was canceled, it has been replaced with a very similar [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program"). The [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_spacecraft "Orion spacecraft") has been left virtually unchanged from its previous design. The planned [Ares V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares_V "Ares V") rocket has been replaced with the smaller [Space Launch System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Launch_System "Space Launch System") (SLS), which is planned to launch both Orion and other necessary hardware.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-58)[Exploration Flight Test-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploration_Flight_Test-1 "Exploration Flight Test-1") (EFT-1), an uncrewed test flight of the Orion spacecraft, launched on December 5, 2014, on a [Delta IV Heavy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_IV_Heavy "Delta IV Heavy") rocket.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-schedule-59)

[Artemis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_I "Artemis I") is the first flight of the SLS and was launched as a test of the completed Orion and SLS system.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-60) During the mission, an uncrewed Orion capsule spent 10 days in a 57,000-kilometer (31,000-nautical-mile)[distant retrograde orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distant_retrograde_orbit "Distant retrograde orbit") around the Moon before returning to Earth.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-a1-1-61)[Artemis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_II "Artemis II"), the first crewed mission of the program, launched on April 1, 2026[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-62) on a [free-return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-return_trajectory "Free-return trajectory") flyby of the Moon at a distance of 8,520 kilometers (4,600 nautical miles).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-64)[Artemis III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_III "Artemis III"), a low Earth orbit mission, is planned to launch in 2027. [Artemis IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_IV "Artemis IV") is planned to touch down on the [lunar south pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_south_pole "Lunar south pole") region in 2028, with two astronauts staying there for about one week.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-a3-1-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-66)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-67)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-a3-2-68)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-69)

For many Artemis missions, the Space Launch System's two solid rocket boosters' engines and casings and four main engines and the Orion spacecraft's main engine will all be previously flown [Space Shuttle main engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RS-25 "RS-25"), [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster"), and [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") engines. They are refurbished legacy engines from the Space Shuttle program, some of which even date back to the early 1980s. For example, Artemis I had components that flew on 83 of the 135 Space Shuttle missions. From Artemis I to Artemis IV recycled Shuttle main engines will be used before manufacturing new engines. From Artemis I to Artemis III recycled Shuttle solid rocket boosters' engines and steel casings will be used before manufacturing new ones. From Artemis I to Artemis VI the Orion main engine will use six previously flown Space Shuttle OMS engines.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-70)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-71)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-72)

## Assets and transition plan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Assets and transition plan")]

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/STS-135_30_mins_after_touchdown2.png/250px-STS-135_30_mins_after_touchdown2.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-135_30_mins_after_touchdown2.png)

_Atlantis_ about 30 minutes after final touchdown

The Space Shuttle program occupied over 654 facilities, used over 1.2 million line items of equipment, and employed over 5,000 people. The total value of equipment was over $12 billion. Shuttle-related facilities represented over a quarter of NASA's inventory. There were over 1,200 active suppliers to the program throughout the United States. NASA's transition plan had the program operating through 2010 with a transition and retirement phase lasting through 2015. During this time, the [Ares I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares_I "Ares I") and [Orion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(Constellation_program) "Orion (Constellation program)") as well as the Altair Lunar Lander were to be under development,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-NTMP-73) although these programs have since been canceled.

In the 2010s, two major programs for human spaceflight are [Commercial Crew Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Crew_Program "Commercial Crew Program") and the [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program"). [Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A") is, for example, used to launch [Falcon Heavy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_Heavy "Falcon Heavy") and [Falcon 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9 "Falcon 9").

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Criticism")]

Main article: [Criticism of the Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criticism_of_the_Space_Shuttle_program "Criticism of the Space Shuttle program")

This section is an excerpt from [Space Shuttle § Criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#Criticism "Space Shuttle").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit)]

The partial reusability of the Space Shuttle was one of the primary design requirements during its initial development.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_dev_space_shuttle-74):164 The technical decisions that dictated the orbiter's return and re-use reduced the per-launch payload capabilities. The original intention was to compensate for this lower payload by lowering the per-launch costs and a high launch frequency. However, the actual costs of a Space Shuttle launch were higher than initially predicted, and the Space Shuttle did not fly the intended 24 missions per year as initially predicted by NASA.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_griffin-75)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III–489–490

The Space Shuttle was originally intended as a launch vehicle to deploy satellites, which it was primarily used for on the missions prior to the _Challenger_ disaster. NASA's pricing, which was below cost, was lower than expendable launch vehicles; the intention was that the high volume of Space Shuttle missions would compensate for early financial losses. The improvement of expendable launch vehicles and the transition away from commercial payloads on the Space Shuttle resulted in expendable launch vehicles becoming the primary deployment option for satellites.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_jenkins2016-30):III–109–112 A key customer for the Space Shuttle was the [National Reconnaissance Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Reconnaissance_Office "National Reconnaissance Office") (NRO) responsible for spy satellites. The existence of NRO's connection was classified through 1993, and secret considerations of NRO payload requirements led to lack of transparency in the program. The proposed [Shuttle-Centaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Centaur "Shuttle-Centaur") program, cancelled in the wake of the _Challenger_ disaster, would have pushed the spacecraft beyond its operational capacity.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-76)

The fatal _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ disasters demonstrated the safety risks of the Space Shuttle that could result in the loss of the crew. The spaceplane design of the orbiter limited the abort options, as the abort scenarios required the controlled flight of the orbiter to a runway or to allow the crew to egress individually, rather than the abort escape options on the [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_(spacecraft) "Apollo (spacecraft)") and [Soyuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)") space capsules.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_shuttle_safety_comparison-77) Early safety analyses advertised by NASA engineers and management predicted the chance of a catastrophic failure resulting in the death of the crew as ranging from 1 in 100 launches to as rare as 1 in 100,000.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_ieee_challenger-78)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_feynman_appendix-79) Following the loss of two Space Shuttle missions, the risks for the initial missions were reevaluated, and the chance of a catastrophic loss of the vehicle and crew was found to be as high as 1 in 9.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_npr_safety-80) NASA management was criticized afterwards for accepting increased risk to the crew in exchange for higher mission rates. Both the _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers\_Commission\_Report "Rogers Commission Report")_ and _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia\_Accident\_Investigation\_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board")_ reports explained that NASA culture had failed to keep the crew safe by not objectively evaluating the potential risks of the missions.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_feynman_appendix-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-Space_Shuttle_columbia_report-81):195–203

## Support vehicles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_program&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Support vehicles")]

Many other vehicles were used in support of the Space Shuttle program, mainly terrestrial transportation vehicles.

*   The [crawler-transporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawler-transporter "Crawler-transporter") carried the [mobile launcher platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_launcher_platform "Mobile launcher platform") and the Space Shuttle from the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) to [Launch Complex 39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_Complex_39 "Launch Complex 39"), originally built for Project Apollo.
*   The [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") (SCA) were two modified [Boeing 747s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747"). Either could fly an orbiter from alternative landing sites back to the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-jenkins2016-82):I–377,382 These aircraft were retired to the [Joe Davies Heritage Airpark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Davies_Heritage_Airpark "Joe Davies Heritage Airpark") at the [Armstrong Flight Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong_Flight_Research_Center "Armstrong Flight Research Center") and [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston").
*   A 36-wheeled transport trailer, the Orbiter Transfer System, originally built for the [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force")'s launch facility at [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") in California (since then converted for [Delta IV rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_IV_rocket "Delta IV rocket")) would transport the orbiter from the landing facility to the launch pad, which allowed both "stacking" and launch without utilizing a separate VAB-style building and crawler-transporter roadway. Prior to the closing of the Vandenberg facility, orbiters were transported from the [OPF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Processing_Facility "Orbiter Processing Facility") to the VAB on their undercarriages, only to be raised when the orbiter was being lifted for attachment to the SRB/ET stack. The trailer allowed the transportation of the orbiter from the OPF to either the SCA ["Mate-Demate"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mate-Demate_Device "Mate-Demate Device") stand or the VAB without placing any additional stress on the undercarriage.
*   The [Crew Transport Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Transport_Vehicle "Crew Transport Vehicle") (CTV), a modified airport [jet bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge"), was used to assist astronauts to egress from the orbiter after landing. Upon entering the CTV, astronauts could take off their launch and reentry suits then proceed to chairs and beds for medical checks before being transported back to the crew quarters in the [Operations and Checkout Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operations_and_Checkout_Building "Operations and Checkout Building"). Originally built for Project Apollo.
*   The [Astrovan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_transfer_van "Astronaut transfer van") was used to transport astronauts from the crew quarters in the Operations and Checkout Building to the launch pad on launch day. It was also used to transport astronauts back again from the Crew Transport Vehicle at the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility").
*   The three locomotives serving the [NASA Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Railroad "NASA Railroad"), used to transport segments of the [Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster"), were determined to be no longer needed for day-to-day operation at the Kennedy Space Center. In April 2015, locomotive No. 1 was sent to [Natchitoches Parish Port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchitoches_Parish_Port "Natchitoches Parish Port") and No. 3 sent to the [Madison Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Railroad "Madison Railroad"). Locomotive No. 2 was sent to the [Gold Coast Railroad Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Railroad_Museum "Gold Coast Railroad Museum") in 2014.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program#cite_note-83)

*   [![Image 37: Crawler-transporter No.2 ("Franz") in a December 2004 road test after track shoe replacement](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Crawler-Transporter.jpg/250px-Crawler-Transporter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crawler-Transporter.jpg "Crawler-transporter No.2 (\"Franz\") in a December 2004 road test after track shoe replacement") Crawler-transporter No.2 ("Franz") in a December 2004 road test after track shoe replacement 
*   [![Image 38: Atlantis being prepared to be mated to the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft using the Mate-Demate Device following STS-44.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Shuttle_mate_demate_facility.jpg/250px-Shuttle_mate_demate_facility.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shuttle_mate_demate_facility.jpg "Atlantis being prepared to be mated to the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft using the Mate-Demate Device following STS-44.") _Atlantis_ being prepared to be mated to the [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") using the [Mate-Demate Device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mate-Demate_Device "Mate-Demate Device") following [STS-44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-44 "STS-44").

Country United States
Organization[NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")
Purpose Crewed orbital flight
Status Completed
Program history

First flight August 12,1977(1977-08-12) ([ALT-12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests"))
First crewed flight April 12,1981(1981-04-12) ([STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1"))
Last flight July 21,2011(2011-07-21) ([STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"))
Successes 133
Failures 2 ([STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L"), [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"))
