## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-26&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Return_to_Flight_Launch_of_Discovery_-_GPN-2000-001871.jpg/250px-Return_to_Flight_Launch_of_Discovery_-_GPN-2000-001871.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Return_to_Flight_Launch_of_Discovery_-_GPN-2000-001871.jpg)

_Discovery_ lifts off from KSC, the first shuttle mission after the _Challenger_ disaster

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B"), [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), at 11:37:00 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on September 29, 1988, 975 days after the _Challenger_ disaster.

The launch was delayed by one hour and thirty-eight minutes due to unseasonable and unusual light winds, and the need to replace fuses in the cooling systems of two crew members' flight suits. The suits were repaired, and a waiver was issued for the wind conditions after officials determined there was a sufficient safety margin for wind loads on the orbiter's wing leading edges. At T−1:30, it was proposed that the launch be delayed at T−0:31 due to a cabin air pressure issue. It was quickly determined that the cabin pressure had been increased slightly by the activation of the oxygen systems in the crew's flight suits, and the launch was conducted without further delay. The shuttle crew—all veteran astronauts—included Commander Frederick H. "Rick" Hauck, Pilot Richard O. Covey, and Mission Specialists John M. "Mike" Lounge, George D. "Pinky" Nelson and David C. Hilmers.

The primary payload for the STS-26 mission, [TDRS-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-3 "TDRS-3"), was successfully deployed, and 11 scheduled mid-deck scientific and technological experiments were carried out. The post-_Challenger_ redesigned [solid rocket booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster") segment joints showed no signs of leakage or overheating.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-3)

Two minor problems occurred during the flight. After ascent, the Flash Evaporator System for cooling the orbiter iced up and shut down, increasing the crew cabin temperature to approximately 31°C (88°F). The problem was resolved on Flight Day 4 and cooler temperatures resulted. A [Ku-band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_band "Ku band") antenna for communications was deployed on Flight Day 2, but it failed to respond properly and had to be stowed for the remainder of the mission.

During STS-26, _Discovery_ became the first spacecraft to fly in space equipped with a VCU (Voice Control Unit), a computer capable of recognising and responding to human speech. The VCU was created by [SCI Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanmina_Corporation "Sanmina Corporation") in [Huntsville, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama "Huntsville, Alabama"), and was based on technology licensed from the [Votan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Votan "Votan") company. This [speech recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition") system controlled the cameras and monitors that were used by the crew to monitor the [Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm") mechanical arm mounted in the cargo bay. Because of the experimental nature of speech recognition at the time, this system was not used for any critical operations. Initial problems almost sidelined the tests when the voice templates that were created prior to liftoff were found to have less than 60% recognition for one crew member and less than 40% recognition for another. This problem was corrected by retraining the templates. It was retested and found to be operational with a recognition success rate of over 96%. It was concluded that [weightless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") conditions caused a fundamental change in human speech, making the templates created prior to liftoff virtually useless when in orbit.

Besides conducting the mission's various experiments, crew members practiced suiting up in new partial-pressure "launch-and-entry" flight suits, and also practiced the unstowing and attaching of the new crew escape system. On October 2, 1988, the day before the mission ended, the five-man crew paid tribute to the seven crew members lost in the _Challenger_ disaster.

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 17, [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at 12:37:11 p.m. EDT on October 3, 1988, after a mission duration of approximately 4 days, 1 hour, 0 minute, and 11 seconds. Capsule Communicator Blaine Hammond Jr. welcomed the crew, saying it was "a great ending to a new beginning".

### Payloads and experiments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-26&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Payloads and experiments")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/TDRS-C_Deployed.jpg/250px-TDRS-C_Deployed.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TDRS-C_Deployed.jpg)

[TDRS-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-3 "TDRS-3") after deployment

TDRS-C, which became TDRS-3 in orbit, and its attached [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS), were deployed from _Discovery_'s cargo bay six hours and 13 minutes into the flight. The first stage of the IUS placed TDRS-3 in a transfer orbit, and the second stage placed it in a [geosynchronous orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit") on September 30, 1988. TDRS-3 moved into position over the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") south of [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") at 171° west [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude "Longitude"). It joined [TDRS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-1 "TDRS-1") in tracking Earth-orbiting spacecraft; a sister satellite, [TDRS-B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-B "TDRS-B"), was lost in the _Challenger_ accident. Also in the payload bay was the Orbiter Experiments Autonomous Supporting Instrumentation System (OASIS). OASIS recorded environmental data on the orbiter and the TDRS payload during various inflight phases.

All the mission's mid-deck experiments were deemed to have been performed successfully. However, there were some glitches with two of the five materials science experiments. In the Protein Crystal Growth (PCG) experiment, two of the 11 [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") processed – including an [enzyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme") believed to be key to the replication of [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") – did not produce crystals suitable for analysis. Also, there were some equipment problems with the Automated Directional Solidification Furnace (ADSF), an experiment to investigate the melting and solidification of various materials in [zero-gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness").

The materials processing experiments included two Shuttle Student Involvement Projects, one on [titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium") grain formation and the other on controlling [crystal growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_growth "Crystal growth") with a membrane. Another materials science experiment, the Physical Vapor Transport of Organic Solids-2 (PVTOS-2), was a joint project of NASA's Office of Commercial Programs and the [3M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M "3M") company.

Three [life sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_life_sciences "List of life sciences") experiments were conducted, including one on the aggregation of [red blood cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cells "Red blood cells"), intended to help determine if microgravity can play a beneficial role in clinical research and medical diagnostic tests. Two further experiments involved atmospheric sciences, while one was in communications research.

### Damage to thermal protection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-26&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Damage to thermal protection")]

_Discovery_ suffered severe damage to its thermal protection tiles in the underwing area. Post-flight analysis showed that the impact of a 30 cm (12 in) long piece of cork insulation during ascent was the culprit. The origin of the debris was the forward field joint on the right-hand SRB. The damage was such that, during re-entry, the thermal protection tile eroded almost completely.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-Young-4) A similar chain of events ultimately led to the [loss of _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") fifteen years later.

Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_D._Sullivan "Kathryn D. **STS-26** was the 26th [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission and the seventh flight of the orbiter _Discovery_. The mission launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on September 29, 1988, and landed four days later on October 3, 1988. STS-26 was declared the "Return to Flight" mission, being the first mission after the [Space Shuttle _Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") of January 28, 1986. It was the first mission since [STS-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-9 "STS-9") to use the original [Space Transportation System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System "Space Transportation System") (STS) numbering system, the first to have all its crew members wear [pressure suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure_suit "Pressure suit") for launch and landing since [STS-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-4 "STS-4"), and the first mission with bailout capacity since STS-4. STS-26 was also the first U.S. space mission with an all-veteran crew since [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11"), with all of its crew members having flown at least one prior mission.

The mission is technically designated **STS-26R**, as the original STS-26 designation previously belonged to [STS-51-F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-F "STS-51-F") (also known as [Spacelab-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-F "STS-51-F")). Likewise all flights with the STS-26 through STS-33 designations would require the **R** in their documentation to avoid conflicts in tracking data between the old and new flight designations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-Jenkins-1)

The crew roster for STS-26 was based on the original crew assignment for [STS-61-F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-F "STS-61-F"), which would have launched the [_Ulysses_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(spacecraft) "Ulysses (spacecraft)") probe from _Challenger_ in 1986. _Ulysses_ was eventually launched on [STS-41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41 "STS-41"). Hauck, Lounge and Hilmers were all assigned to that flight, with [Roy D. Bridges Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_D._Bridges_Jr. "Roy D. Bridges Jr.") as pilot. Bridges never flew again after the _Challenger_ disaster, but would eventually become the director of [Langley Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langley_Research_Center "Langley Research Center") (LRC).

Covey was the [CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller "Flight controller") operator during the [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") launch who uttered the words, "_Challenger_, go at throttle up" to commander [Francis R. Scobee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Scobee "Dick Scobee"), shortly after which the orbiter disintegrated. He also would have been the CAPCOM operator for the canceled STS-61-F mission during launch and landing.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-26&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Return_to_Flight_Launch_of_Discovery_-_GPN-2000-001871.jpg/250px-Return_to_Flight_Launch_of_Discovery_-_GPN-2000-001871.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Return_to_Flight_Launch_of_Discovery_-_GPN-2000-001871.jpg)

_Discovery_ lifts off from KSC, the first shuttle mission after the _Challenger_ disaster

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B"), [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), at 11:37:00 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on September 29, 1988, 975 days after the _Challenger_ disaster.

The launch was delayed by one hour and thirty-eight minutes due to unseasonable and unusual light winds, and the need to replace fuses in the cooling systems of two crew members' flight suits. The suits were repaired, and a waiver was issued for the wind conditions after officials determined there was a sufficient safety margin for wind loads on the orbiter's wing leading edges. At T−1:30, it was proposed that the launch be delayed at T−0:31 due to a cabin air pressure issue. It was quickly determined that the cabin pressure had been increased slightly by the activation of the oxygen systems in the crew's flight suits, and the launch was conducted without further delay. The shuttle crew—all veteran astronauts—included Commander Frederick H. "Rick" Hauck, Pilot Richard O. Covey, and Mission Specialists John M. "Mike" Lounge, George D. "Pinky" Nelson and David C. Hilmers.

The primary payload for the STS-26 mission, [TDRS-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-3 "TDRS-3"), was successfully deployed, and 11 scheduled mid-deck scientific and technological experiments were carried out. The post-_Challenger_ redesigned [solid rocket booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster") segment joints showed no signs of leakage or overheating.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-3)

Two minor problems occurred during the flight. After ascent, the Flash Evaporator System for cooling the orbiter iced up and shut down, increasing the crew cabin temperature to approximately 31°C (88°F). The problem was resolved on Flight Day 4 and cooler temperatures resulted. A [Ku-band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_band "Ku band") antenna for communications was deployed on Flight Day 2, but it failed to respond properly and had to be stowed for the remainder of the mission.

During STS-26, _Discovery_ became the first spacecraft to fly in space equipped with a VCU (Voice Control Unit), a computer capable of recognising and responding to human speech. The VCU was created by [SCI Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanmina_Corporation "Sanmina Corporation") in [Huntsville, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama "Huntsville, Alabama"), and was based on technology licensed from the [Votan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Votan "Votan") company. This [speech recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition") system controlled the cameras and monitors that were used by the crew to monitor the [Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm") mechanical arm mounted in the cargo bay. Because of the experimental nature of speech recognition at the time, this system was not used for any critical operations. Initial problems almost sidelined the tests when the voice templates that were created prior to liftoff were found to have less than 60% recognition for one crew member and less than 40% recognition for another. This problem was corrected by retraining the templates. It was retested and found to be operational with a recognition success rate of over 96%. It was concluded that [weightless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") conditions caused a fundamental change in human speech, making the templates created prior to liftoff virtually useless when in orbit.

Besides conducting the mission's various experiments, crew members practiced suiting up in new partial-pressure "launch-and-entry" flight suits, and also practiced the unstowing and attaching of the new crew escape system. On October 2, 1988, the day before the mission ended, the five-man crew paid tribute to the seven crew members lost in the _Challenger_ disaster.

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 17, [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at 12:37:11 p.m. EDT on October 3, 1988, after a mission duration of approximately 4 days, 1 hour, 0 minute, and 11 seconds. Capsule Communicator Blaine Hammond Jr. welcomed the crew, saying it was "a great ending to a new beginning".

### Payloads and experiments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-26&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Payloads and experiments")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/TDRS-C_Deployed.jpg/250px-TDRS-C_Deployed.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TDRS-C_Deployed.jpg)

[TDRS-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-3 "TDRS-3") after deployment

TDRS-C, which became TDRS-3 in orbit, and its attached [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS), were deployed from _Discovery_'s cargo bay six hours and 13 minutes into the flight. The first stage of the IUS placed TDRS-3 in a transfer orbit, and the second stage placed it in a [geosynchronous orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit") on September 30, 1988. TDRS-3 moved into position over the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") south of [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") at 171° west [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude "Longitude"). It joined [TDRS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-1 "TDRS-1") in tracking Earth-orbiting spacecraft; a sister satellite, [TDRS-B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-B "TDRS-B"), was lost in the _Challenger_ accident. Also in the payload bay was the Orbiter Experiments Autonomous Supporting Instrumentation System (OASIS). OASIS recorded environmental data on the orbiter and the TDRS payload during various inflight phases.

All the mission's mid-deck experiments were deemed to have been performed successfully. However, there were some glitches with two of the five materials science experiments. In the Protein Crystal Growth (PCG) experiment, two of the 11 [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") processed – including an [enzyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme") believed to be key to the replication of [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") – did not produce crystals suitable for analysis. Also, there were some equipment problems with the Automated Directional Solidification Furnace (ADSF), an experiment to investigate the melting and solidification of various materials in [zero-gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness").

The materials processing experiments included two Shuttle Student Involvement Projects, one on [titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium") grain formation and the other on controlling [crystal growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_growth "Crystal growth") with a membrane. Another materials science experiment, the Physical Vapor Transport of Organic Solids-2 (PVTOS-2), was a joint project of NASA's Office of Commercial Programs and the [3M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M "3M") company.

Three [life sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_life_sciences "List of life sciences") experiments were conducted, including one on the aggregation of [red blood cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cells "Red blood cells"), intended to help determine if microgravity can play a beneficial role in clinical research and medical diagnostic tests. Two further experiments involved atmospheric sciences, while one was in communications research.

### Damage to thermal protection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-26&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Damage to thermal protection")]

_Discovery_ suffered severe damage to its thermal protection tiles in the underwing area. Post-flight analysis showed that the impact of a 30 cm (12 in) long piece of cork insulation during ascent was the culprit. The origin of the debris was the forward field joint on the right-hand SRB. The damage was such that, during re-entry, the thermal protection tile eroded almost completely.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-Young-4) A similar chain of events ultimately led to the [loss of _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") fifteen years later.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-26&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to awaken a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-Wakeup_Calls-5) Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-Wakeup_Calls-5)[Kathryn D. Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_D._Sullivan "Kathryn D. Sullivan") chose the wakeup music for STS-26, including a contribution from [Robin Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Williams "Robin Williams"), who provided a pastiche of his _[Good Morning, Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Morning,\_Vietnam "Good Morning, Vietnam")_ radio greeting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26#cite_note-Sullivan-6)

**STS-42** was a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ mission with the [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") module. Liftoff was originally scheduled for 8:45 [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") (13:45 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")) on January 22, 1992, but the launch was delayed due to weather constraints. _Discovery_ successfully lifted off an hour later at 9:52:33 EST (14:52:33 UTC) on her 14th flight.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-NASASummary-1) The main goal of the mission was to study the effects of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") on a variety of [organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism"). The shuttle landed at 8:07:17 [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") (16:07:17 UTC) on January 30, 1992, on Runway 22, [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-NASASummary-1) STS-42 was the first of two flights in 1992 of _Discovery_, the second of which occurred during [STS-53](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53 "STS-53"), which launched on December 2, 1992. The mission was also the last mission of the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ to have a seven-member crew until [STS-82](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82"), which was launched on February 11, 1997.

The astronauts were divided into a red team and a blue team to allow around-the-clock monitoring of experiments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-2)

The crew of STS-42 included the first non-American astronauts on a shuttle mission since the _Challenger_ disaster, [Ulf D. Merbold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulf_Merbold "Ulf Merbold") and [Roberta Bondar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberta_Bondar "Roberta Bondar"). Merbold was [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany") first astronaut and was making his second flight on the shuttle. Bondar was [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada")'s first female astronaut.

[Mary L. Cleave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_L._Cleave "Mary L. Cleave") was originally selected to fly as Mission Specialist 3 for this mission but withdrew herself for personal reasons. She was replaced by [Manley Lanier "Sonny" Carter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Carter "Sonny Carter"), who died seven months prior to the launch in a plane crash. David Hilmers was then chosen to replace him.

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-42&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/STS-42_Launch.jpg/250px-STS-42_Launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-42_Launch.jpg)

_Discovery_ lifts off at the start of STS-42.

STS-42 was launched on January 22, 1992, 9:52:33 a.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"). The launch was delayed by one hour due to weather constraints. The launch weight was 243,396 lb (110,403 kg).

_Discovery_ carried into orbit the [International Microgravity Laboratory-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") (IML-1), a pressurized crewed [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") module, to explore in depth the complex effects of [weightlessness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") on [living organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism") and materials processing. The international crew, divided into Red and Blue teams, conducted experiments on the human nervous system's adaptation to low gravity and the effects of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") on other life forms such as [shrimp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrimp "Shrimp")[eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg "Egg"), [lentil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lentil "Lentil") seedlings, [fruit fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drosophila_melanogaster "Drosophila melanogaster") eggs and [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria"). Low gravity materials processing experiments included [crystal growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_growth "Crystal growth") from a variety of substances such as [enzymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme"), [mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element) "Mercury (element)"), [iodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine "Iodine") and a [virus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virus "Virus"). Other [payloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload "Payload") included 10 [Get Away Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Away_Special "Get Away Special") (GAS) canisters, a number of middeck payloads, two Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) experiments, and an [Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") developed [ultraviolet telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet_astronomy "Ultraviolet astronomy")_Endeavour_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-4) Middeck payloads included Gelation of SOLS: Applied Microgravity Research (GOSAMR), Investigations into [Polymer Membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymeric_membrane "Polymeric membrane") Processing (IPMP) and the Radiation Monitoring Experiment (RME-III).

The mission landed on January 30, 1992, 8:07:17 a.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone"), Runway 22, [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), after being extended by a day for continued scientific experimentation. The rollout distance was 9,811 ft (2,990 m). The orbiter returned to [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on February 16, 1992. The landing weight was 218,016 lb (98,890 kg).

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-42&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The four stars in the lower blue field and two stars in the upper blue field of the insignia symbolize the flight's numerical designation in the Space Transportation System's mission sequence. The single gold star above the horizon on the right is in honor of [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut")[Manley Lanier "Sonny" Carter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Carter "Sonny Carter"), who was killed in the crash of [Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Southeast_Airlines_Flight_2311 "Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311") in [Brunswick, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick,_Georgia "Brunswick, Georgia") while on a commercial airplane traveling for NASA. Carter was originally assigned as a mission specialist on STS-42 at the time of his death.

**STS-42** was a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ mission with the [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") module. Liftoff was originally scheduled for 8:45 [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") (13:45 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")) on January 22, 1992, but the launch was delayed due to weather constraints. _Discovery_ successfully lifted off an hour later at 9:52:33 EST (14:52:33 UTC) on her 14th flight.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-NASASummary-1) The main goal of the mission was to study the effects of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") on a variety of [organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism"). The shuttle landed at 8:07:17 [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") (16:07:17 UTC) on January 30, 1992, on Runway 22, [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-NASASummary-1) STS-42 was the first of two flights in 1992 of _Discovery_, the second of which occurred during [STS-53](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53 "STS-53"), which launched on December 2, 1992. The mission was also the last mission of the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ to have a seven-member crew until [STS-82](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82"), which was launched on February 11, 1997.

The astronauts were divided into a red team and a blue team to allow around-the-clock monitoring of experiments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-2)

The crew of STS-42 included the first non-American astronauts on a shuttle mission since the _Challenger_ disaster, [Ulf D. Merbold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulf_Merbold "Ulf Merbold") and [Roberta Bondar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberta_Bondar "Roberta Bondar"). Merbold was [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany") first astronaut and was making his second flight on the shuttle. Bondar was [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada")'s first female astronaut.

[Mary L. Cleave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_L._Cleave "Mary L. Cleave") was originally selected to fly as Mission Specialist 3 for this mission but withdrew herself for personal reasons. She was replaced by [Manley Lanier "Sonny" Carter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Carter "Sonny Carter"), who died seven months prior to the launch in a plane crash. David Hilmers was then chosen to replace him.

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-42&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/STS-42_Launch.jpg/250px-STS-42_Launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-42_Launch.jpg)

_Discovery_ lifts off at the start of STS-42.

STS-42 was launched on January 22, 1992, 9:52:33 a.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"). The launch was delayed by one hour due to weather constraints. The launch weight was 243,396 lb (110,403 kg).

_Discovery_ carried into orbit the [International Microgravity Laboratory-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") (IML-1), a pressurized crewed [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") module, to explore in depth the complex effects of [weightlessness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") on [living organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism") and materials processing. The international crew, divided into Red and Blue teams, conducted experiments on the human nervous system's adaptation to low gravity and the effects of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") on other life forms such as [shrimp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrimp "Shrimp")[eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg "Egg"), [lentil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lentil "Lentil") seedlings, [fruit fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drosophila_melanogaster "Drosophila melanogaster") eggs and [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria"). Low gravity materials processing experiments included [crystal growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_growth "Crystal growth") from a variety of substances such as [enzymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme"), [mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element) "Mercury (element)"), [iodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine "Iodine") and a [virus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virus "Virus"). Other [payloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload "Payload") included 10 [Get Away Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Away_Special "Get Away Special") (GAS) canisters, a number of middeck payloads, two Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) experiments, and an [Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") developed [ultraviolet telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet_astronomy "Ultraviolet astronomy")_Endeavour_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-42#cite_note-4) Middeck payloads included Gelation of SOLS: Applied Microgravity Research (GOSAMR), Investigations into [Polymer Membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymeric_membrane "Polymeric membrane") Processing (IPMP) and the Radiation Monitoring Experiment (RME-III).

The mission landed on January 30, 1992, 8:07:17 a.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone"), Runway 22, [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), after being extended by a day for continued scientific experimentation. The rollout distance was 9,811 ft (2,990 m). The orbiter returned to [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on February 16, 1992. The landing weight was 218,016 lb (98,890 kg).

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-42&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The four stars in the lower blue field and two stars in the upper blue field of the insignia symbolize the flight's numerical designation in the Space Transportation System's mission sequence. The single gold star above the horizon on the right is in honor of [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut")[Manley Lanier "Sonny" Carter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Carter "Sonny Carter"), who was killed in the crash of [Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Southeast_Airlines_Flight_2311 "Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311") in [Brunswick, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick,_Georgia "Brunswick, Georgia") while on a commercial airplane traveling for NASA. Carter was originally assigned as a mission specialist on STS-42 at the time of his death.

**STS-29** was the 28th [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission, during which Space Shuttle _Discovery_ inserted a [Tracking and Data Relay Satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._tracking_and_data_relay_satellite "U.S. tracking and data relay satellite") (TDRS) into [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") orbit.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STS-29_Press_Kit-1) It was the third shuttle mission following the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on March 13, 1989.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-LATimes_1989-03-14-2)**STS-29R** was the eighth flight of _Discovery_ and the 28th Space Shuttle mission overall; its planned predecessor, [STS-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-28 "STS-28"), was delayed until August 1989.

The mission was technically designated **STS-29R** as the original STS-29 designator belonged to [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A"), the 22nd Space Shuttle mission. Official documentation and paperwork for that mission contained the designator STS-29 when it was allocated to Space Shuttle _Columbia_ and later as STS-30 when allocated to _Challenger_. As [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") was designated STS-33, future flights with the STS-26 through [STS-33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-33 "STS-33") designators would require the **R** in their documentation to avoid conflicts in tracking data from one mission to another.

Prior to the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), this mission was slated to launch in June 1986 as [STS-61-H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-H "STS-61-H") with _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ as the spacecraft. [Anna L. Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Lee_Fisher "Anna Lee Fisher") was originally assigned to be as mission specialist, which would have been her second spaceflight. Fisher chose to leave from NASA in order to be with her family and was replaced by rookie [James P. Bagian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_P._Bagian "James P. Bagian"). This mission would include payload specialists from [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), however, they did not have a chance to fly again.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-29&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

_Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B"), Kennedy Space Center, at 9:57:00 a.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on March 13, 1989.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-Chen_2012-4) The launch was originally scheduled for February 18, 1989, but was postponed to allow for the replacement of faulty [liquid oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_oxygen "Liquid oxygen") turbopumps on the three main engines. The amended target date of March 11, 1989, was postponed by 1 day, because of the failure of a master event controller (MEC); #2 when it was powered up during prelaunch checkout,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) as well as an additional day to replace a faulty fuel preburner oxidizer valve (FPOV).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) On the rescheduled launch day of March 13, 1989, the launch was delayed for nearly two hours because of ground fog and high upper winds.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) A waiver was approved for the orbiter's wing loads.

The primary payload was [TDRS-D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-4 "TDRS-4"), the third and final component of the [Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") (TDRSS) constellation in [geosynchronous orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STS-29_Press_Kit-1) The three on-orbit satellites were stationed over the [equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator "Equator") at about 35,900 km (22,300 mi) above Earth; two of them were positioned 130° apart, while the third was located between them as an on-orbit spare.

On Flight Day 1, one of three cryogenic hydrogen tanks which supplied shuttle's electricity-generating fuel cells exhibited erratic pressure fluctuations. It was deactivated while engineers studied the problem, and the crew was told to conserve electrical power. The tank was reactivated on Flight Day 3, March 15, 1989, and operated successfully thereafter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-MSER_STS-29-6)

_Discovery_ landed on March 18, 1989, after orbit 80, one orbit earlier than planned, in order to avoid possible excessive wind buildup expected at the landing site. The shuttle touched down on Runway 22 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at 9:35:51 a.m. EST. The total mission duration was 4 days, 23 hours, 38 minutes, and 52 seconds.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5)

### Payload and experiments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-29&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Payload and experiments")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/TDRS_horizon.jpg/250px-TDRS_horizon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TDRS_horizon.jpg)

[TDRS-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-4 "TDRS-4") after deployment

The mission's primary payload was TDRS-D,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) which became TDRS-4 after deployment, and its attached [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS). The satellite was deployed from the shuttle's payload bay less than six hours after launch, at 3:12 a.m. EST. The first-stage orbit burn of the IUS took place an hour later, and the second burn to circularize the orbit occurred 12 hours and 30 minutes into the mission. The satellite was stationed at 41.0° West [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude "Longitude").

_Discovery_ also carried eight [secondary payloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_payload "Secondary payload"), including two Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) experiments. One student experiment, using four live [rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat "Rat") with tiny pieces of bone removed from their bodies, was to test whether the environmental effects of space flight inhibit bone healing. The other student experiment was to fly 32 [chicken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken "Chicken")[eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg_(food) "Egg (food)") to determine the effects of space flight on fertilized chicken [embryos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryo "Embryo").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-Brown_1990-7)

One experiment, mounted in the payload bay, was only termed "partially successful". The Space Station Heat Pipe Advanced Radiator Element (SHARE), a potential cooling system for the planned [Space Station _Freedom_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Station_Freedom "Space Station Freedom"), operated continuously for less than 30 minutes under powered electrical loads. The failure was blamed on the faulty design of the equipment, especially the manifold section.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-AIAA_Share_Paper-8)

All other experiments operated successfully. [Crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") were obtained from all the [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") in the Protein Crystal Growth (PCG) experiment. The Chromosomes and Plant Cell Division in Space (CHROMEX), a life sciences experiment, was designed to show the effects of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") on root development. An [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") (70 mm) camera was used to film a variety of scenes for the 1990 IMAX film [_Blue Planet_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Planet_(1990_film) "Blue Planet (1990 film)"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-LATimes_1989-03-18-9) including the effects of floods, hurricanes, wildfires and volcanic eruptions on Earth. A ground-based [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") experiment used the orbiter as a calibration target for the [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) in [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-SOAR_90-10)

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-29&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-Wakeup_Calls-11)

**STS-29** was the 28th [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission, during which Space Shuttle _Discovery_ inserted a [Tracking and Data Relay Satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._tracking_and_data_relay_satellite "U.S. tracking and data relay satellite") (TDRS) into [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") orbit.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STS-29_Press_Kit-1) It was the third shuttle mission following the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on March 13, 1989.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-LATimes_1989-03-14-2)**STS-29R** was the eighth flight of _Discovery_ and the 28th Space Shuttle mission overall; its planned predecessor, [STS-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-28 "STS-28"), was delayed until August 1989.

The mission was technically designated **STS-29R** as the original STS-29 designator belonged to [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A"), the 22nd Space Shuttle mission. Official documentation and paperwork for that mission contained the designator STS-29 when it was allocated to Space Shuttle _Columbia_ and later as STS-30 when allocated to _Challenger_. As [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") was designated STS-33, future flights with the STS-26 through [STS-33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-33 "STS-33") designators would require the **R** in their documentation to avoid conflicts in tracking data from one mission to another.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-29&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Crew")]

Prior to the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), this mission was slated to launch in June 1986 as [STS-61-H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-H "STS-61-H") with _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ as the spacecraft. [Anna L. Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Lee_Fisher "Anna Lee Fisher") was originally assigned to be as mission specialist, which would have been her second spaceflight. Fisher chose to leave from NASA in order to be with her family and was replaced by rookie [James P. Bagian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_P._Bagian "James P. Bagian"). This mission would include payload specialists from [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), however, they did not have a chance to fly again.

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-29&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

_Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B"), Kennedy Space Center, at 9:57:00 a.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on March 13, 1989.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-Chen_2012-4) The launch was originally scheduled for February 18, 1989, but was postponed to allow for the replacement of faulty [liquid oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_oxygen "Liquid oxygen") turbopumps on the three main engines. The amended target date of March 11, 1989, was postponed by 1 day, because of the failure of a master event controller (MEC); #2 when it was powered up during prelaunch checkout,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) as well as an additional day to replace a faulty fuel preburner oxidizer valve (FPOV).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) On the rescheduled launch day of March 13, 1989, the launch was delayed for nearly two hours because of ground fog and high upper winds.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) A waiver was approved for the orbiter's wing loads.

The primary payload was [TDRS-D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-4 "TDRS-4"), the third and final component of the [Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") (TDRSS) constellation in [geosynchronous orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosynchronous_orbit "Geosynchronous orbit").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STS-29_Press_Kit-1) The three on-orbit satellites were stationed over the [equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator "Equator") at about 35,900 km (22,300 mi) above Earth; two of them were positioned 130° apart, while the third was located between them as an on-orbit spare.

On Flight Day 1, one of three cryogenic hydrogen tanks which supplied shuttle's electricity-generating fuel cells exhibited erratic pressure fluctuations. It was deactivated while engineers studied the problem, and the crew was told to conserve electrical power. The tank was reactivated on Flight Day 3, March 15, 1989, and operated successfully thereafter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-MSER_STS-29-6)

_Discovery_ landed on March 18, 1989, after orbit 80, one orbit earlier than planned, in order to avoid possible excessive wind buildup expected at the landing site. The shuttle touched down on Runway 22 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at 9:35:51 a.m. EST. The total mission duration was 4 days, 23 hours, 38 minutes, and 52 seconds.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5)

### Payload and experiments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-29&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Payload and experiments")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/TDRS_horizon.jpg/250px-TDRS_horizon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TDRS_horizon.jpg)

[TDRS-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TDRS-4 "TDRS-4") after deployment

The mission's primary payload was TDRS-D,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-STIsummary-5) which became TDRS-4 after deployment, and its attached [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS). The satellite was deployed from the shuttle's payload bay less than six hours after launch, at 3:12 a.m. EST. The first-stage orbit burn of the IUS took place an hour later, and the second burn to circularize the orbit occurred 12 hours and 30 minutes into the mission. The satellite was stationed at 41.0° West [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude "Longitude").

_Discovery_ also carried eight [secondary payloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_payload "Secondary payload"), including two Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) experiments. One student experiment, using four live [rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat "Rat") with tiny pieces of bone removed from their bodies, was to test whether the environmental effects of space flight inhibit bone healing. The other student experiment was to fly 32 [chicken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken "Chicken")[eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg_(food) "Egg (food)") to determine the effects of space flight on fertilized chicken [embryos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryo "Embryo").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-Brown_1990-7)

One experiment, mounted in the payload bay, was only termed "partially successful". The Space Station Heat Pipe Advanced Radiator Element (SHARE), a potential cooling system for the planned [Space Station _Freedom_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Station_Freedom "Space Station Freedom"), operated continuously for less than 30 minutes under powered electrical loads. The failure was blamed on the faulty design of the equipment, especially the manifold section.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-AIAA_Share_Paper-8)

All other experiments operated successfully. [Crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") were obtained from all the [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") in the Protein Crystal Growth (PCG) experiment. The Chromosomes and Plant Cell Division in Space (CHROMEX), a life sciences experiment, was designed to show the effects of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") on root development. An [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") (70 mm) camera was used to film a variety of scenes for the 1990 IMAX film [_Blue Planet_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Planet_(1990_film) "Blue Planet (1990 film)"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-LATimes_1989-03-18-9) including the effects of floods, hurricanes, wildfires and volcanic eruptions on Earth. A ground-based [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") experiment used the orbiter as a calibration target for the [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) in [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-SOAR_90-10)

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-29&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-29#cite_note-Wakeup_Calls-11)

**STS-31** was the 35th mission of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s Space Shuttle program and the tenth flight of the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_. The primary purpose of this mission was the deployment of the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") (HST) into [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit"). _Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") on April 24, 1990, from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida").

Following the Challenger accident clarification was required on mission numbering. As [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") was also designated STS-33, future flights with the previous STS-26 through [STS-33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-33 "STS-33") designators would require the **R** in their documentation to avoid conflicts in tracking data from one mission to another.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_Discovery_'s crew deployed the Hubble Space Telescope on April 25, 1990, and then spent the rest of the mission tending to various scientific experiments in the Shuttle's payload bay as well as operating a set of [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") cameras to record the mission. _Discovery_'s launch marked the first time since January 1986 that two Space Shuttles had been on the launch pad at the same time – _Discovery_ on 39B and [_Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on 39A.

### Crew notes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-31&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Crew notes")]

This mission was originally to be flown in August 1986 as [STS-61-J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-J "STS-61-J") using [_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis"), but was postponed due to the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"). [John W. Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Young_(astronaut) "John Young (astronaut)") was originally assigned to command this mission,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-2) which would have been his seventh spaceflight, but was reassigned to an administrative position and was replaced by [Loren J. Shriver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loren_Shriver "Loren Shriver") in 1988.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-JSC_Press_1988-3)

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-31&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/STS-31_Launch_-_GPN-2000-000684.jpg/330px-STS-31_Launch_-_GPN-2000-000684.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-31_Launch_-_GPN-2000-000684.jpg)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launches from LC-39B for STS-31 with _Columbia_ on LC-39A in preparation for [STS-35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-35 "STS-35").

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/1990_s31_IMAX_view_of_HST_in_payload_bay.jpg/330px-1990_s31_IMAX_view_of_HST_in_payload_bay.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1990_s31_IMAX_view_of_HST_in_payload_bay.jpg)

Hubble Space Telescope in the cargo bay of _Discovery_

STS-31 was launched on April 24, 1990, at 12:33:51[UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time") (8:33:51 am[EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Daylight_Time "Eastern Daylight Time"), local time at the launch site). A launch attempt on April 10, 1990, was scrubbed at T _−_ 4 minutes for a faulty valve in [auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit") (APU) number one. The APU was eventually replaced, and the Hubble Space Telescope's batteries were recharged. On launch day, the countdown was briefly halted at T _−_ 31 seconds when _Discovery_'s computers failed to shut down a fuel valve line on ground support equipment. Engineers manually commanded the valve to close and the countdown continued.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-MSER_STS-31-4)

The main purpose of this mission was to deploy Hubble. It was designed to operate above the Earth's turbulent and obscuring atmosphere to observe celestial objects at [ultraviolet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet "Ultraviolet"), [visible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visible_spectrum "Visible spectrum") and [near-infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared")[wavelengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength "Wavelength"). The Hubble mission was a joint NASA-ESA ([European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency")) effort going back to the late 1970s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-NewScientist_1990-07-07-5) The rest of the mission was devoted to photography and onboard experiments. To launch HST into an orbit that guaranteed longevity, _Discovery_ entered an orbit of around 613×615 km (381×382 mi). At one point during the mission, _Discovery_ briefly reached an [apogee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apsis "Apsis") of 621 km (386 mi), the highest altitude ever reached by a Shuttle orbiter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-6) The record height also permitted the crew to photograph Earth's large-scale geographic features not apparent from lower orbits. Motion pictures were recorded by two IMAX cameras, and the results appeared in the 1994 IMAX film _[Destiny in Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny\_in\_Space "Destiny in Space")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Smithsonian_IMAX_Camera-7) Experiments on the mission included a biomedical technology study, advanced materials research, particle contamination and ionizing radiation measurements, and a student science project studying zero-gravity effects on electronic arcs. _Discovery_'s reentry from its higher-than-usual orbit required a deorbit burn of 4 minutes and 58 seconds, the longest in Shuttle history up to that time.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-STS-31_SSMR-8)_Discovery_ orbited the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") 80 times during the mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-STS-31_SSMR-8)

During the deployment of Hubble, one of the observatory's solar arrays stopped as it unfurled. While ground controllers searched for a way to command HST to unreel the [solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panels_on_spacecraft "Solar panels on spacecraft"), Mission Specialists McCandless and Sullivan began preparing for a contingency [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") in the event that the array could not be deployed through ground control. The array eventually came free and unfurled through ground control while McCandless and Sullivan were pre-breathing inside the partially depressurized airlock.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Goodman_2009-9)

Secondary payloads included the [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") Cargo Bay Camera (ICBC) to document operations outside the crew cabin and a handheld IMAX camera for use inside the orbiter. Also included were the Ascent Particle Monitor (APM) to detect particulate matter in the payload bay; a Protein Crystal Growth (PCG) experiment to provide data on growing [protein crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_crystallization "Protein crystallization") in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment"), [Radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation "Radiation") Monitoring Equipment III (RME III) to measure [gamma ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray") levels in the crew cabin; Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP) to determine porosity control in the microgravity environment, and an [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) experiment.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-STS-31_SSMR-8)

The mission marked the flight of an 5 kg (11 lb)[human skull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_skull "Human skull"), which served as the primary element of "Detailed Secondary Objective 469", also known as the In-flight Radiation Dose Distribution (IDRD) experiment. This joint NASA/[DoD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") experiment was designed to examine the penetration of [radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation "Radiation") into the human cranium during spaceflight. The female skull was seated in a plastic matrix, representative of tissue, and sliced into ten layers. Hundreds of thermo-luminescent [dosimeters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dosimeters "Dosimeters") were mounted in the skull's layers to record radiation levels at multiple depths. This experiment, which also flew on [STS-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-28 "STS-28") and [STS-36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-36 "STS-36"), was located in the shuttle's mid-deck lockers on all three flights, recording radiation levels at different orbital inclinations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-MacKnight_1991-10)

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 22 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") on April 29, 1990, at 13:49:57 UTC (6:49:57 am[PDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Daylight_Time "Pacific Daylight Time"), local time at the landing site). The landing had a rollout distance of 2,705 m (8,875 ft), took 61 seconds, and marked the first use of carbon brakes on a shuttle. _Discovery_ was returned to Kennedy Space Center after STS-31 on May 7, 1990.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Archives_STS-31-11)

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-31&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), which was first used to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by their families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Wakeup_Calls-12)

**STS-31** was the 35th mission of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s Space Shuttle program and the tenth flight of the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_. The primary purpose of this mission was the deployment of the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") (HST) into [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit"). _Discovery_ lifted off from [Launch Complex 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") on April 24, 1990, from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida").

Following the Challenger accident clarification was required on mission numbering. As [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L") was also designated STS-33, future flights with the previous STS-26 through [STS-33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-33 "STS-33") designators would require the **R** in their documentation to avoid conflicts in tracking data from one mission to another.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_Discovery_'s crew deployed the Hubble Space Telescope on April 25, 1990, and then spent the rest of the mission tending to various scientific experiments in the Shuttle's payload bay as well as operating a set of [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") cameras to record the mission. _Discovery_'s launch marked the first time since January 1986 that two Space Shuttles had been on the launch pad at the same time – _Discovery_ on 39B and [_Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on 39A.
