### Crew notes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-31&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Crew notes")]

This mission was originally to be flown in August 1986 as [STS-61-J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-J "STS-61-J") using [_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis"), but was postponed due to the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"). [John W. Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Young_(astronaut) "John Young (astronaut)") was originally assigned to command this mission,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-2) which would have been his seventh spaceflight, but was reassigned to an administrative position and was replaced by [Loren J. Shriver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loren_Shriver "Loren Shriver") in 1988.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-JSC_Press_1988-3)

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-31&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/STS-31_Launch_-_GPN-2000-000684.jpg/330px-STS-31_Launch_-_GPN-2000-000684.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-31_Launch_-_GPN-2000-000684.jpg)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launches from LC-39B for STS-31 with _Columbia_ on LC-39A in preparation for [STS-35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-35 "STS-35").

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/1990_s31_IMAX_view_of_HST_in_payload_bay.jpg/330px-1990_s31_IMAX_view_of_HST_in_payload_bay.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1990_s31_IMAX_view_of_HST_in_payload_bay.jpg)

Hubble Space Telescope in the cargo bay of _Discovery_

STS-31 was launched on April 24, 1990, at 12:33:51[UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time") (8:33:51 am[EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Daylight_Time "Eastern Daylight Time"), local time at the launch site). A launch attempt on April 10, 1990, was scrubbed at T _−_ 4 minutes for a faulty valve in [auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit") (APU) number one. The APU was eventually replaced, and the Hubble Space Telescope's batteries were recharged. On launch day, the countdown was briefly halted at T _−_ 31 seconds when _Discovery_'s computers failed to shut down a fuel valve line on ground support equipment. Engineers manually commanded the valve to close and the countdown continued.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-MSER_STS-31-4)

The main purpose of this mission was to deploy Hubble. It was designed to operate above the Earth's turbulent and obscuring atmosphere to observe celestial objects at [ultraviolet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet "Ultraviolet"), [visible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visible_spectrum "Visible spectrum") and [near-infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared")[wavelengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength "Wavelength"). The Hubble mission was a joint NASA-ESA ([European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency")) effort going back to the late 1970s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-NewScientist_1990-07-07-5) The rest of the mission was devoted to photography and onboard experiments. To launch HST into an orbit that guaranteed longevity, _Discovery_ entered an orbit of around 613×615 km (381×382 mi). At one point during the mission, _Discovery_ briefly reached an [apogee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apsis "Apsis") of 621 km (386 mi), the highest altitude ever reached by a Shuttle orbiter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-6) The record height also permitted the crew to photograph Earth's large-scale geographic features not apparent from lower orbits. Motion pictures were recorded by two IMAX cameras, and the results appeared in the 1994 IMAX film _[Destiny in Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny\_in\_Space "Destiny in Space")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Smithsonian_IMAX_Camera-7) Experiments on the mission included a biomedical technology study, advanced materials research, particle contamination and ionizing radiation measurements, and a student science project studying zero-gravity effects on electronic arcs. _Discovery_'s reentry from its higher-than-usual orbit required a deorbit burn of 4 minutes and 58 seconds, the longest in Shuttle history up to that time.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-STS-31_SSMR-8)_Discovery_ orbited the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") 80 times during the mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-STS-31_SSMR-8)

During the deployment of Hubble, one of the observatory's solar arrays stopped as it unfurled. While ground controllers searched for a way to command HST to unreel the [solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panels_on_spacecraft "Solar panels on spacecraft"), Mission Specialists McCandless and Sullivan began preparing for a contingency [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") in the event that the array could not be deployed through ground control. The array eventually came free and unfurled through ground control while McCandless and Sullivan were pre-breathing inside the partially depressurized airlock.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Goodman_2009-9)

Secondary payloads included the [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") Cargo Bay Camera (ICBC) to document operations outside the crew cabin and a handheld IMAX camera for use inside the orbiter. Also included were the Ascent Particle Monitor (APM) to detect particulate matter in the payload bay; a Protein Crystal Growth (PCG) experiment to provide data on growing [protein crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_crystallization "Protein crystallization") in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment"), [Radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation "Radiation") Monitoring Equipment III (RME III) to measure [gamma ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray") levels in the crew cabin; Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP) to determine porosity control in the microgravity environment, and an [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) experiment.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-STS-31_SSMR-8)

The mission marked the flight of an 5 kg (11 lb)[human skull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_skull "Human skull"), which served as the primary element of "Detailed Secondary Objective 469", also known as the In-flight Radiation Dose Distribution (IDRD) experiment. This joint NASA/[DoD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") experiment was designed to examine the penetration of [radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation "Radiation") into the human cranium during spaceflight. The female skull was seated in a plastic matrix, representative of tissue, and sliced into ten layers. Hundreds of thermo-luminescent [dosimeters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dosimeters "Dosimeters") were mounted in the skull's layers to record radiation levels at multiple depths. This experiment, which also flew on [STS-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-28 "STS-28") and [STS-36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-36 "STS-36"), was located in the shuttle's mid-deck lockers on all three flights, recording radiation levels at different orbital inclinations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-MacKnight_1991-10)

_Discovery_ landed on Runway 22 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") on April 29, 1990, at 13:49:57 UTC (6:49:57 am[PDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Daylight_Time "Pacific Daylight Time"), local time at the landing site). The landing had a rollout distance of 2,705 m (8,875 ft), took 61 seconds, and marked the first use of carbon brakes on a shuttle. _Discovery_ was returned to Kennedy Space Center after STS-31 on May 7, 1990.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Archives_STS-31-11)

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-31&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), which was first used to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by their families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31#cite_note-Wakeup_Calls-12)

**STS-41** was the 36th [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission and the eleventh mission of the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_. The four-day mission had a primary objective of launching the [_Ulysses_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(spacecraft) "Ulysses (spacecraft)") probe as part of the "[International Solar Polar Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(spacecraft) "Ulysses (spacecraft)")" (ISPM).

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/STS-41_launch.jpg/250px-STS-41_launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-41_launch.jpg)

STS-41 launches from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), on October 6, 1990.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/STS-41_Ulysses_deployment.jpg/250px-STS-41_Ulysses_deployment.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-41_Ulysses_deployment.jpg)

_Ulysses_ after deployment

_Discovery_ lifted off on October 6 1990 at 7:47:16 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"). Liftoff occurred 12 minutes after a two-and-a-half-hour launch window opened that day at 7:35 a.m. EDT. STS-41 featured the heaviest payload to date; _Discovery_ weighed 117,749 kg (259,592 lb).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41#cite_note-lsda_sts41-2)

The primary payload was the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency") (ESA)-built _Ulysses_ spacecraft to explore the polar regions of the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"). Attached to _Ulysses_ were two upper stages, the [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS) and a mission-specific [Payload Assist Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Assist_Module "Payload Assist Module")-S (PAM-S), combined for the first time to send _Ulysses_ toward an out-of-ecliptic trajectory. Other payloads and experiments included the Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultraviolet (SSBUV) experiment, Intelsat Solar Array Coupon (ISAC), Chromosome and Plant Cell Division Experiment (CHROMEX), Voice Command System (VCS), Solid Surface Combustion Experiment (SSCE), Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP), Physiological Systems Experiment (PSE), Radiation Monitoring Experiment III (RME III), Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) and [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS).

Six hours after _Discovery_'s launch, _Ulysses_ was deployed from the payload bay. _Ulysses_, a joint project between the European Space Agency and NASA, was the first spacecraft to study the Sun's polar regions. Its voyage to the Sun began with a sixteen-month trip to Jupiter, where the planet's gravitational energy was used to fling _Ulysses_ southward out of the orbital plane of the planets and on toward a solar south pole passage in 1994. The spacecraft crossed back over the orbital plane and made a solar north pole passage in 1995. By the time _Discovery_ touched down at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), _Ulysses_ had already traversed 1,600,000 km (990,000 mi) on its five-year mission.

With _Ulysses_ on its way, the STS-41 crew began an ambitious schedule of science experiments. Flowering plant samples were grown in the CHROMEX-2 module in a [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") and [Stony Brook University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stony_Brook_University "Stony Brook University") experiment. An earlier version of the experiment flown on STS-29 revealed [chromosome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromosome "Chromosome") damage in root tip cells but no damage to control plants on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). By studying plant samples carried on _Discovery_, researchers hoped to determine how the genetic material in the root cells respond to [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment"). The information gained was of importance to future space travelers on long-term expeditions, researchers on the planned [Space Station Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Station_Freedom "Space Station Freedom"), and may contribute to advances in [intensive farming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intensive_farming "Intensive farming") practices on Earth.

Understanding fire behavior in microgravity was part of the continuing research to improve Space Shuttle safety. In a specially designed chamber called the Solid Surface Combustion Experiment (SSCE), a strip of paper was burned and filmed to gain an understanding of the development of flame and its movement in the absence of convection currents. This experiment was sponsored by the [Lewis Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Research_Center "Glenn Research Center") (LeRC) and [Mississippi State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_University "Mississippi State University").

[Atmospheric ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone") depletion is an environmental problem of worldwide concern. At the time, NASA's [Nimbus 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimbus_7 "Nimbus 7") satellite and [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")'s (NOAA) [Television Infrared Observation Satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_Infrared_Observation_Satellite "Television Infrared Observation Satellite") (TIROS) satellites provided daily data to permit researchers to detect ozone trends. The Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultraviolet (SSBUV) instrument from the [Goddard Space Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddard_Space_Flight_Center "Goddard Space Flight Center") carried an ozone detector instrument identical to those on the satellites. By comparing _Discovery_'s measurements with coordinated satellite observations, scientists were able to calibrate their satellite instruments to ensure the most accurate readings possible.

In 1990, a commercial expendable launch vehicle stranded an [INTELSAT VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelsat_VI "Intelsat VI")[communications satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") in [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit"). Before STS-41, NASA was evaluating a possible Shuttle rescue mission in 1992. In preparation for this rescue, [solar arrays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_system "Photovoltaic system"), similar to those on the satellite, were exposed to the conditions of low orbit to determine if they were in any way altered by the [atomic oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_oxygen "Allotropes of oxygen") present. When the returned arrays were closely examined, it was found that the arrays were not significantly damaged. Based on this finding, NASA went ahead and carried out [STS-49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-49 "STS-49") in 1992.

Until STS-41, previous research had shown that during the process of adapting to microgravity, animals and humans experienced loss of [bone mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_density "Bone density"), cardiac [deconditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deconditioning "Deconditioning"), and after prolonged periods (over 30 days), developed [symptoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signs_and_symptoms "Signs and symptoms") similar to that of [terrestrial disuse osteoporosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis "Osteoporosis"). The goal of the STS-41 Physiological Systems Experiment (PSE), sponsored by the [Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames_Research_Center "Ames Research Center") and [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University")'s Center for Cell Research, was to determine if pharmacological treatments would be effective in reducing or eliminating some of these disorders. [Proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein"), developed by [Genentech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genentech "Genentech") of [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), were administered to eight [rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat "Rat") during the flight while another eight rats accompanying them on the flight did not receive the treatment.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/S90-48650.jpg/250px-S90-48650.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S90-48650.jpg)

A view of two [Space Shuttles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") on adjacent KSC Launch Complex 39 pads. _Discovery_ (STS-41) is on [LC-39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") in the background, _Columbia_ ([STS-35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-35 "STS-35")) is on [LC-39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A") in the foreground.

The Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP) experiment was conducted to determine the role convection currents play in membrane formation. Membranes are used in commercial applications for [purification of medicines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), [kidney dialysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_dialysis "Kidney dialysis"), and [water desalination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desalination "Desalination"). This experiment was sponsored in part by the Battelle Advanced Materials Center for the Commercial Development of Space in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio").

During open periods in the STS-41 crew schedule, the astronauts videotaped a number of demonstrations in an effort to create an educational video tape for middle school students. The tape was later distributed nationwide through NASA's Teacher Resource Center network.

The astronauts evaluated the suitability of [graphical user interfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface"). Previous shuttle crews used [Grid Systems laptop computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_Systems_Corporation "Grid Systems Corporation") with command-line interfaces. The evaluation used mostly commercially available hardware and software, including a [Macintosh Portable laptop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_Portable "Macintosh Portable"). The astronauts found the Portable's trackball did not work well in weightlessness. The evaluation was continued on [STS-43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-43 "STS-43"), this time using a Macintosh Portable with a modified trackball.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41#cite_note-3)

Additional crew activities included experimenting with a voice command system (VCS) to control onboard [television cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_video_camera "Professional video camera") and monitoring [ionizing radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionizing_radiation "Ionizing radiation") exposure to the crew within the orbiter cabin.

On October 10,1990, at 6:57:19 a.m. [PDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone"), _Discovery_ landed at Edwards Air Force Base, California, on runway 22. Rollout distance was 2,523 m (8,278 ft), and the rollout time was 49 seconds (including a braking test). _Discovery_ was returned to Kennedy Space Center on October 16,1990.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), which was first used to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by their families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41#cite_note-chronology-4)

**STS-41** was the 36th [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission and the eleventh mission of the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_. The four-day mission had a primary objective of launching the [_Ulysses_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(spacecraft) "Ulysses (spacecraft)") probe as part of the "[International Solar Polar Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(spacecraft) "Ulysses (spacecraft)")" (ISPM).

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/STS-41_launch.jpg/250px-STS-41_launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-41_launch.jpg)

STS-41 launches from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), on October 6, 1990.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/STS-41_Ulysses_deployment.jpg/250px-STS-41_Ulysses_deployment.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-41_Ulysses_deployment.jpg)

_Ulysses_ after deployment

_Discovery_ lifted off on October 6 1990 at 7:47:16 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"). Liftoff occurred 12 minutes after a two-and-a-half-hour launch window opened that day at 7:35 a.m. EDT. STS-41 featured the heaviest payload to date; _Discovery_ weighed 117,749 kg (259,592 lb).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41#cite_note-lsda_sts41-2)

The primary payload was the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency") (ESA)-built _Ulysses_ spacecraft to explore the polar regions of the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"). Attached to _Ulysses_ were two upper stages, the [Inertial Upper Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_Upper_Stage "Inertial Upper Stage") (IUS) and a mission-specific [Payload Assist Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Assist_Module "Payload Assist Module")-S (PAM-S), combined for the first time to send _Ulysses_ toward an out-of-ecliptic trajectory. Other payloads and experiments included the Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultraviolet (SSBUV) experiment, Intelsat Solar Array Coupon (ISAC), Chromosome and Plant Cell Division Experiment (CHROMEX), Voice Command System (VCS), Solid Surface Combustion Experiment (SSCE), Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP), Physiological Systems Experiment (PSE), Radiation Monitoring Experiment III (RME III), Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) and [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS).

Six hours after _Discovery_'s launch, _Ulysses_ was deployed from the payload bay. _Ulysses_, a joint project between the European Space Agency and NASA, was the first spacecraft to study the Sun's polar regions. Its voyage to the Sun began with a sixteen-month trip to Jupiter, where the planet's gravitational energy was used to fling _Ulysses_ southward out of the orbital plane of the planets and on toward a solar south pole passage in 1994. The spacecraft crossed back over the orbital plane and made a solar north pole passage in 1995. By the time _Discovery_ touched down at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), _Ulysses_ had already traversed 1,600,000 km (990,000 mi) on its five-year mission.

With _Ulysses_ on its way, the STS-41 crew began an ambitious schedule of science experiments. Flowering plant samples were grown in the CHROMEX-2 module in a [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") and [Stony Brook University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stony_Brook_University "Stony Brook University") experiment. An earlier version of the experiment flown on STS-29 revealed [chromosome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromosome "Chromosome") damage in root tip cells but no damage to control plants on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). By studying plant samples carried on _Discovery_, researchers hoped to determine how the genetic material in the root cells respond to [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment"). The information gained was of importance to future space travelers on long-term expeditions, researchers on the planned [Space Station Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Station_Freedom "Space Station Freedom"), and may contribute to advances in [intensive farming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intensive_farming "Intensive farming") practices on Earth.

Understanding fire behavior in microgravity was part of the continuing research to improve Space Shuttle safety. In a specially designed chamber called the Solid Surface Combustion Experiment (SSCE), a strip of paper was burned and filmed to gain an understanding of the development of flame and its movement in the absence of convection currents. This experiment was sponsored by the [Lewis Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Research_Center "Glenn Research Center") (LeRC) and [Mississippi State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_University "Mississippi State University").

[Atmospheric ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone") depletion is an environmental problem of worldwide concern. At the time, NASA's [Nimbus 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimbus_7 "Nimbus 7") satellite and [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")'s (NOAA) [Television Infrared Observation Satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_Infrared_Observation_Satellite "Television Infrared Observation Satellite") (TIROS) satellites provided daily data to permit researchers to detect ozone trends. The Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultraviolet (SSBUV) instrument from the [Goddard Space Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddard_Space_Flight_Center "Goddard Space Flight Center") carried an ozone detector instrument identical to those on the satellites. By comparing _Discovery_'s measurements with coordinated satellite observations, scientists were able to calibrate their satellite instruments to ensure the most accurate readings possible.

In 1990, a commercial expendable launch vehicle stranded an [INTELSAT VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelsat_VI "Intelsat VI")[communications satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") in [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit"). Before STS-41, NASA was evaluating a possible Shuttle rescue mission in 1992. In preparation for this rescue, [solar arrays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_system "Photovoltaic system"), similar to those on the satellite, were exposed to the conditions of low orbit to determine if they were in any way altered by the [atomic oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_oxygen "Allotropes of oxygen") present. When the returned arrays were closely examined, it was found that the arrays were not significantly damaged. Based on this finding, NASA went ahead and carried out [STS-49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-49 "STS-49") in 1992.

Until STS-41, previous research had shown that during the process of adapting to microgravity, animals and humans experienced loss of [bone mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_density "Bone density"), cardiac [deconditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deconditioning "Deconditioning"), and after prolonged periods (over 30 days), developed [symptoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signs_and_symptoms "Signs and symptoms") similar to that of [terrestrial disuse osteoporosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis "Osteoporosis"). The goal of the STS-41 Physiological Systems Experiment (PSE), sponsored by the [Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames_Research_Center "Ames Research Center") and [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University")'s Center for Cell Research, was to determine if pharmacological treatments would be effective in reducing or eliminating some of these disorders. [Proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein"), developed by [Genentech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genentech "Genentech") of [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), were administered to eight [rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat "Rat") during the flight while another eight rats accompanying them on the flight did not receive the treatment.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/S90-48650.jpg/250px-S90-48650.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S90-48650.jpg)

A view of two [Space Shuttles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") on adjacent KSC Launch Complex 39 pads. _Discovery_ (STS-41) is on [LC-39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") in the background, _Columbia_ ([STS-35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-35 "STS-35")) is on [LC-39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A") in the foreground.

The Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP) experiment was conducted to determine the role convection currents play in membrane formation. Membranes are used in commercial applications for [purification of medicines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), [kidney dialysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_dialysis "Kidney dialysis"), and [water desalination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desalination "Desalination"). This experiment was sponsored in part by the Battelle Advanced Materials Center for the Commercial Development of Space in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio").

During open periods in the STS-41 crew schedule, the astronauts videotaped a number of demonstrations in an effort to create an educational video tape for middle school students. The tape was later distributed nationwide through NASA's Teacher Resource Center network.

The astronauts evaluated the suitability of [graphical user interfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface"). Previous shuttle crews used [Grid Systems laptop computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_Systems_Corporation "Grid Systems Corporation") with command-line interfaces. The evaluation used mostly commercially available hardware and software, including a [Macintosh Portable laptop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_Portable "Macintosh Portable"). The astronauts found the Portable's trackball did not work well in weightlessness. The evaluation was continued on [STS-43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-43 "STS-43"), this time using a Macintosh Portable with a modified trackball.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41#cite_note-3)

Additional crew activities included experimenting with a voice command system (VCS) to control onboard [television cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_video_camera "Professional video camera") and monitoring [ionizing radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionizing_radiation "Ionizing radiation") exposure to the crew within the orbiter cabin.

On October 10,1990, at 6:57:19 a.m. [PDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone"), _Discovery_ landed at Edwards Air Force Base, California, on runway 22. Rollout distance was 2,523 m (8,278 ft), and the rollout time was 49 seconds (including a braking test). _Discovery_ was returned to Kennedy Space Center on October 16,1990.

**STS-48** was a [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission that launched on September 12, 1991, from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). The orbiter was [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ on her 13th flight. The primary payload was the [Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Atmosphere_Research_Satellite "Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite") (UARS). The mission landed on September 18 at 12:38 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") on runway 22. The mission was completed in 81 revolutions of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") and traveled 3,530,369 km (2,193,670 mi). The 5 astronauts carried out a number of experiments and deployed several satellites. The total launch mass was 108,890 kg (240,060 lb) and the landing mass was 87,440 kg (192,770 lb).

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-48&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/STS48_launch.jpg/250px-STS48_launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS48_launch.jpg)

Liftoff of STS-48

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Upperatmosphereresearchsatellite.jpg/250px-Upperatmosphereresearchsatellite.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Upperatmosphereresearchsatellite.jpg)

UARS on the remote manipulator ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) prior to deployment

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ was launched into a 57.00° [inclination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_inclination "Orbital inclination") orbit from the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) [Launch Complex 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A") at 7:11 p.m. EDT on September 12, 1991. Launch was delayed for 14 minutes at the T−5 minute mark due to a noise problem in the air-to-ground link. The noise cleared itself, and the countdown proceeded normally to launch.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-Clatterbuck_&_Hill_1991-2):15

On the third day of the mission, the Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite (UARS) was deployed from Discovery's payload bay 650 km (400 mi; 350 nmi) above Earth to study human effects on the planet's atmosphere and its shielding [ozone layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_layer "Ozone layer"). The UARS mission objectives were to provide an increased understanding of the energy input into the [upper atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_atmosphere "Upper atmosphere"), [global photochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photochemistry "Photochemistry") of the upper atmosphere, dynamics of the upper atmosphere, the coupling among these processes, and the coupling between the upper and lower atmosphere. This provided data for a coordinated study of the structure, chemistry, energy balance, and physical action of the Earth's middle atmosphere – that slice of air between 16 km (9.9 mi; 8.6 nmi) and 97 km (60 mi; 52 nmi) above the Earth. The UARS was the first major flight element of NASA's Mission to Planet Earth, a multi-year global research program that would use ground-based, airborne, and space-based instruments to study the Earth as a complete environmental system.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-Clatterbuck_&_Hill_1991-2):28 UARS had ten sensing and measuring devices: Cryogenic Limb Array Etalon Spectrometer (CLAES); Improved Stratospheric and Mesospheric Sounder (ISAMS); [Microwave Limb Sounder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave_limb_sounder "Microwave limb sounder") (MLS); Halogen Occultation Experiment (HALOE); High Resolution Doppler Imager (HRDI); Wind Imaging Interferometer (WlNDII); Solar Ultraviolet Spectral Irradiance Monitor (SUSIM); Solar/Stellar Irradiance Comparison Experiment (SOLSTICE); Particle Environment Monitor (PEM) and [Active Cavity Radiometer Irradiance Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACRIMSAT "ACRIMSAT") (ACRIM II). UARS's initial 18-month mission was extended several times – it was finally retired after 14 years of service.

Secondary payloads were: Ascent Particle Monitor (APM); Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE); Shuttle Activation Monitor (SAM); Cosmic Ray Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM); Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment (PARE); Protein Crystal Growth (PCG II-2); Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP); and the [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) experiment.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-sts-48-press-kit-3)

The flight was the first to test an electronic still camera in space, a modified [Nikon NASA F4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikon_NASA_F4 "Nikon NASA F4"). Images obtained during the flight were [monochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monochrome "Monochrome") with 8 bits of digital information per pixel (256 gray levels) and stored on a removable hard disk. The images could be viewed and enhanced on board using a [modified lap-top computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laptop "Laptop") before being transmitted to the ground via the orbiter digital downlinks.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-sts-48-press-kit-3):40

STS-48 was the second post-_Challenger_ mission to have Kennedy Space Center as the planned End-Of-Mission landing site, and the first mission to have a planned night landing at KSC. However, due to weather conditions at KSC in Florida, Discovery flew one extra orbit and landed at Edwards Air Force Base, [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at 3:38 a.m. EDT on September 18, 1991. The orbiter returned to KSC on September 26, 1991.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-4):2

## Ice particles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-48&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ice particles")]

Video while in orbit on September 15, 1991, shows a flash of light and several objects that appear to be flying in an artificial or controlled fashion. NASA explained the objects as ice particles reacting to engine jets.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-7)[Philip C. Plait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Plait "Phil Plait") discussed the issue in his book _[Bad Astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad\_Astronomy "Bad Astronomy")_, agreeing with NASA.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-8) This topic was also discussed in an episode of _[UFO Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO\_Hunters "UFO Hunters")_.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-48&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-:0-9) Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.

| Day | Song | Artist/Composer | Played For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Day 2 | Hound Dog | [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") |  |
| Day 3 | Release Me | Elvis Presley | In anticipation of the release of the UARS |
| Day 4 | [The Bare Necessities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bare_Necessities "The Bare Necessities") | [The Sherman Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sherman_Brothers "The Sherman Brothers") | Ken Reightler, chosen by his daughters (who were in the control room, from the animated 1967 [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney "Disney") film _[The Jungle Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jungle\_Book\_(1967\_film) "The Jungle Book (1967 film)")_, sung by [Phil Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Harris "Phil Harris") as [Baloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baloo "Baloo") and [Bruce Reitherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Reitherman "Bruce Reitherman") as [Mowgli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mowgli "Mowgli")) |
| Day 5 | [Are You Lonesome Tonight?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are_You_Lonesome_Tonight%3F "Are You Lonesome Tonight?") | Elvis Presley | Chosen for its line "Are you sorry we drifted apart?" referring to Discovery's separation from its payload ([UARS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Atmosphere_Research_Satellite "Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite")) |
| Day 6 | [Return to Sender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Sender_(song) "Return to Sender (song)") | Elvis Presley | In anticipation of their landing that day |

**STS-48** was a [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission that launched on September 12, 1991, from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). The orbiter was [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ on her 13th flight. The primary payload was the [Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Atmosphere_Research_Satellite "Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite") (UARS). The mission landed on September 18 at 12:38 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") on runway 22. The mission was completed in 81 revolutions of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") and traveled 3,530,369 km (2,193,670 mi). The 5 astronauts carried out a number of experiments and deployed several satellites. The total launch mass was 108,890 kg (240,060 lb) and the landing mass was 87,440 kg (192,770 lb).

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-48&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/STS48_launch.jpg/250px-STS48_launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS48_launch.jpg)

Liftoff of STS-48

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Upperatmosphereresearchsatellite.jpg/250px-Upperatmosphereresearchsatellite.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Upperatmosphereresearchsatellite.jpg)

UARS on the remote manipulator ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) prior to deployment

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ was launched into a 57.00° [inclination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_inclination "Orbital inclination") orbit from the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) [Launch Complex 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A") at 7:11 p.m. EDT on September 12, 1991. Launch was delayed for 14 minutes at the T−5 minute mark due to a noise problem in the air-to-ground link. The noise cleared itself, and the countdown proceeded normally to launch.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-Clatterbuck_&_Hill_1991-2):15

On the third day of the mission, the Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite (UARS) was deployed from Discovery's payload bay 650 km (400 mi; 350 nmi) above Earth to study human effects on the planet's atmosphere and its shielding [ozone layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_layer "Ozone layer"). The UARS mission objectives were to provide an increased understanding of the energy input into the [upper atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_atmosphere "Upper atmosphere"), [global photochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photochemistry "Photochemistry") of the upper atmosphere, dynamics of the upper atmosphere, the coupling among these processes, and the coupling between the upper and lower atmosphere. This provided data for a coordinated study of the structure, chemistry, energy balance, and physical action of the Earth's middle atmosphere – that slice of air between 16 km (9.9 mi; 8.6 nmi) and 97 km (60 mi; 52 nmi) above the Earth. The UARS was the first major flight element of NASA's Mission to Planet Earth, a multi-year global research program that would use ground-based, airborne, and space-based instruments to study the Earth as a complete environmental system.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-Clatterbuck_&_Hill_1991-2):28 UARS had ten sensing and measuring devices: Cryogenic Limb Array Etalon Spectrometer (CLAES); Improved Stratospheric and Mesospheric Sounder (ISAMS); [Microwave Limb Sounder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave_limb_sounder "Microwave limb sounder") (MLS); Halogen Occultation Experiment (HALOE); High Resolution Doppler Imager (HRDI); Wind Imaging Interferometer (WlNDII); Solar Ultraviolet Spectral Irradiance Monitor (SUSIM); Solar/Stellar Irradiance Comparison Experiment (SOLSTICE); Particle Environment Monitor (PEM) and [Active Cavity Radiometer Irradiance Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACRIMSAT "ACRIMSAT") (ACRIM II). UARS's initial 18-month mission was extended several times – it was finally retired after 14 years of service.

Secondary payloads were: Ascent Particle Monitor (APM); Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE); Shuttle Activation Monitor (SAM); Cosmic Ray Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM); Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment (PARE); Protein Crystal Growth (PCG II-2); Investigations into Polymer Membrane Processing (IPMP); and the [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) experiment.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-sts-48-press-kit-3)

The flight was the first to test an electronic still camera in space, a modified [Nikon NASA F4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikon_NASA_F4 "Nikon NASA F4"). Images obtained during the flight were [monochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monochrome "Monochrome") with 8 bits of digital information per pixel (256 gray levels) and stored on a removable hard disk. The images could be viewed and enhanced on board using a [modified lap-top computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laptop "Laptop") before being transmitted to the ground via the orbiter digital downlinks.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-sts-48-press-kit-3):40

STS-48 was the second post-_Challenger_ mission to have Kennedy Space Center as the planned End-Of-Mission landing site, and the first mission to have a planned night landing at KSC. However, due to weather conditions at KSC in Florida, Discovery flew one extra orbit and landed at Edwards Air Force Base, [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at 3:38 a.m. EDT on September 18, 1991. The orbiter returned to KSC on September 26, 1991.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-4):2

## Ice particles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-48&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ice particles")]

Video while in orbit on September 15, 1991, shows a flash of light and several objects that appear to be flying in an artificial or controlled fashion. NASA explained the objects as ice particles reacting to engine jets.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-7)[Philip C. Plait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Plait "Phil Plait") discussed the issue in his book _[Bad Astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad\_Astronomy "Bad Astronomy")_, agreeing with NASA.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-8) This topic was also discussed in an episode of _[UFO Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO\_Hunters "UFO Hunters")_.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-48&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-48#cite_note-:0-9) Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.

**STS-53** was a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ mission in support of the [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD). It was Discovery's 15th flight. The mission was launched on December 2, 1992, from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). This was also the last mission to have been operated via [MCR-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_C._Kraft_Jr._Mission_Control_Center "Christopher C. Kraft Jr. Mission Control Center") in JSC. Afterwards the room was restored entirely to its Apollo era appearance.

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-53&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

_Discovery_ carried a classified primary payload (DOD-1) for the United States Department of Defense (DoD), two unclassified secondary payloads and nine unclassified middeck experiments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

_Discovery_'s primary payload, [USA-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites") (1992-086B) is also known as ["DoD-1"](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=STSDOD1), and was the shuttle's last major payload for the Department of Defense. The satellite was the third launch of a [Satellite Data System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_Data_System "Satellite Data System")-2 (SDS 2-3) [military communications satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_satellite "Military satellite"), after [USA-40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites") on [STS-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-28 "STS-28") and [STS-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-38 "STS-38")'s deployment of [USA-67](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

Secondary payloads contained in or attached to [Get Away Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Away_Special "Get Away Special") (GAS) hardware in the cargo bay included the Orbital Debris Radar Calibration Spheres ([ODERACS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ODERACS_2A "ODERACS 2A")) satellites and the combined Shuttle Glow Experiment/Cryogenic Heat Pipe Experiment (GCP).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

Middeck experiments included Microcapsules in Space (MIS-l); Space Tissue Loss (STL); Visual Function Tester (VFT-2); Cosmic Radiation Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM); Radiation Monitoring Equipment (RME-III); Fluid Acquisition and Resupply Experiment (FARE); Hand-held, Earth-oriented, Real-time, Cooperative, User-friendly, Location-targeting and Environmental System ([HERCULES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikon_NASA_F4 "Nikon NASA F4")); Battlefield Laser Acquisition Sensor Test (BLAST); and the Cloud Logic to Optimize Use of Defense Systems (CLOUDS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-53&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The five sides represent [the Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon"), the Department of Defense headquarters. The five stars and three stripes of the insignia symbolize the flight's numerical designation in the [Space Transportation System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System "Space Transportation System")'s mission sequence.

**STS-53** was a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ mission in support of the [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD). It was Discovery's 15th flight. The mission was launched on December 2, 1992, from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). This was also the last mission to have been operated via [MCR-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_C._Kraft_Jr._Mission_Control_Center "Christopher C. Kraft Jr. Mission Control Center") in JSC. Afterwards the room was restored entirely to its Apollo era appearance.

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-53&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

_Discovery_ carried a classified primary payload (DOD-1) for the United States Department of Defense (DoD), two unclassified secondary payloads and nine unclassified middeck experiments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

_Discovery_'s primary payload, [USA-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites") (1992-086B) is also known as ["DoD-1"](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=STSDOD1), and was the shuttle's last major payload for the Department of Defense. The satellite was the third launch of a [Satellite Data System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_Data_System "Satellite Data System")-2 (SDS 2-3) [military communications satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_satellite "Military satellite"), after [USA-40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites") on [STS-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-28 "STS-28") and [STS-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-38 "STS-38")'s deployment of [USA-67](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_USA_satellites "List of USA satellites").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

Secondary payloads contained in or attached to [Get Away Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Away_Special "Get Away Special") (GAS) hardware in the cargo bay included the Orbital Debris Radar Calibration Spheres ([ODERACS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ODERACS_2A "ODERACS 2A")) satellites and the combined Shuttle Glow Experiment/Cryogenic Heat Pipe Experiment (GCP).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

Middeck experiments included Microcapsules in Space (MIS-l); Space Tissue Loss (STL); Visual Function Tester (VFT-2); Cosmic Radiation Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM); Radiation Monitoring Equipment (RME-III); Fluid Acquisition and Resupply Experiment (FARE); Hand-held, Earth-oriented, Real-time, Cooperative, User-friendly, Location-targeting and Environmental System ([HERCULES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikon_NASA_F4 "Nikon NASA F4")); Battlefield Laser Acquisition Sensor Test (BLAST); and the Cloud Logic to Optimize Use of Defense Systems (CLOUDS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-53#cite_note-STS53KSC-2)

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-53&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The five sides represent [the Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon"), the Department of Defense headquarters. The five stars and three stripes of the insignia symbolize the flight's numerical designation in the [Space Transportation System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System "Space Transportation System")'s mission sequence.

**STS-56** was a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ mission to perform special experiments. It was Discovery's 16th flight. The mission was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on April 8, 1993.

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-56&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

| Attempt | Planned | Result | Turnaround | Reason | Decision point | Weather go (%) | Notes |

| 1 | 6 Apr 1993, 2:32:00 am | Scrubbed | — | Technical | 6 Apr 1993, 2:31 am​(T−00:00:11) | 80[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-2) | T−9 minute hold extended for one hour due to high temperatures on SSME 1.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Report-3):2 The launch was scrubbed when a liquid hydrogen bleed valve was indicated as open when it was actually closed as required.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4) The erroneous indication was caused by a faulty relay.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-5) |
| 2 | 8 Apr 1993, 1:29:00 am | Success | 1 day 22 hours 57 minutes |  |  | 90[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-6) | Flash evaporator system shut down four minutes into flight, but was manually restarted by the crew.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Report-3):2 |

The primary payload of the flight was the [Atmospheric Laboratory for Applications and Science-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") (ATLAS-2),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Report-3):1 designed to collect data on the relationship between the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun")'s energy output and [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s middle atmosphere and how these factors affect the [ozone layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_layer "Ozone layer"). It included six instruments mounted on a Spacelab pallet in the cargo bay, with the seventh mounted on the wall of the bay in two [Get Away Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Away_Special "Get Away Special") (GAS) canisters. Atmospheric instruments included the Atmospheric Trace Molecule Spectroscopy (ATMOS) experiment, the Millimeter Wave Atmospheric Sounder (MAS), and the Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultraviolet (SSBUV/A) spectrometer (on the cargo bay wall). Solar science instruments were the solar spectrometry instrument SOLSPEC,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-SOLSPEC-7) the Solar Ultraviolet Irradiance Monitor (SUSIM), and the Active Cavity Radiometer (ACR) and Solar Constant (SOLCON) experiments.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

ATLAS-2 is one element of NASA's Mission to Planet Earth program. All seven ATLAS-2 instruments first flew on [ATLAS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") during [STS-45](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-45 "STS-45"), and flew a third time in late 1994 on [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

On April 11, 1993, the crew used the remote manipulator arm ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) to deploy the Shuttle Point Autonomous Research Tool for Astronomy-201 (SPARTAN-201), a free-flying science instrument platform designed to study velocity and acceleration of the [solar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind "Solar wind") and observe the [Sun's corona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_corona "Stellar corona"). Collected data was stored on tape for playback after return to Earth. SPARTAN-201 was retrieved on April 13, 1993.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

The crew also made numerous radio contacts to schools around the world using the Shuttle Amateur Radio Experiment (SAREX II), including brief radio contact with the [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia")[Mir space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir"), the first such contact between Space Shuttle and Mir using amateur radio equipment.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STIsummary-8)

Other cargo bay payloads were the Solar Ultraviolet Experiment (SUVE), sponsored by [Colorado Space Grant Consortium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Space_Grant_College_and_Fellowship_Program "National Space Grant College and Fellowship Program") and located in a GetAway Special canister on the cargo bay wall.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

The middeck payloads were the Commercial Materials Dispersion Apparatus Instrumentation Technology Associates Experiment (CMIX), the Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment (PARE), Space Tissue Loss (STL-1) experiment, the Cosmic Ray Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM) experiment. the Hand-held, Earth-oriented, Real-time, Cooperative, User-friendly, Location-targeting and Environmental System ([HERCULES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikon_NASA_F4 "Nikon NASA F4")), Radiation Monitoring Equipment (RME III), and an [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) calibration test.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

**STS-56** was a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")_Discovery_ mission to perform special experiments. It was Discovery's 16th flight. The mission was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on April 8, 1993.

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-56&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

| Attempt | Planned | Result | Turnaround | Reason | Decision point | Weather go (%) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 6 Apr 1993, 2:32:00 am | Scrubbed | — | Technical | 6 Apr 1993, 2:31 am​(T−00:00:11) | 80[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-2) | T−9 minute hold extended for one hour due to high temperatures on SSME 1.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Report-3):2 The launch was scrubbed when a liquid hydrogen bleed valve was indicated as open when it was actually closed as required.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4) The erroneous indication was caused by a faulty relay.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-5) |
| 2 | 8 Apr 1993, 1:29:00 am | Success | 1 day 22 hours 57 minutes |  |  | 90[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-6) | Flash evaporator system shut down four minutes into flight, but was manually restarted by the crew.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Report-3):2 |

The primary payload of the flight was the [Atmospheric Laboratory for Applications and Science-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") (ATLAS-2),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Report-3):1 designed to collect data on the relationship between the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun")'s energy output and [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s middle atmosphere and how these factors affect the [ozone layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_layer "Ozone layer"). It included six instruments mounted on a Spacelab pallet in the cargo bay, with the seventh mounted on the wall of the bay in two [Get Away Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Away_Special "Get Away Special") (GAS) canisters. Atmospheric instruments included the Atmospheric Trace Molecule Spectroscopy (ATMOS) experiment, the Millimeter Wave Atmospheric Sounder (MAS), and the Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultraviolet (SSBUV/A) spectrometer (on the cargo bay wall). Solar science instruments were the solar spectrometry instrument SOLSPEC,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-SOLSPEC-7) the Solar Ultraviolet Irradiance Monitor (SUSIM), and the Active Cavity Radiometer (ACR) and Solar Constant (SOLCON) experiments.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

ATLAS-2 is one element of NASA's Mission to Planet Earth program. All seven ATLAS-2 instruments first flew on [ATLAS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") during [STS-45](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-45 "STS-45"), and flew a third time in late 1994 on [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

On April 11, 1993, the crew used the remote manipulator arm ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) to deploy the Shuttle Point Autonomous Research Tool for Astronomy-201 (SPARTAN-201), a free-flying science instrument platform designed to study velocity and acceleration of the [solar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind "Solar wind") and observe the [Sun's corona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_corona "Stellar corona"). Collected data was stored on tape for playback after return to Earth. SPARTAN-201 was retrieved on April 13, 1993.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

The crew also made numerous radio contacts to schools around the world using the Shuttle Amateur Radio Experiment (SAREX II), including brief radio contact with the [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia")[Mir space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir"), the first such contact between Space Shuttle and Mir using amateur radio equipment.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STIsummary-8)

Other cargo bay payloads were the Solar Ultraviolet Experiment (SUVE), sponsored by [Colorado Space Grant Consortium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Space_Grant_College_and_Fellowship_Program "National Space Grant College and Fellowship Program") and located in a GetAway Special canister on the cargo bay wall.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)

The middeck payloads were the Commercial Materials Dispersion Apparatus Instrumentation Technology Associates Experiment (CMIX), the Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment (PARE), Space Tissue Loss (STL-1) experiment, the Cosmic Ray Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM) experiment. the Hand-held, Earth-oriented, Real-time, Cooperative, User-friendly, Location-targeting and Environmental System ([HERCULES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikon_NASA_F4 "Nikon NASA F4")), Radiation Monitoring Equipment (RME III), and an [Air Force Maui Optical Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Maui_Optical_and_Supercomputing_observatory "Air Force Maui Optical and Supercomputing observatory") (AMOS) calibration test.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-56#cite_note-STS-56_Mission_Summary-4)
